records.content:
This empirical example uses the CC0 Kaggle snapshot from 

Zhu (2021)
of Amazon book sales and weekly average sales ranks from 2001.  The cleaned
snapshot is committed at data/incerto/snapshots/amazon_bookrank_2001.csv because it
is small and redistributable.

The example asks two related questions:

Does weekly sales volume have a heavy right tail?

Does the sales-rank relation look approximately log-linear, as one would
expect from a rough power-law ranking rule?

The rank variable is inverse popularity: rank 1 is better than rank 1000.

hierarchy.lvl2: Why book ranks suggest a tail question

records.content:
Book sales are a natural “winner-take-more” setting.  Most titles sell little
in a given week, while a few sell much more.  A rank is not the same object as
a sales count, but if sales approximately follow a power law, a log-log plot of
sales against rank can look close to linear over part of the range.

The important word is “approximately.”  Amazon’s ranking algorithm is not a
statistical law of nature, and this old dataset is small.  The example is a
real-data bridge from the 

Pareto pages to
rank-size empirical work.

A descriptive log-log regression fits sales s_i>0 against ranks r_i>0:\log s_i=b_0+b_1\log r_i+\varepsilon_i.

Here b_0,b_1 and the residuals \varepsilon_i are local regression notation;
the fitted slope is not automatically a Pareto exponent.

There is no proof that the data are Pareto.  The computation is a reproducible
diagnostic:

Load the CC0 snapshot.

Plot weekly sales against weekly average rank on log-log axes.

Plot empirical sales survival on log-log axes.

Apply 

Hill Estimator sensitivity checks to
positive weekly sales above a small reporting cutoff.

Any resulting exponent is sample-specific and should be read as an empirical
description, not a structural parameter of Amazon.

Use 

load_amazon_bookrank, 

hill_alpha_estimator.from xmath.incerto.datasets import load_amazon_bookrank
from xmath.incerto.estimators import hill_alpha_estimator

data = load_amazon_bookrank()
sales = data.weekly_sales[data.weekly_sales > 10]
print(f"Snapshot rows: {data.weekly_sales.size:d}")
for k in (10, 20, 40, 80, 120):
    print(f"{k} {hill_alpha_estimator(sales, k):.3f}")

OutputSnapshot rows: 861
10 3.670
20 2.509
40 2.270
80 2.116
120 2.066

Run in an editable checkout with the bundled CC0 snapshot; the estimates
are threshold-sensitive descriptions of this sample.

Figure regeneration: uv run python demos/incerto/amazon_bookrank.py.

The log-log fit captures a broad rank-size direction, but
the survival and Hill panels make the tail sensitivity visible.  The
calculation is a diagnostic bridge, not proof of a generative Pareto law.

The snapshot is old and small.  It should not be used to infer current Amazon
ranking behavior.

The sample appears to be a narrow book universe rather than all books on
Amazon.

A rank is generated by a platform algorithm and can be affected by time
windows, category rules, stock status, and measurement conventions.

Weekly sales are discrete and bounded in this sample.  That makes the far
right tail short.

A log-log line over ranks is descriptive.  It does not prove a generative
Pareto mechanism.

Zhu (2021), “Amazon Book Sales VS Rank” Kaggle dataset.

Hill (1975), “A Simple General Approach to Inference About the Tail of a
Distribution”.

The installed distribution is xshi-math; these helpers are imported as
xmath.incerto. Install the numerical and plotting extra with:uv sync --locked --extra incerto

Run page examples in Python after installing from a repository checkout.
Every fenced python block on the Incerto pages is executed by pytest;
examples do not fetch data or save files. Each Output block is captured
from its preceding example and checked against stdout, ignoring trailing
whitespace only. Bundled dataset examples require an
editable checkout (or a populated INCERTO_DATA_DIR). Longer examples expand
under a Code dropdown.

Numeric output uses about four significant digits or three to four decimal
places, with scientific notation for small probabilities. Counts remain
integers; vectors print as short lists and dictionaries as key: value lines.
Mathematical infinities and missing values print as inf and nan.

The base xmath helpers require only NumPy. The Incerto extra adds SciPy and
Matplotlib; graph generation uses NetworkX and PyYAML from the development
group. Dataset fetching uses standard-library urllib. The Python modules
contain the full signatures and docstrings; there is no separate Sphinx build.

Module: xmath.incerto.distributions.

Call an object below with its shape parameters to freeze a law; then use
pdf(x), logpdf(x), cdf(x), sf(x), logsf(x), ppf(q),
rvs(size=..., random_state=rng) or stats(moments="mv").
These methods belong to the linked distribution entry. scale is a
positive scale multiplier, and loc shifts the support.

pareto_type1(alpha, loc=0, scale=1)

Pareto Type I with positive exponent alpha; at loc=0, scale is the lower cutoff.

double_pareto(alpha, loc=0, scale=1)

Symmetric shifted double Pareto with positive exponent alpha; ordinary mean exists only above one.

hypsecant2(loc=0, scale=1)

Density 0.5 / cosh(x)**2 at default location and scale (logistic scale one half).

simple_normal_mixture(a, loc=0, scale=1)

Equal centered normal mixture with component variances 1-a and 1+a, for 0 <= a < 1.

univariate_variance_gamma(alpha, beta, lam, loc=0, scale=1)

Variance–gamma law requiring alpha > abs(beta) and lam > 0; this alpha is a decay parameter, not a Pareto exponent.

hypsecant2.chf(t, loc=0.0, scale=1.0)from xmath.incerto.distributions import hypsecant2

values = hypsecant2.chf([0, 1, 2]).real
print("[" + ", ".join(f"{v:.4g}" for v in values) + "]")

Output[1, 0.6826, 0.272]

generalized_pareto(xi, beta=1.0)

Returns a frozen zero-location GPD with finite scalar shape \xi and
finite scale \beta>0. Methods include pdf, cdf, sf, logsf,
ppf, rvs and support. Support is [0,\infty) for \xi\ge0 and
[0,-\beta/\xi] for \xi<0. CDF/survival extend continuously at
support boundaries. Endpoint densities can be infinite when \xi<-1.
Invalid parameters raise ValueError.from xmath.incerto.distributions import generalized_pareto

law = generalized_pareto(-0.4)
print("Survival: [" + ", ".join(f"{v:.4g}" for v in law.sf([-1, 0, 1, 2.5, 3])) + "]")

OutputSurvival: [1, 1, 0.2789, 0, 0]

generalized_extreme_value(xi, mu=0.0, sigma=1.0)

Returns a frozen GEV with the 

page’s shape convention:
positive \xi is heavy-tailed, zero is Gumbel, negative has a finite
right endpoint. The adapter uses scipy.stats.genextreme(c=-xi) and
exposes the same methods as the GPD adapter. Require finite scalar
parameters and \sigma>0. Outside support, density is zero and
CDF/survival have their limiting values. For \xi<-1, the density
diverges as the right endpoint is approached, although SciPy 1.18 returns
zero at the endpoint itself. This single-point convention does not change
probabilities. Invalid parameters raise ValueError.from xmath.incerto.distributions import generalized_extreme_value

for xi in (-0.3, 0, 0.3):
    law = generalized_extreme_value(xi)
    print(f"xi={xi:.4g}: cdf(0)={law.cdf(0):.4g}, sf(4)={law.sf(4):.4g}")

Outputxi=-0.3: cdf(0)=0.3679, sf(4)=0
xi=0: cdf(0)=0.3679, sf(4)=0.01815
xi=0.3: cdf(0)=0.3679, sf(4)=0.06966

frechet(alpha, scale=1.0)

Returns a frozen zero-location Fréchet law with CDF
\exp[-(y/\mathrm{scale})^{-\alpha}] for y>0. Both parameters are
finite positive scalars. Uses SciPy invweibull, including pdf, cdf,
sf, logsf, ppf, rvs and support. At and below zero,
density and CDF are zero, survival one. Use sf rather than subtracting
cdf from one when the right tail is small. Invalid parameters raise ValueError.
The adapter inherits SciPy’s numerical limits: for example, SciPy 1.18
returns nan for frechet(3).pdf(1e-100) because intermediate powers
overflow, although the true density rounds to zero. The P1 figure grids
avoid this range.from xmath.incerto.distributions import frechet

law = frechet(1.5)
for y in (0, 1, 10):
    print(f"y={y:d}: pdf={law.pdf(y):.4g}, cdf={law.cdf(y):.4g}, sf={law.sf(y):.4g}")

Outputy=0: pdf=0, cdf=0, sf=1
y=1: pdf=0.5518, cdf=0.3679, sf=0.6321
y=10: pdf=0.004596, cdf=0.9689, sf=0.03113

max_to_sum_path(x)

Returns the maximum divided by the sum for every prefix of a nonempty,
finite, real, nonnegative one-dimensional list. Zero-total prefixes return
nan. Log accumulation avoids overflow of the sum and avoids scaling early
prefixes by a much larger future observation. Negative/nonfinite/complex
values and wrong dimensions raise ValueError; ordinary rounding remains.from xmath.incerto.estimators import max_to_sum_path

path = max_to_sum_path([0, 1, 1, 8])
print("Prefix ratios: [" + ", ".join(f"{v:.4g}" for v in path) + "]")

OutputPrefix ratios: [nan, 1, 0.5, 0.8]

gpd_threshold_fit(x, threshold, *, min_exceedances=30)

Numerically fits a zero-location GPD to strict excesses above a finite
threshold. Returns threshold, integer count, xi, beta,
modified_scale (\widehat\beta-\widehat\xi u), success and status.
Finite real one-dimensional data are required; invalid input raises.
Insufficient or constant excesses, overflow when forming excesses, and failed
numerical fits retain counts but report nan parameters and an explanatory
status. The optimizer stops
at 2,000 iterations or 4,000 evaluations. Checks cover numerical convergence,
finite parameters/log density, positive scale and every excess’s support.
Success is no guarantee of a global MLE, a valid tail model or an appropriate
threshold. No confidence interval is returned.from xmath.incerto.estimators import gpd_threshold_fit

fit = gpd_threshold_fit([1, 2, 2, 4], 2, min_exceedances=2)
print(f"Count: {fit['count']:d}; status: {fit['status']}")
print(f"xi: {fit['xi']:.4g}; beta: {fit['beta']:.4g}")

OutputCount: 1; status: insufficient count
xi: nan; beta: nan

must not be constant. Locations of positive families are fixed at zero.

the transformation’s Jacobian is independent of its parameters.

The GIG fit includes normalizable Gamma and inverse Gamma boundaries.
An inward score test certifies a boundary maximum using concavity in natural
parameters, as proved in the 

note.
Otherwise SciPy’s interior optimizer must converge within 4,000 iterations
and 8,000 evaluations, and its likelihood must match or beat both boundaries
to within 

10-7. This numerical branch does not certify a global optimum.
The frozen interior law uses SciPy’s geninvgauss(p, b, scale=scale):
the note’s canonical parameters are a=b/\mathrm{scale} and
b_{\rm canonical}=b\,\mathrm{scale}.

Nonfinite diagnostics and optimizer failures raise. Large interior GIG
samples may be slow because their CDF uses quadrature. GIG’s AIC retains
the nominal three-parameter penalty on a boundary; its usual regular-model
interpretation is not asserted there. KS uses the ordinary exact finite-n
distribution for a specified continuous CDF, without adjusting for the
estimated parameters. Very small p-values may underflow to zero.

fit_tail_model(x, xmin, model="powerlaw", *, discrete=False) -> dict
fits one common conditional tail. Models are powerlaw, lognormal,
exponential, stretched_exponential (the full Weibull family), and
truncated_powerlaw (an exponential cutoff, no finite upper endpoint).
Discrete mode supports powerlaw only and rejects continuous alternatives.
The result contains model, xmin, discrete, n_tail, parameters,
per-observation loglik in retained input order, loglikelihood, success,
boundary, and status. Below-cutoff values do not enter the scores.

Parameters are alpha for a pure power law; mu, sigma for the parent
lognormal; rate for exponential; shape, scale for Weibull; and density
exponent a, rate for the cutoff family. The interior cutoff exponent a
can be any real number mathematically. Lognormal/Weibull/cutoff fits use
multi-start numerical optimization; convergence is not a global-MLE proof.

Numerical search boxes use dimensionless coordinates: lognormal
mu-log(xmin) in [-100,100] and log(sigma) in [-6,5]; Weibull
log(shape) in [-5,5], profiling out scale. The cutoff search starts with
a-1 in [-20,100] and log(rate*xmin) covering both [-18,8] and the
sample’s inverse mean excess scale. It expands the bounds over at most eight
search rounds; log rates stay within [-700,700]. Each start permits 2000
iterations. An unresolved search or artificial bound sets success=False.
These bounds are numerical limits, not definitions of the families.
The pure-law boundary rate=0 is accepted only after verifying its inward
score, returning boundary=True with status pure-power-law boundary.
An inferior numerical fit can return the pure law with success=False and
an explicit uncertified-boundary status. Cutoff quadrature is centered and
scaled around its mode; unresolved integration raises or fails the fit.
Exponential fitting accepts constant observations above the threshold when
their mean excess is positive. Lognormal, Weibull, and cutoff fitting reject
constant tails.from xmath.incerto.powerlaw import fit_tail_model

fit = fit_tail_model([0.5, 1, 2, 3, 6], 1, "exponential")

print(f"Conditional log likelihood: {fit['loglikelihood']:.3f}")

likelihood_ratio_test(loglik1, loglik2, *, nested=False, calibration=None, df=1) -> dict accepts paired finite real score vectors of
length at least two, from the same ordered observations and reference measure.
Positive R=sum(loglik1-loglik2) favors model 1. Non-nested mode returns
normalized_R=R/(sqrt(n)*std(d,ddof=0)) and a two-sided normal p_value.
Zero contrast variance gives nan statistic/p with an explanatory status.
Results also contain n, statistic, and status; statistic is the nested
LR statistic and is nan for non-nested comparisons.

beyond numerical tolerance raises ValueError. The statistic is -2R, while
the default p-value is nan pending calibration. Explicit calibration="chi2"
uses a chi-square reference with positive integer df;
calibration="boundary" requires df=1 and uses the regular half-point-mass,
half-chi-square reference, with inclusive p-value one at statistic zero.
These options assert conditions; they do not diagnose them. See the


boundary and infinite-information caveats.
No automatic AIC/BIC correction, multiple-testing adjustment, dependence
correction, or selected-threshold calibration is performed.from xmath.incerto.powerlaw import likelihood_ratio_test

A forecast of an event and the payoff attached to that event answer different
questions. Let X be a real random variable with CDF F and let g(X)
be its payoff. We use g for the transformation, reserving F for the CDF
as in the 

shared notation.
An ordinary finite expected payoff requires \mathbb E|g(X)|<\infty.

hierarchy.lvl2: The frequency of gains does not determine their mean
The frequency of gains does not determine their mean

records.content:
Consider this finite payoff table, in arbitrary payoff units:

Outcome probability

Payoff A

Payoff B

0.98

1

Direct summation gives \mathbb E[A]=-0.62 and \mathbb E[B]=0.62.
The higher probability of a gain belongs to the lower expected payoff.
Both payoffs are bounded; fat tails are unnecessary for this distinction.
More generally, a payoff equal to a>0 with probability 1-q and to
-b<0 with probability q has mean (1-q)a-qb.

This is a one-period expectation calculation. A repeated strategy with a
finite resource constraint needs a model of 

ruin as well.

Suppose X takes values in an open interval I, its mean
\mu=\mathbb E X belongs to I, and \mathbb E|X|<\infty.
If g:I\to\mathbb R is differentiable and convex, and
\mathbb E|g(X)|<\infty, then\mathbb E g(X)\ge g(\mathbb E X).

We prove this differentiable case. Convexity gives the supporting-line
inequality g(x)\ge g(\mu)+g'(\mu)(x-\mu) for every x\in I:
the secant slopes on either side of \mu bracket g'(\mu).
Taking expectations of this integrable inequality proves the claim.
Applying it to -g reverses the inequality for concave g.

For a symmetric two-point perturbation X=\mu\pm s, each with probability
1/2, the mean remains \mu. With \mu=4 and s=2,\mathbb E X^2=20>16=(\mathbb E X)^2,
\qquad
\mathbb E\sqrt X=\frac{\sqrt2+\sqrt6}{2}<2.

For the quadratic payoff g(x)=x^2, the gain in expectation is exactly
s^2; for g(x)=-x^2, it is -s^2. These are changes relative to the
constant input \mu. Comparing two arbitrary distributions requires a
specified ordering of their spreads; variance alone does not order
expectations of every convex function.

For example, compare the symmetric law at \pm1 with the law assigning
probability 3/4 to zero and 1/8 to each of \pm2. Both have mean
zero and variance one. Their expectations of |X| are 1 and 1/2,
whereas their expectations of X^4 are 1 and 4. Both functions are
convex, so neither law gives the larger expectation for every convex payoff.

For exact Pareto X with x_m>0, \alpha>0, and a power payoff
g(x)=x^r with r>0, direct inversion of the event givesP(g(X)>y)=P(X>y^{1/r})
=\left(\frac{x_m^r}{y}\right)^{\alpha/r},
\qquad y\ge x_m^r.

The payoff exponent is \alpha/r. Its mean is finite exactly when
r<\alpha, by the 

Pareto moment proof.
For example, \alpha=3/2 gives a finite mean for X and an infinite mean
for X^2. The finite-expectation version of Jensen above cannot be applied
to that quadratic payoff with both sides finite.

If instead g(x)=\min(x,c) on x\ge0 with c>0, the payoff lies in
[0,c], so \mathbb E e^{t g(X)}\le e^{|t|c} for every real t.
For X Pareto with x_m=1, \alpha=3/2, and c=4, integration of
the survival gives\mathbb E\min(X,4)=\int_0^4P(X>v)\,dv
=1+\int_1^4v^{-3/2}\,dv=2,
\qquad \mathbb E X=3.

This cap bounds the realized payoff and changes its mean. It does not
estimate the uncapped mean. The


inference note
shows why bounded payoffs have a different contamination sensitivity.

Convexity alone does not bound downside: g(x)=e^x+x has
g''(x)=e^x>0 but tends to -\infty as x\to-\infty. An explicit bound such as
g(x)=\max(x-u,0)-d\ge-d, for fixed u and d\ge0, is a separate
property. Repetition, costs and the distribution of X still matter.

0\le s\le3. Reproduce the figure and finite payoff table with

The source context is 

Taleb (2025), ch. 3, §3.4.1, pp. 41–43,
and §3.10, pp. 60–63. The chapter motivates distinguishing state from
exposure. The finite-table calculation, differentiable Jensen argument,
power-tail transformation and capped-mean calculation are proved here.

For a centered normal density parameterized by variance v>0g_v(x)=
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi v}}
\exp\left(-\frac{x^2}{2v}\right),

the body-shoulder-tail diagnostic asks where a small, mean-preserving
randomization of v adds density and where it removes density.  A local
version is the sign of\frac{\partial^2 g_v(x)}{\partial v^2}.

For the standard normal density, this second derivative changes sign at\pm\sqrt{3-\sqrt6},
\qquad
\pm\sqrt{3+\sqrt6}.

These four points split the line into left tail, left shoulder, peak, right
shoulder, and right tail regions.  Positive variance curvature means a local
variance mixture raises density there; negative variance curvature means it
lowers density there.

The notation g_v denotes the density at fixed variance v; a mixture
averages these densities over a positive random variance Y. The


Normix normal-mixtures note supplies the
complementary conditional construction. See the 

shared notation canon.

For the standard normal density under variance perturbation, the inner
shoulder boundaries are about \pm0.742, and the outer tail boundaries are
about \pm2.334.

If one perturbs the normal scale \sigma rather than the variance v, the
corresponding boundaries are different: about \pm0.662 and \pm2.136 for
the standard normal.

For Student-t densities, a scale-curvature version applies, but the boundary
values depend on the degrees of freedom.

These boundaries are not Pareto thresholds; threshold selection for


regular variation is a separate problem.

If a Gaussian variance is randomized while keeping the center fixed, the
resulting mixture does not simply “spread out” everywhere.  It tends to add mass near the
peak and in the far tails, while taking mass from the shoulders.  The shoulders
are the moderate-deviation region that looks ordinary under a single scale but
is depleted when variance uncertainty is introduced.

This diagnoses the geometry of a specified population density, not its tail index.
It explains why stochastic volatility can create both a sharper center and
fatter-looking tails without producing a 

Pareto tail.
Choosing a threshold for tail estimation remains the separate judgment handled
by 

Tail Threshold Selection.

We derive the standard-normal variance-curvature boundaries by differentiating
the density with respect to variance and solving the resulting quadratic in
x^2.  The Taylor expansion explains the local mixture interpretation.  The
comparison with scale perturbation below uses a different derivative; none
of these boundaries is a rule for selecting a Pareto threshold.

For the normal density with variance parameter v, writeg_v(x)=
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi v}}
\exp\left(-\frac{x^2}{2v}\right).

Set y=x/\sqrt v.  A direct differentiation gives\frac{\partial g_v(x)}{\partial v}
=
\frac{g_v(x)}{2v}(y^2-1),

and a second differentiation gives\frac{\partial^2 g_v(x)}{\partial v^2}
=
\frac{g_v(x)}{4v^2}(y^4-6y^2+3).

At v=1, the sign changes wherex^4-6x^2+3=0.

Solving the quadratic in x^2 givesx^2=3\pm\sqrt6.

This is a local Taylor diagnostic. A sufficient small-perturbation model isY_\tau=v_0+\tau H,\qquad v_0>0,\quad
\mathbb E[H]=0,\quad \mathbb E[H^2]=1,

with bounded local perturbation H and \tau small enough that Y_\tau>0. For each fixed x,
Taylor’s theorem, with bounded third derivative near v_0, gives\mathbb E[g_{Y_\tau}(x)]-g_{v_0}(x)
=\frac{\tau^2}{2}
\frac{\partial^2g_v(x)}{\partial v^2}\bigg|_{v=v_0}
+O(\tau^3).

Thus the curvature sign determines the leading local density change away
from its zeros. Small variance of a perturbation alone would not justify
this remainder without control of the perturbation family. The expansion
is pointwise in x, not uniform arbitrarily far into the tails.

At v=1, put a=\sqrt{3-\sqrt6}\approx0.742 and
b=\sqrt{3+\sqrt6}\approx2.334.

Leading change under small mean-preserving variance mixing

Positive

Density increases

Negative

Density decreases

\lvert x\rvert>b (tails)

Positive

For a concrete finite mixture, definef_{\mathrm{mix}}(x)=\tfrac12 g_{0.2}(x)+\tfrac12 g_{1.8}(x).

records.content:
For x>0, the two-sided normal survival at variance v is
T_v(x)=2\bar\Phi(x/\sqrt v), where \bar\Phi is standard normal survival
and \phi is its density. Differentiation gives\frac{\partial^2 T_v(x)}{\partial v^2}
=\frac{x\phi(x/\sqrt v)}{2v^{5/2}}\left(\frac{x^2}{v}-3\right).

Its positive-threshold curvature boundary is x=\sqrt{3v}, about 1.732
when v=1. It differs from both density boundaries.

For scale perturbation, write h_\sigma(x)=g_{\sigma^2}(x) and
z=x/\sigma. Then\frac{\partial^2h_\sigma(x)}{\partial\sigma^2}
=\frac{h_\sigma(x)}{\sigma^2}(z^4-5z^2+2).

At \sigma=1, its positive zeros are
\sqrt{(5-\sqrt{17})/2}\approx0.662 and
\sqrt{(5+\sqrt{17})/2}\approx2.136. Mean-preserving scale mixing is a
different operation from mean-preserving variance mixing. Student scale-curvature comparisons depend on degrees of freedom, as derived below.

The scale calculation also has a closed form for a Student density. Write
h_s(x)=C_\nu s^{-1}(1+x^2/(\nu s^2))^{-(\nu+1)/2}, where s>0 is
scale, \nu>1 is degrees of freedom, and C_\nu normalizes the density.
Set z=x/s and t=z^2/\nu. Logarithmic differentiation givess\,\partial_s\log h_s=\frac{\nu t-1}{1+t},\qquad
\frac{s^2\partial_s^2h_s}{h_s}
=\frac{\nu(\nu-1)t^2-(5\nu+1)t+2}{(1+t)^2}.

For the second formula, differentiate the first, using
\partial_st=-2t/s, and add the square of the log derivative.
The numerator is a quadratic with two positive roots when \nu>1.
Solving in z^2 gives the four density-curvature boundariesx=\pm s\sqrt{
\frac{5\nu+1\pm\sqrt{(\nu+1)(17\nu+1)}}{2(\nu-1)}}.

The leading coefficient and the value at zero are positive, so curvature
is positive inside the inner pair and beyond the outer pair, and negative
between them. At \nu=3,s=1, the positive boundaries are
\sqrt{4-\sqrt{13}}\approx0.628 and
\sqrt{4+\sqrt{13}}\approx2.758. The standard deviation is \sqrt3;
these numbers are in scale units. For \nu\le2, the variance is not
finite, although the four-boundary formula still applies when 1<\nu\le2.
At \nu=1 the quadratic loses its leading term, so that formula’s domain
must not be extended through the zero denominator.

Dividing numerator and denominator of the root formula by \nu shows
that its two positive roots tend to the Gaussian scale-curvature roots
as \nu\to\infty. This is an algebraic limit, not a fitted threshold rule.
The 

gamma-precision construction
explains the Student tail exponent and moment conditions separately.

mixtures at perturbations 0.1 and 0.6. Vertical lines mark the variance
curvature zeros; finite-mixture crossings need not stay on those lines.
The lower panel places normal variance, normal scale, and Student-three
scale boundaries on the same dimensionless axis. Student scale is 1,
so its standard deviation is the square root of 3.

Let X_1,X_2,\ldots be iid Cauchy variables with location \mu and
scale \sigma>0. Their density and characteristic function are\begin{gathered}
f(x)=\frac{\sigma}{\pi((x-\mu)^2+\sigma^2)},\\
\varphi(t)=\exp(i\mu t-\sigma|t|).
\end{gathered}

The characteristic function is a cited identity
(

Durrett (2019), §3.3.1, Example 3.3.16, p. 131). The positive and negative
parts both have infinite expectation: integrating |x|f(x) on either
tail gives logarithmic divergence. Thus \mu is a location and median,
not an expectation. See the 

stable-law convention
for the shared scale parameterization.

records.content:
We prove this finite-sample identity from the stated characteristic function.
Independence gives, for every integer n\ge1,\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E e^{it\bar X_n}&=\varphi(t/n)^n\\
&=\exp(i\mu t-\sigma|t|).
\end{aligned}

Uniqueness of characteristic functions therefore gives
\bar X_n\overset d=X_1. In particular,\begin{gathered}
P(|\bar X_n-\mu|>\varepsilon)\\
=1-\frac2\pi\arctan(\varepsilon/\sigma)>0\\
(\varepsilon>0).
\end{gathered}

The average does not converge in probability to \mu, or to any finite
constant. This argument alone does not classify every possible pathwise
limit. It also does not say that successive running averages are independent:
they share observations.

The population quantile is
Q(p)=\mu+\sigma\tan(\pi(p-1/2)), 0<p<1.
Consequently the interquartile range of every \bar X_n is 2\sigma.
By contrast, sample medians consistently estimate \mu. For fixed
\varepsilon>0, the strong law applied to the indicators
\mathbf1_{\{X_i\le\mu-\varepsilon\}} and
\mathbf1_{\{X_i\le\mu+\varepsilon\}} eventually puts fewer than half the observations at or below the lower
endpoint and more than half at or below the upper endpoint. Every sample
median is then inside that interval. Intersect over rational positive \varepsilon to
obtain almost-sure convergence. This is a proof about the median, not a
restoration of the missing mean.

Standard Cauchy draws, \mu=0, \sigma=1. The first panel retains all
10,000 prefixes of three paths (PCG64 seed 20261071); the signed logarithmic
vertical axis has a linear region between −2 and 2. The second shows
pointwise 10th/50th/90th sampling percentiles over 600 independent samples
at each of five sizes (seed 20261072). Dashed horizontal lines are the
exact 10th/90th quantiles of the mean. Bands are sampling quantiles, not
confidence intervals or simultaneous path bands. No draws are capped or
removed; the computation, not the distribution, is bounded.

For finite real observations x_1,\ldots,x_n with n\geq 1, define the fraction
strictly above a finite threshold t by\widehat S_n(t)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf{1}\{x_i>t\}.

Here t is the local name for the threshold u in the


shared notation.
\widehat S_n describes the observations; \bar F(u)=P(X>u) describes a
population law. The symbol S_n without a hat denotes a sample sum elsewhere.

The strict inequality matters when an observation equals the threshold. For
(1,2,2,4) at t=2, only the last observation contributes, so the fraction is
1/4. Counting observations greater than or equal to 2 would give 3/4 and
answer a different question.

Each indicator is either zero or one, so 0\leq\widehat S_n(t)\leq1. If
s<t, every observation exceeding t also exceeds s. Therefore
\widehat S_n(t)\leq\widehat S_n(s). These statements follow directly from
counting; they are exact finite-sample arguments.

Use

print("Strict survival: [" + ", ".join(f"{v:.4g}" for v in survival) + "]")

\bar F(u)=P(X>u), even when X has atoms. For the empirical law that
assigns mass 1/n to each observation,\begin{gathered}

\widehat S_n(u)=1-\widehat F_n(u).

We prove this identity by partitioning the observations into x_i\le u
and x_i>u. The alternative count with x_i\ge u adds the empirical

Now assume X_1,\ldots,X_n are iid from F, and fix a nonrandom threshold
u. Put q=\bar F(u). Each indicator I_i=\mathbf1_{\{X_i>u\}} has
\mathbb E I_i=q and \operatorname{Var}(I_i)=q(1-q) because I_i^2=I_i.
Independence makes the cross-covariances zero. Consequently,\begin{gathered}
\mathbb E\widehat S_n(u)=q,\\
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat S_n(u))=\frac{q(1-q)}n.
\end{gathered}

These are exact finite-sample identities, proved by summing the indicators.
For any fixed \varepsilon>0, Chebyshev’s inequality gives
P(|\widehat S_n(u)-q|>\varepsilon)\le q(1-q)/(n\varepsilon^2),
which tends to zero. No moment assumption on X is needed: the indicators
are bounded. This argument is pointwise in a fixed u; it proves neither a
uniform-in-threshold theorem nor consistency of an unbounded payoff average.

A random variable X satisfies a right-tail Cramér condition when there is
some \theta>0 such that\mathbb E[e^{\theta X}]<\infty.

For two-sided large-deviation statements, one usually asks for the moment
generating function M(\theta)=\mathbb E[e^{\theta X}] to be finite in an
open neighborhood of 0.  Equivalently, the cumulant generating function
\Lambda(\theta)=\log \mathbb E[e^{\theta X}] is finite near zero, and
the Cramér rate function isI(x)=\sup_\theta\{\theta x-\Lambda(\theta)\}.

We use the one-sided version when the question is upper-tail
concentration; the classical two-sided Cramér large-deviation theorem requires
stronger mgf control.

The condition gives the elementary Chernoff bound\mathbb P(X>x)\le e^{-\theta x}\mathbb E[e^{\theta X}],

so the upper-tail probability is bounded above by an exponentially decaying
function.  Equivalently, \bar F(x)=O(e^{-\theta x}) for that value of
\theta.

Here \bar F(x)=\mathbb P(X>x) is the survival function, \mathbb E
is expectation, and \theta is the exponential-tilting parameter. All symbols needed here are defined locally; see also


Shared notation.

The Cramér condition is a thin-tail gate.  If exponential moments exist, then
exponential tilting, Chernoff bounds, and classical large-deviation rates have
room to operate.  If no positive exponential moment exists, those tools may
give a false sense of security.

This is the clean contrast with 

Pareto-type fat
tails.  A 

regularly varying tail can have many finite
ordinary moments, but multiplying by e^{\theta X} eventually overwhelms
every power-law decay. Failure of the Cramér condition does not require
infinite variance: it can also occur when both the mean and variance are finite.

We prove the displayed Chernoff bound from Markov’s inequality.  The right-tail
and two-sided Cramér conditions are definitions or standard large-deviation
hypotheses; the larger Cramér theorem is cited rather than proved here.  The
normal, exponential, and Pareto cases below are direct checks of the condition.

The Chernoff bound follows from Markov’s inequality applied to the nonnegative
random variable e^{\theta X}:\begin{aligned}
\mathbb P(X>x)&=\mathbb P(e^{\theta X}>e^{\theta x})\\
&\le e^{-\theta x}\mathbb E[e^{\theta X}].
\end{aligned}

A standard normal random variable satisfies the two-sided version because
\mathbb E[e^{\theta X}]=e^{\theta^2/2} for all real \theta.  An exponential
random variable with rate \lambda>0 has mgf
\lambda/(\lambda-\theta) for \theta<\lambda, so it also satisfies
the two-sided neighborhood condition. Its positive exponential moments exist
exactly for 0<\theta<\lambda.

For a 

Pareto Type I random variable,\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb E[e^{\theta X}]\\
&\quad=\int_{x_m}^{\infty} e^{\theta x}\alpha x_m^\alpha x^{-(\alpha+1)}\,dx.
\end{aligned}

For every \theta>0, the exponential factor dominates the polynomial decay,
so the integral diverges.  Thus Pareto tails fail the right-tail Cramér
condition for every positive \theta.

For an exponential variable of rate \lambda and c\ge0,\begin{gathered}
\mathbb E[e^{\theta X}\mathbf 1_{\{X\le c\}}]\\
=\frac{\lambda}{\lambda-\theta}
  \left(1-e^{-(\lambda-\theta)c}\right),\\
0<\theta<\lambda.
\end{gathered}

For example, \lambda=1 and \theta=0.12 give a finite limit
1/0.88\approx1.13636 as c\to\infty.

For Pareto Type I with \alpha>0, every \theta>0 instead gives a
lower bound that diverges. For c\ge2x_m, retain only the interval (c/2,c]:\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb E[e^{\theta X}\mathbf 1_{\{X\le c\}}]\\
&\quad\ge e^{\theta c/2}\mathbb P(c/2<X\le c)\\
&\quad=(2^\alpha-1)\left(\frac{x_m}{c}\right)^\alpha e^{\theta c/2}\\
&\quad\longrightarrow\infty.
\end{aligned}

These are population calculations, independent of simulation. Even a Pareto
law with \alpha=2.5, finite mean, and finite variance has no positive
exponential moment.

An optimized bound for Bernoulli averages

records.content:
For iid X_i\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p), 0<p<1, independence gives
\mathbb Ee^{tS_n}=(1-p+pe^t)^n. Markov therefore proves, for p<q<1,\begin{aligned}
&P(S_n\ge nq)\\
&\quad\le\inf_{t>0}\exp\Bigl\{-n\bigl[tq\\
&\qquad-\log(1-p+pe^t)\bigr]\Bigr\}\\
&\quad=e^{-nD(q\Vert p)},
\end{aligned}

where\begin{aligned}
D(q\Vert p)&=q\log(q/p)\\
&\quad+(1-q)\log\frac{1-q}{1-p}.
\end{aligned}

To verify the optimum, differentiate the bracket: its derivative vanishes
at e^t=q(1-p)/(p(1-q))>1, and its second derivative is negative.
Substitution yields the displayed expression. At q=1 the bound is
p^n, exactly the all-success probability. At q\le p we use the trivial
upper bound one. If nq is not an integer, the event is
S_n\ge\lceil nq\rceil; the bound at the unrounded q is still valid.

For p=1/2, q=3/4, D(q\Vert p)\approx0.130812.
This is an upper bound, not a finite-n equality or a tail-probability
approximation with a proved relative error. Appendix D, pp. 187–188 of


Taleb (2025) is the context; the optimization here is proved directly.
It also avoids identifying a two-sided Chernoff bound with a one-sided
probability or dropping its prefactor.

bernoulli_chernoff_log_bound
returns the log upper bound, which remains useful when probabilities underflow.import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import binom

for n in (20, 100, 1000):
    exact = binom.sf(int(np.ceil(.75*n))-1, n, .5)
    bound = np.exp(bernoulli_chernoff_log_bound(.5, .75, n))
    print(f"n={n}: exact={exact:.4g}, bound={bound:.4g}")

The general large-deviation principle instead gives logarithmic upper bounds
on closed sets and lower bounds on open sets. It does not generally assert
P(\bar X_n>x)/e^{-nI(x)}\to1. Our Bernoulli calculation needs only
Markov, independence, and elementary optimization, not that general theorem.

The condition is direction-specific unless the moment generating function is
finite around both sides of zero.

Failure of the Cramér condition does not by itself prove regular variation
or subexponentiality.  A lognormal distribution has every positive polynomial
moment finite but no positive exponential moment, so “all moments finite” is
not enough for the Cramér condition.

Empirical samples cannot prove that an exponential moment exists; a finite
sample always has a finite empirical exponential average.

Large-deviation results need more than the one-line condition here.  This
page records the gate and the thin-tail contrast, not the full theorem.

simultaneous losses. These are separate mechanisms. We compare systems
with the same total exposure, explicitly specifying their response to a
shock and their dependence. None of the calculations identifies a real
institution’s failure law.

records.content:
Let h:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty) be convex with h(0)=0.
For integer m\ge1 and z\ge0,m h(z/m)\le h(z).

We prove the inequality directly: convexity at
z/m=(1/m)z+(1-1/m)0 gives h(z/m)\le h(z)/m.
It applies to a model where total input z is divided equally and the
resulting module damages add. It assumes that division does not change
h, add costs, or cause damage to propagate between modules.

For h(z)=z^r, r>1, total exposure a>0 and a common nonnegative
shock X, compareD_1=(aX)^r,\qquad
D_m=m(aX/m)^r=a^r m^{1-r}X^r.

The reduction factor m^{1-r} holds on every path, even with this perfectly
common shock. It comes from the local nonlinear response, not independence.
If the response is applied after pooling all inputs, the result is again
(aX)^r and there is no reduction. For a linear response (r=1),
splitting has no effect; for 0<r<1 and m>1 the factor instead exceeds one.

The tail exponent need not improve

records.content:
Suppose now that X is exact 

Pareto with
x_m>0 and \alpha>0. Put d_m=a^r m^{1-r}x_m^r.
By solving the event D_m>u for X,P(D_m>u)=\left(\frac{d_m}{u}\right)^{\alpha/r},
\qquad u\ge d_m.

Below d_m the survival is one. Above both minima, the split-to-unsplit
tail-probability ratio is m^{-\alpha(r-1)/r}. The exponent remains
\alpha/r for every finite m. Consequently \mathbb E D_m is finite
exactly when \alpha>r, by the


power-payoff calculation.
If \alpha\le r, every finite split still has infinite mean in this model.

With a=x_m=1, \alpha=3/2, r=2 and m=16, damage at each
fixed shock is reduced by 1/16; for u\ge1 the survival is reduced
by 1/8. Both damage laws still have infinite mean. A reduction in scale
does not by itself change the moment-existence boundary.

Consider a second, bounded model. Each of m equal modules loses its
entire exposure a/m if an indicator B_i is one, with
P(B_i=1)=q\in(0,1). Total damage is
D_m=(a/m)\sum_{i=1}^m B_i.

If the indicators are independent, finite sums and independence give\mathbb E D_m=aq,\quad
\operatorname{Var}(D_m)=\frac{a^2q(1-q)}m,\quad
P(D_m=a)=q^m,\quad P(D_m>0)=1-(1-q)^m.

For perfect dependence, B_i=B for all i, we instead have D_m=aB,
the same mean, variance a^2q(1-q), and probability q of either a
positive loss or total failure. These formulas follow from Bernoulli
moments and the all-fail/all-survive intersections; no limit theorem is used.

For m=10, q=0.02, independent total failure has probability
0.02^{10}=1.024\times10^{-17}, while some loss has probability
1-0.98^{10}\approx0.182927. Under a common shock both probabilities
are 0.02. Splitting reduces one event probability and increases another;
the event being protected against must be specified. All these finite
Bernoulli sums are bounded, even when dependent.

Intermediate cases can be represented by k independent equal-size
blocks, with perfect dependence within each block. Replacing m by k
in these formulas gives the total damage law. Adding nominal modules
inside an unchanged block does not increase the number of independent risks.
This is a finite dependence comparison, not a model of contagion dynamics.

Top: exact survivals for \alpha=3/2, r=2, a=x_m=1 and
m=1,4,16. Middle and bottom: bounded block failures at q=0.02.
A shared logarithmic axis would compress the any-loss and common-shock
curves near its upper edge because total-loss probabilities reach about

any loss has probability about 0.554, versus 0.02 under a common shock.
They agree exactly at k=1. Separate linear and logarithmic panels retain
both comparisons. The Bernoulli model is bounded and is not heavy-tailed.

Let x_1,\dots,x_n be observed data, and compare the sample standard
deviation with absolute-deviation scale estimates.  The repository uses
normal-scaled versions\operatorname{MeanAD}
=
\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n |x_i-\bar x|,

and\operatorname{MedianAD}
=
\frac{\operatorname{median}_i |x_i-\operatorname{median}(x)|}
{\Phi^{-1}(0.75)}.

For Gaussian data, both are calibrated to estimate the same \sigma as the
standard deviation.  Under fat-tailed or contaminated data, the ratios\frac{\operatorname{Std}}{\operatorname{MeanAD}},
\qquad
\frac{\operatorname{Std}}{\operatorname{MedianAD}}

can rise because sample standard deviation is more sensitive to isolated extremes.
The mean absolute deviation uses all observations; the median absolute
deviation depends on their central order statistics.

The sample notation X_1,\dots,X_n and expectation notation follow the shared


notation table.  The scale symbol \sigma and the
names MeanAD and MedianAD are local conventions for this page.

For Gaussian data, the standard deviation, normal-scaled mean absolute
deviation, and normal-scaled median absolute deviation target the same
\sigma, so the ratios should be near 1.

For Student-t or Pareto samples, large observations can push the standard
deviation much higher than the absolute-deviation scales.

We justify the Gaussian scale constants here; these identities do not
establish a tail class. Integrating the standard normal density on the
positive half-line gives \mathbb E|Z|=2\int_0^\infty z\phi(z)\,dz=\sqrt{2/\pi}.
The equation P(|Z|\le m)=2\Phi(m)-1=1/2 gives m=\Phi^{-1}(0.75).
Here Z is standard normal and \phi is its density.

For X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2),\mathbb E|X-\mu|
=
\sigma\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}.

Thus multiplying the mean absolute deviation by \sqrt{\pi/2} calibrates it
to \sigma under a normal model.  Also,\operatorname{median}(|X-\mu|)
=
\sigma\Phi^{-1}(0.75),

so dividing the raw median absolute deviation by \Phi^{-1}(0.75) gives the
same normal calibration.

These identities are normal-model calibrations, not tail theorems.  If the
sample has extreme observations, the standard deviation’s quadratic loss gives
those observations much more weight than either absolute-deviation statistic.

We use the symmetric shifted convention defined below; the
name “double Pareto” is overloaded in the literature and can also refer to
positive-valued size distributions with different left and right exponents.
Let Y have a 

Pareto Type I distribution with lower cutoff 1 and
tail exponent \alpha>0.  Let B be independent of Y with
\mathbb P(B=1)=\mathbb P(B=-1)=1/2.  The shifted symmetric double Pareto
variable isX = B(Y-1).

Its density on the real line isf(x;\alpha)=\frac{\alpha}{2}(1+|x|)^{-(\alpha+1)},\qquad x\in\mathbb R.

The CDF isF(x)=
\begin{cases}
\frac12(1-x)^{-\alpha}, & x<0,\\
1-\frac12(1+x)^{-\alpha}, & x\ge 0.
\end{cases}

For x\ge0, each one-sided tail has probability\mathbb P(X>x)=\frac12(1+x)^{-\alpha},
\qquad
\mathbb P(X<-x)=\frac12(1+x)^{-\alpha}.

Consequently,\mathbb P(|X|>x)=(1+x)^{-\alpha}.

More generally, a location-scale version Z=\mu+sX with s>0 has densityf_Z(z)=\frac{\alpha}{2s}
\left(1+\frac{|z-\mu|}{s}\right)^{-(\alpha+1)}.

The ordinary mean exists and equals 0 exactly when \alpha>1.  For
\alpha\le1, the positive and negative parts are both infinite, so symmetry
gives a center but not an ordinary expectation.  The variance is finite exactly
when \alpha>2, in which case\operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac{2}{(\alpha-1)(\alpha-2)}.

The absolute moments unify these thresholds:\mathbb E|X|^p
=\frac{\Gamma(p+1)\Gamma(\alpha-p)}{\Gamma(\alpha)},
\qquad 0<p<\alpha.

Here F and f denote the CDF and density; B is an independent sign.
\Gamma denotes the gamma function. Absolute moments diverge for
p\ge\alpha; the displayed gamma expression only applies for 0<p<\alpha.

The ordinary 

Pareto distribution is one-sided: the rare extreme is always on
the right.  The double Pareto keeps the same power-law magnitude but gives the
shock a sign.  This makes it useful for toy return models where both large gains
and large losses are possible, while preserving a transparent tail exponent.

The density is symmetric, with peak f(0)=\alpha/2 and\frac{f(x)}{f(0)}=(1+|x|)^{-(\alpha+1)}.

Smaller \alpha lowers the central density and puts more probability far
from zero on both sides. The chance of a large positive value and the chance
of an equally large negative value decay at the same power rate.



Figure 1:The page’s shifted symmetric law X=B(Y-1), with unit Pareto minimum
and \alpha=0.8,1.5,3. Support is the whole real line, so there is no
finite support endpoint. The log-log panel shows the right-tail
probability P(X>x)=\tfrac12(1+x)^{-\alpha} for x>0;
the absolute-tail probability would be twice as large. The shift causes

We derive the symmetric shifted construction used here from the signed
Pareto magnitude X=B(Y-1).  The tail, density, and CDF formulas follow
directly from symmetry.  The moment thresholds use the same Pareto moment
logic as 

Pareto Moment Existence.

For x\ge0,\mathbb P(X>x)
=\mathbb P(B=1, Y-1>x)
=\frac12\mathbb P(Y>1+x)
=\frac12(1+x)^{-\alpha}.

The negative tail is identical by symmetry.  Differentiating the CDF on either
side gives the density.  The expectation is zero only when the first absolute
moment exists.  When \alpha\le1,
\mathbb E[X^+]=\mathbb E[X^-]=\infty, so the ordinary mean is undefined even
though the distribution is symmetric.  Since X^2=(Y-1)^2,\mathbb E[X^2]
=\mathbb E[Y^2]-2\mathbb E[Y]+1
=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha-2}-2\frac{\alpha}{\alpha-1}+1
=\frac{2}{(\alpha-1)(\alpha-2)}

for \alpha>2. For 1<\alpha\le2, the mean exists but the variance
is infinite. For \alpha\le1, the ordinary mean, and hence variance
about that mean, is undefined; the second raw moment is still infinite.

SCoFT v4 §5.3, p. 101 

Taleb, 2025, compares a symmetric shifted
power law with a Student law. We keep the normalized density \alpha/2
above on each side and derive both matching scales. Equal exponents do
not imply equal moments or equal leading tail constants.

Let T_\nu have the unit-scale Student density, with \nu=\alpha>0,
and let Z=sT_\alpha, s>0. Its right tail satisfiesP(Z>x)\sim C_\alpha s^\alpha x^{-\alpha},\qquad
C_\alpha=\frac{\Gamma((\alpha+1)/2)\alpha^{\alpha/2-1}}
                  {\sqrt\pi\,\Gamma(\alpha/2)}.

We prove the constant from the density. Factoring x^2/(\alpha s^2)
out of 1+x^2/(\alpha s^2) in the Student density gives
f_Z(x)\sim\alpha C_\alpha s^\alpha x^{-\alpha-1}.
For each \varepsilon>0, this density lies between 1\pm\varepsilon
times its leading power beyond a fixed threshold. Integrating those bounds
from x to infinity and letting \varepsilon\downarrow0 gives the
displayed survival asymptotic. For positive orders p, the same comparison
proves \mathbb E|Z|^p<\infty exactly when p<\alpha; the density is
bounded near zero.

The double-Pareto right-tail constant is 1/2 at scale one. Matching it
requiress_{\rm tail}=(2C_\alpha)^{-1/\alpha}.

For \alpha>2, the Student variance is
s^2\alpha/(\alpha-2) (the beta-integral moment calculation is also
given in the 

mixture note).
Equating that to 2/[(\alpha-1)(\alpha-2)] instead givess_{\rm var}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\alpha(\alpha-1)}}.

At \alpha=3, C_3=2\sqrt3/\pi. Variance matching uses
s_{\rm var}=1/\sqrt3 and gives Student right-tail constant
2/(3\pi), versus 1/2 for double Pareto. Their asymptotic survival
ratio is 4/(3\pi)\approx0.424413 even though both variances are one.
Tail matching uses s_{\rm tail}=(\pi/(4\sqrt3))^{1/3} and gives
Student variance about 1.770683, versus one for double Pareto.
Matching tails thus leaves a substantial variance difference in this example.

For a stationary process (X_k), an ensemble mean is \mathbb E[g(X_0)];
a time average is n^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}g(X_k) along one realization.
The observable g and its integrability are part of the question.
Stationarity means that shifting every time index preserves joint laws.
Ergodicity means that events invariant under that shift have probability
zero or one.

For an integrable observable of a stationary process, Birkhoff’s theorem
gives the almost-sure limit \mathbb E[g(X_0)\mid\mathcal I], where
\mathcal I is the invariant sigma-field. Under ergodicity this is the
constant \mathbb E[g(X_0)]. This general theorem is cited, not proved:


Durrett (2019), Theorem 6.2.1, p. 335. The following finite examples
are proved directly.

For a stationary nonergodic example, draw B\in\{0,1\} once with equal
probabilities and put X_k=B at every time. The time average is B,
whereas the ensemble mean is 1/2. The event \{B=1\} is invariant
and has probability 1/2. Independence fails even though all moments exist.

Let A_1,A_2,\ldots be iid positive multipliers with
\mathbb E|\log A_1|<\infty and \mathbb E A_1<\infty.
For initial wealth w_0>0, define W_n=w_0\prod_{i=1}^n A_i.
Independence and the strong law give, respectively,\begin{gathered}
\mathbb E W_n=w_0(\mathbb E A_1)^n,\\
\frac1n\log(W_n/w_0)\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}\mathbb E\log A_1.
\end{gathered}

The first formula follows by factoring the expectation of a finite product.
The second follows by taking logarithms and averaging integrable iid
increments. Concavity of log gives
\mathbb E\log A_1\le\log\mathbb E A_1, strictly for a nonconstant
positive multiplier. These statements concern expected wealth and realized
log growth. They are not two competing values for the same time average.
Wealth itself generally is not stationary, so the stationary ergodic theorem
cannot be applied to W_n without additional structure.

Take A_i=1.8 or 0.6, each with probability 1/2. Then\begin{gathered}
\mathbb E A_i=1.2,\\
\mathbb E\log A_i=\tfrac12\log(1.08)>0.
\end{gathered}

Both targets grow, at different exponential rates. For the equally likely
pair 1.5,0.6, expected wealth grows at rate \log(1.05)>0, while
the path log-growth rate is \tfrac12\log(0.9)<0, so W_n\to0 almost
surely. A positive expected payoff therefore does not determine long-run
multiplicative growth. Choosing expected utility, expected wealth or growth
as an objective is a further decision, not an ergodic theorem.



The 1.5/0.6 example with w_0=1, 200 steps, 800 independent paths,
PCG64 seed 20261073. Four paths and pointwise 10th/50th/90th sampling
quantiles use log wealth, avoiding numerical overflow. The rising line is
\log\mathbb EW_n=n\log1.05; the falling line is
\mathbb E\log W_n=(n/2)\log0.9. Neither line is the empirical mean of
the displayed paths. The finite ensemble does not estimate rare wealth
contributions accurately merely because its median is stable.

For a fixed horizon T>0, initial size x_m>0, and a random constant
rate R\sim\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda), let X=x_m e^{TR}. For x\ge x_m,\begin{aligned}
P(X>x)&=P\!\left(R>\frac{\log(x/x_m)}T\right)\\
&=\left(\frac{x_m}{x}\right)^{\lambda/T}.
\end{aligned}

Thus the outcome is exactly Pareto with \alpha=\lambda/T, despite the
exponential rate having all power moments. Integrating the exponential
density gives, for p>0,\mathbb EX^p=
\begin{cases}
x_m^p\lambda/(\lambda-pT),&pT<\lambda,\\
\infty,&pT\ge\lambda.

The extreme-value index \xi is the tail-shape parameter of an extreme-value
domain of attraction.  It is not defined by assuming a


Pareto-type tail.  Let H_\xi denote the
standardized generalized extreme-value (GEV)
CDF,H_\xi(z)=\exp\left[-(1+\xi z)^{-1/\xi}\right],
\qquad 1+\xi z>0,\quad \xi\ne0,

with the Gumbel boundary caseH_0(z)=\exp(-e^{-z}).

The formula for H_\xi is written on its support; outside the support it takes
the usual endpoint CDF values.  In the block-maxima view, if
X_1,\dots,X_n are iid with distribution F, M_n=\max_i X_i, and there are
normalizing constants a_n>0 and b_n such that, at every continuity point
z of H_\xi,\mathbb P\left(\frac{M_n-b_n}{a_n}\le z\right)
\to
H_\xi(z),

then \xi is the extreme-value index of that tail.  The arrow \to means
ordinary convergence of the CDF values at continuity points of H_\xi;
equivalently,
(M_n-b_n)/a_n converges in distribution to a random variable with CDF
H_\xi.  The


Pickands-Balkema-de Haan theorem
then says that the same \xi appears as the generalized Pareto shape
parameter in threshold-excess limits.

Estimating \xi means choosing a tail region and reporting an estimate of
\xi together with the sensitivity of that estimate to the threshold choice.
If a distribution is not in a stable extreme-value domain of attraction, then
there is no single population EVI for these estimators to target; fitted
values are finite-sample diagnostics rather than estimates of a well-defined
limit parameter.

For the positive, Frechet-type case, a common calibration is a
Pareto-type right tail with\bar F(x)=x^{-\alpha}L(x),\qquad \alpha>0,

where L is 

slowly varying, the
extreme-value index is\xi=\frac1\alpha>0.

This Pareto-type formula is a special case, not the definition.  More
generally, \xi>0 corresponds to a heavy right tail with
Frechet-type limits, \xi=0 to the
Gumbel domain, and \xi<0 to a finite right endpoint. The Gumbel domain
includes both exponential and lognormal tails; \xi=0 does not require an
exactly exponential tail. These notes focus on \xi>0, often reported
through the reciprocal Pareto exponent \alpha=1/\xi.

Here \bar F(x)=\mathbb P(X>x) and L is slowly varying. The
standardized GEV CDF H_\xi, normalizing constants a_n, b_n, and
argument z belong to the block-maxima statement; k and x_{i:n}
are defined with the estimators below.

We prove \xi=1/\alpha for iid exact Pareto variables with \alpha>0 and
x_m>0. Set c_n=x_m n^{1/\alpha}. For y\ge n^{-1/\alpha},
independence gives the exact finite-n CDFP(M_n/c_n\le y)=\left(1-\frac{y^{-\alpha}}n\right)^n.

Below that support boundary the CDF is zero. For each fixed y>0 the
displayed expression tends to \exp(-y^{-\alpha}) by
n\log(1-y^{-\alpha}/n)\to-y^{-\alpha}. The limit is zero for y\le0.
To match the GEV convention above, choose b_n=c_n and a_n=c_n/\alpha.
Then y=1+z/\alpha=1+\xi z, and the limiting CDF is H_{1/\alpha}(z).
This proves the claimed EVI for exact Pareto. The general regular-variation
characterization and the threshold-limit theorem are cited results, not
proved by this special case.

SCoFT v4 §2.2.22, p. 17, motivates the domain-of-attraction terminology


Taleb, 2025. Approaching a support endpoint alone does not define a
maximum domain of attraction. If x_F=\sup\{x:F(x)<1\}, then iid sampling
gives P(M_n\le r)=F(r)^n\to0 for every r<x_F, even without a
nondegenerate normalized limit. The EVI definition needs that additional
limit and its normalizing constants.

Here “coordinate” means a one-dimensional tail coordinate, not a two-dimensional
(x,y) coordinate system.  The parameter \xi puts several tail descriptions
on the same scalar scale.  In a 

Pareto tail, it
is just the inverse of the familiar tail exponent: smaller \alpha means
larger \xi and heavier extremes.  For non-Pareto domains, \xi is still the
GEV/GPD shape coordinate: \xi=0 describes the Gumbel boundary and \xi<0
describes finite-endpoint tails.  There is then no reciprocal Pareto exponent
\alpha=1/\xi to report.

The logical order is therefore not circular.  First, a distribution may belong
to an extreme-value domain of attraction with index \xi.  Second, the
Pickands-Balkema-de Haan theorem transfers that same \xi to the
peaks-over-threshold generalized Pareto limit.  Third, exact Pareto and
Pareto-type tails provide a convenient \xi=1/\alpha calibration for the
positive-tail case.

In a generalized Pareto approximation for threshold excesses, the same \xi
is the shape parameter that controls whether excesses look heavy-tailed,
exponential-like, or endpoint-bounded.

That makes EVI estimation useful because many downstream questions are really
questions about \xi: Do moments exist?  Are threshold exceedances plausibly
Pareto-like?  Is a Hill estimate stable across a range of k?  Is a fitted
peaks-over-threshold model trying to put the sample in the \xi\ge1 infinite
mean region, the 1/2\le\xi<1 finite-mean but infinite-variance region, or a
thinner regime? These moment boundaries are exact for a GPD model. For a
general regularly varying tail, the boundary cases also depend on the slowly
varying factor, as explained by 

Karamata.

The danger is that \xi is a tail parameter, while data are finite and mostly
not tail.  Choosing the threshold too high gives little data and high variance.
Choosing it too low mixes body observations into a tail calculation.

For a realized positive right-tail sample
x_{1:n}\le \cdots \le x_{n:n}, the Hill estimate is\widehat\xi_{k,n}^{H}
=
\frac1k\sum_{j=1}^{k}
\log\left(\frac{x_{n-j+1:n}}{x_{n-k:n}}\right),
\qquad 1\le k<n.

The value of k selects the number of upper order statistics.  An EVI estimate
should therefore be reported as a threshold-indexed diagnostic, not as a
threshold-free constant.

The same tail coordinate appears in threshold-excess modeling.  Under the
conditions of the
Pickands-Balkema-de Haan theorem, cited in the references below,
for high thresholds u the excess X-u\mid X>u is approximated by a
generalized Pareto distribution with shape \xi and scale \beta(u)>0.
Fitting that shape parameter across several thresholds is another way to
estimate or diagnose the extreme-value index.

The three sign regimes have simple generalized Pareto representatives. An
exact Pareto calibration then connects Hill and GPD shape estimates.

The exact distribution of excesses above any u\ge x_m is GPD with

Positive \xi leaves a power tail, \xi=0 gives exponential GPD
excesses, and negative \xi ends at a finite endpoint. Agreement between
finite-sample estimates would be a diagnostic, not proof of the tail model.

EVI estimation is threshold-sensitive.  Report the chosen k or threshold
u, the sample transformation, and a stability diagnostic.

Hill estimates are designed for positive right-tail data and \xi>0.
They should not be used blindly for two-sided returns, zero-heavy data,
exponential-type tails, or finite-endpoint tails.

A stable region is not proof of a Pareto model.  Dependence, volatility
clustering, mixtures, truncation, censoring, and measurement limits can all
distort the apparent tail index.

The reciprocal \widehat\alpha=1/\widehat\xi is unstable when
\widehat\xi is close to zero.  Moment claims near \xi=1 or \xi=1/2
need special caution.

The GPD shape parameter is asymptotic in the threshold.  A fitted value from
one finite threshold is a model diagnostic, not a theorem about the data.

The Frechet distribution is the positive-shape extreme-value law for normalized
maxima with heavy right tails.  In the standard one-parameter form with shape
\alpha>0, its CDF is\Phi_\alpha(y)
=
\begin{cases}
0, & y\le0,\\
\exp(-y^{-\alpha}), & y>0.
\end{cases}

For y>0, the density is\phi_\alpha(y)
=
\alpha y^{-\alpha-1}\exp(-y^{-\alpha}).

It is the \xi>0 member of the


generalized extreme-value distribution.  With
\xi=1/\alpha, location \mu=1, and scale \sigma=\xi,H_{\xi,1,\xi}(y)
=
\exp\left[-y^{-1/\xi}\right]
=
\Phi_\alpha(y),
\qquad y>0.

The phrase Frechet-type refers to distributions whose normalized maxima
converge to this law.  In the usual right-tail setting, this is the


regularly varying maximum-domain-of-attraction
case: a 

Pareto-type survival tail with exponent \alpha has
extreme-value index \xi=1/\alpha>0. Here F is the parent CDF,
\bar F=1-F its survival function, X_i its iid draws, and x_m>0
the lower cutoff in the exact Pareto example. \Phi_\alpha and
\phi_\alpha denote the Frechet CDF and density.



Figure 1:Unit-scale Fréchet laws with \alpha=0.8,1.5,3, using the same exponent
colors as the Pareto card. The boundary is zero. Survival approaches a
power tail at large positive thresholds; it is not an exact power over
the whole support. The last panel’s lower visible probability is 

10-8.

Frechet-type behavior is a statement about extremes, not necessarily about the
full parent distribution.  If X_1,\dots,X_n are iid and the right tail is
regularly varying with exponent \alpha>0, then an appropriate positive
normalization a_n puts the maximumM_n=\max_{1\le i\le n} X_i

on the Frechet scale.  The full regular-variation domain-of-attraction theorem
is cited in the references; the exact Pareto calculation below shows the core
mechanism.

For 

Pareto Type I with lower cutoff x_m and exponent \alpha,
take a_n=x_m n^{1/\alpha}.  Then for fixed y>0 and all large enough n,\mathbb P(M_n/a_n\le y)
=
\left(1-\frac{1}{ny^\alpha}\right)^n
\to
\exp(-y^{-\alpha})
=
\Phi_\alpha(y).

The same shape parameter is therefore seen in two coordinates:\alpha \quad \text{for the Pareto-type survival exponent},
\qquad
\xi=\frac1\alpha \quad \text{for the extreme-value index}.

Although the Frechet law is a limit law for maxima, it is itself heavy-tailed.
Its survival function satisfies\bar\Phi_\alpha(y)
=
1-\exp(-y^{-\alpha})
\sim
y^{-\alpha},
\qquad y\to\infty.

Thus the Frechet survival tail is regularly varying with index -\alpha.
This is why the \xi>0 GEV regime is also the Pareto-type regime: the
block-maximum limit and the parent survival tail share the same reciprocal
coordinate \xi=1/\alpha.

For any \alpha>0, the exact Pareto probability at y=1 is (1-1/n)^n.
The limit is e^{-1}, independently of \alpha because the normalization
already includes n^{1/\alpha}.

The ordinary central limit theorem uses finite variance and normalizes sums by
\sqrt{n}.  The substantive generalized central limit theorem is a
classification theorem: a nondegenerate distribution can occur as a weak limit
of centered and normalized iid sums if and only if it is stable.  In other
words, if there are constants a_n>0 and b_n such that\frac{X_1+\cdots+X_n-b_n}{a_n}
\Rightarrow Z,

for a nondegenerate limit Z, then Z must be stable; conversely, stable laws
arise as such limits for suitable iid summands.  The Gaussian law is the stable
case \alpha=2.  The heavy-tailed stable cases have index 0<\alpha<2.

For a two-sided regularly varying sufficient condition, assume\begin{gathered}
\mathbb P(|X|>x)=x^{-\alpha}L(x),\\
0<\alpha<2,
\end{gathered}

where L is slowly varying at infinity, with tail balance\begin{gathered}
\frac{\mathbb P(X>x)}{\mathbb P(|X|>x)}\to p,\\
\frac{\mathbb P(X<-x)}{\mathbb P(|X|>x)}\to q,\\
p+q=1.
\end{gathered}

Choose a_n so that n\mathbb P(|X|>a_n)\to1.  Then, with suitable
centering constants b_n,\frac{X_1+\cdots+X_n-b_n}{a_n}
\Rightarrow Z_\alpha,

where Z_\alpha is an \alpha-stable law whose skewness is determined by
p-q.  For nonnegative Pareto-type examples this reduces to a strongly
right-skewed stable limit, and the scaling is of order n^{1/\alpha} up to a
slowly varying factor.  When 1<\alpha<2, the mean exists but the variance is
infinite, so a common centering choice is b_n=n\mathbb E[X].

A common centering summary is\begin{gathered}
b_n=\\
\begin{cases}
0, & 0<\alpha<1,\\
n\mathbb E[X\mathbf 1_{\{|X|\le a_n\}}], & \alpha=1,\\
n\mathbb E[X], & 1<\alpha<2.
\end{cases}
\end{gathered}

The first row applies in the usual nonnegative case; the second is a
standard choice at \alpha=1.

Here S_n=\sum_{i=1}^n X_i is the sum, M_n=\max_{1\le i\le n}X_i
is the maximum, \mathbb E is expectation, and \Rightarrow denotes
convergence in distribution. The tail exponent \alpha, norming constants
a_n, centering constants b_n, tail-balance weights p,q, and stable limit
Z_\alpha are defined above. See 

Shared notation.

We record the stable-limit contrast needed by the site’s heavy-tail
pages.  We do not classify every possible domain of attraction or every
parameterization of stable laws.

The classification and tail condition are cited from 

Durrett (2019),
Theorems 3.8.8 (p. 191) and 3.8.2 (p. 186), with characteristic functions
in §3.8, p. 189. That theorem uses truncated centering; the conventions
above can change the limit’s location. For exact Pareto with 1<\alpha<2
and a_n=x_m n^{1/\alpha}, the difference between full and truncated centering divided by a_n is
the constant \alpha/(\alpha-1), since
n\mathbb E[X\mathbf1_{\{X>a_n\}}]/a_n=\alpha/(\alpha-1).
For a scale satisfying only nP(X>a_n)\to1, this ratio converges to
the same constant. Thus full-mean centering preserves convergence, with
the limit shifted downward by \alpha/(\alpha-1).
These theorems are not proved by the maximum calculation below.

The normal law is not the only possible attractor for sums.  It is the
finite-variance attractor. For the regularly varying tails with 0<\alpha<2
considered here, the largest observations remain visible at the scale of the
centered sum, and \sqrt{n} is no longer the right normalization.

For a 

Pareto-type tail with exponent
\alpha<2, the natural scale of the maximum is about n^{1/\alpha}.  Stable
normalization puts the centered sum on that same order. This is why infinite-variance
sums can keep producing large jumps instead of smoothing into Gaussian-looking
noise.

The full generalized central limit theorem is a stable-law classification
result, so we cite it rather than reproduce the proof.  What we prove
directly is the exact Pareto maximum scaling calculation, which shows why the
usual \sqrt n scale is too small when \alpha<2.

For a 

Pareto Type I variable with survival
\bar F(x)=(x_m/x)^\alpha, choose a_n=x_m n^{1/\alpha}.  Then for y>0 and sufficiently large n such that a_n y\ge x_m,\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb P(M_n/a_n\le y)\\
&\quad=\left(1-\frac{1}{ny^\alpha}\right)^n\\
&\quad\to e^{-y^{-\alpha}}.
\end{aligned}

The maximum remains of order a_n.  Since a_n grows faster than
\sqrt{n} when \alpha<2, the Gaussian finite-variance scaling is not the
right asymptotic scale for such tails.  This maximum calculation identifies the
right order of extreme observations; it is a scaling heuristic, not a proof of
stable convergence for sums.

Take exact Pareto Type I with x_m=1 and \alpha=1.5. Its mean is 3
and its variance is infinite. With S_n=\sum_{i=1}^n X_i, compare\begin{gathered}
T_n=\frac{S_n-3n}{n^{2/3}},\\
G_n=\frac{S_n-3n}{\sqrt n}=n^{1/6}T_n.
\end{gathered}

The identity holds for every sample. Consequently, whenever its interquartile
range is nonzero, the spread of G_n is exactly n^{1/6} times that of
T_n. Here are the normalization factors, rounded to three decimals:

We use a symmetric stable law with characteristic function\begin{gathered}
\varphi_X(t)=\exp(i\mu t-|\sigma t|^\alpha),\\
0<\alpha\le2,\quad\sigma>0.
\end{gathered}

Here \alpha is the stability index; for \alpha<2 it is also the
power-tail exponent. At \alpha=2 this is N(\mu,2\sigma^2),
so \sigma is not its standard deviation. The existence of these stable
laws is a cited input from 

Durrett (2019), Example 3.3.23,
pp. 138–139 (with the Gaussian endpoint immediate).
Multiplying characteristic functions proves, for iid copies,\begin{gathered}
S_n-n\mu\overset d=n^{1/\alpha}(X_1-\mu),\\
\bar X_n-\mu\overset d=n^{1/\alpha-1}(X_1-\mu).
\end{gathered}

For 1<\alpha\le2 the scale shrinks. The finite absolute moment proved
below also makes the strong law applicable, so \bar X_n\to\mu almost
surely. At \alpha=1 the average keeps its Cauchy law; at \alpha<1
the scale grows and \mu is only a location. These exact identities must
not be transferred to a Pareto parent merely because its normalized sums
have a stable limit.

For the preceding parameterization and 1<\alpha\le2, we prove\begin{gathered}
\mathbb E|X-\mu|=\frac{2\sigma}{\pi}\Gamma(1-1/\alpha),\\
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb E|\bar X_n-\mu|\\
&\quad=\frac{2\sigma}{\pi}\Gamma(1-1/\alpha)n^{1/\alpha-1}.
\end{aligned}
\end{gathered}

Start with |x|=(2/\pi)\int_0^\infty(1-\cos(tx))/t^2\,dt.
For completeness, the integral at x=1 equals \pi/2: write
u^{-2}=\int_0^\infty s e^{-su}\,ds and use Tonelli to get
\int_0^\infty (1+s^2)^{-1}\,ds=\pi/2. Scaling gives the identity
for all x. Tonelli again, followed by v=(\sigma t)^\alpha, gives\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb E|X-\mu|\\
&\quad=\frac{2\sigma}{\pi\alpha}
\int_0^\infty(1-e^{-v})v^{-1-1/\alpha}\,dv.
\end{aligned}

Integration by parts makes the integral
\alpha\Gamma(1-1/\alpha); both boundary terms vanish when \alpha>1.
For \alpha\le1, the integrand near zero is asymptotic to
v^{-1/\alpha}, so the absolute moment is infinite. Symmetry and
integrability give \mathbb EX=\mu in the finite case. The average’s
formula now follows from the exact scale identity.

Let the iid summands have mean \mu, variance 0<\sigma^2<\infty,
and finite absolute moment of integer order r\ge3. Define the local
rth cumulant by \kappa_r(X)=i^{-r}(\log\varphi_X)^{(r)}(0),
using the continuous logarithm near \varphi_X(0)=1. For
T_n=(S_n-n\mu)/(\sigma\sqrt n), multiplication of characteristic
functions and the chain rule prove\kappa_r(T_n)=n^{1-r/2}\frac{\kappa_r(X)}{\sigma^r}.

Thus standardized skewness decays as n^{-1/2} and excess kurtosis as
n^{-1}. Direct integration gives zero skewness and excess -6/5 for
U(0,1); differentiating -\log(1-t) gives skewness 2 and excess
6 for \mathrm{Exp}(1). For iid sums, divide these excesses by n.
These calculations describe moments, not a distance between CDFs.
Zero excess kurtosis does not identify a Gaussian law: a variable taking
0,\sqrt3,-\sqrt3 with probabilities 2/3,1/6,1/6 has variance one
and fourth moment three, but is discrete.

For a CDF error bound, the cited Berry–Esseen theorem
(

Durrett (2019), Theorem 3.4.17, p. 157) requires
\rho=\mathbb E|X-\mu|^3<\infty and gives
\sup_x|P(T_n\le x)-\Phi(x)|\le3\rho/(\sigma^3\sqrt n).
The constant is sufficient, not optimal. For U(0,1),
\rho/\sigma^3=3\sqrt3/4; for \mathrm{Exp}(1) it is 12/e-2,
obtained by splitting the centered absolute-moment integral at one.
These upper bounds do not prove a universal ranking of convergence speeds.

For exact Pareto, the 

moment gate
requires \alpha>2 for finite variance, \alpha>3 for Berry–Esseen’s
third absolute moment, and \alpha>4 for excess kurtosis. The source’s
\alpha=2 example has infinite variance. Its Gaussian-domain scaling
requires an additional logarithmic factor; it is not a finite-variance
\sqrt n example. For 1<\alpha<2, the non-Gaussian limit above applies.
The Lyapunov and Lindeberg extensions in SCoFT §7.5 need their own
array/moment conditions; the iid examples here do not prove those theorems.

Stable-law parameterizations vary across books and software. The exact
symmetric calculations specify their characteristic function; the general
attraction statement does not fix a software skew/location convention.

The displayed regular-variation and tail-balance condition covers the
non-Gaussian stable range 0<\alpha<2; the Gaussian boundary needs a
different criterion.

Right-tail regular variation alone is not enough for a general two-sided
variable; the left tail can change the scale or skewness of the limit.

Some infinite-variance distributions can still be in the Gaussian domain of
attraction when their truncated second moment is slowly varying.

For 0<\alpha<1, the absolute first moment is infinite. At \alpha=1,
its finiteness depends on the slowly varying factor: the tail-integral
criterion is \int^\infty L(x)/x\,dx<\infty. For example, a nonnegative
variable with survival 1/[x(\log x)^2] for x\ge e has a finite mean,
since that tail integral equals 1. Exact Pareto tails have infinite mean
at \alpha=1. See the boundary discussion in 

Karamata’s theorem.
The truncated centering above remains a standard choice at this boundary;
finite mean alone does not justify replacing it by n\mathbb E[X] without
checking the resulting location shift on the a_n scale.

Finite samples can look calmer than the asymptotic theory suggests until a
large observation arrives.

1971, 2nd ed., Wiley.

Resnick (2007).

The generalized extreme-value distribution is the standard limit family for
normalized block maxima.  With location \mu, scale \sigma>0, shape
\xi, and standardized variable z=(x-\mu)/\sigma, its CDF is\begin{gathered}
H_{\xi,\mu,\sigma}(x)\\
=\exp\left[-\left(1+\xi z\right)^{-1/\xi}\right],\\
\xi\ne0,
\end{gathered}

where 1+\xi z>0. For \xi>0, extend the CDF by zero at and
below \mu-\sigma/\xi; for \xi<0, extend it by one at and above
\mu-\sigma/\xi. The boundary case is the Gumbel law,H_{0,\mu,\sigma}(x)
=
\exp\left[-e^{-z}\right].

The shape parameter \xi is the same extreme-value index used in threshold
excesses: \xi>0 is 

Frechet-type heavy-tail behavior,
\xi=0 is Gumbel-type behavior, and \xi<0 is
Weibull-type finite endpoint.
Here X_i are observations and M_n=\max_{1\le i\le n}X_i. The Pareto
example below uses lower cutoff x_m>0 and exponent \alpha>0.
Gumbel attraction is broader than exponential parent tails: normal and
lognormal parents are examples, despite their different tail decay.

The distribution is to block maxima what the 

Generalized Pareto Distribution
is to threshold exceedances. For iid observations, if there are constants
a_n>0 and b_n such that (M_n-b_n)/a_n converges to a nondegenerate
law, that law is a GEV distribution up to location and scale. Existence
of such a limit is an assumption; it does not hold for every parent law.

For fat-tail work, \xi>0 is the main case.  A 

Pareto tail with exponent
\alpha has \xi=1/\alpha, so the fitted block-maximum shape should point to
the same tail coordinate as a Hill or GPD threshold analysis when the modeling
assumptions are reasonable.

With \mu=0 and \sigma=1, the support makes the three shapes explicit.

Shape \xi

Interior CDF

Support

x<10/3; CDF is one above

All real x

\exp[-(1+0.3x)^{-10/3}]

x>-10/3; CDF is zero below

Every curve passes through H(0)=e^{-1}. Positive shape gives a power-law
right tail; negative shape gives a finite right endpoint.



Figure 1:Exact GEV laws with (\mu,\sigma)=(0,1) and \xi=-0.3,0,0.3.
The dotted boundaries are -10/3 for positive shape and 10/3 for
negative shape. The Gumbel law has no finite endpoint. The log-log panel
shows only positive thresholds, with survival below

If X_1,\dots,X_n are iid 

Pareto Type I with lower cutoff x_m and exponent
\alpha, then for x\ge x_m,\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb P(M_n\le x)\\
&\quad=\left(1-\left(\frac{x_m}{x}\right)^\alpha\right)^n.
\end{aligned}

With a_n=x_m n^{1/\alpha}, for fixed y>0 and sufficiently large n,\begin{gathered}
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb P(M_n/a_n\le y)\\
&\quad=\left(1-\frac{1}{ny^\alpha}\right)^n\\
&\quad\to\exp(-y^{-\alpha}),
\end{aligned}\\
y>0.
\end{gathered}

This is the 

Frechet member of the GEV family with
\xi=1/\alpha after a standard location-scale reparameterization.

For an exact Pareto parent with \alpha=1.8=9/5, the limiting shape is
\xi=5/9. At block size n=250, the normalizing scale is
a_n=x_m250^{5/9}. At the normalized threshold y=1,\begin{gathered}
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb P(M_{250}/a_{250}\le1)\\
&\quad=(249/250)^{250}\approx0.367142,
\end{aligned}\\
\Phi_{1.8}(1)=e^{-1}\approx0.367879.
\end{gathered}

This compares an exact finite-block CDF with its limit; it is not a GEV fit
or an assessment of sampling uncertainty. The standard Frechet limit has GEV
parameters (\xi,\mu,\sigma)=(5/9,1,5/9) on the normalized scale.

Block maxima discard within-block information.  Threshold methods may use
extremes more efficiently, but they require a threshold choice.

Blocks should be chosen with dependence and seasonality in mind.  Overlapping
or strongly dependent blocks can make fitted uncertainty too optimistic.

A GEV fit describes maxima, not the entire parent distribution.

Software may use a different shape sign convention. Translate fitted
parameters into the displayed CDF before comparing maxima and excesses.

The generalized Pareto distribution is the standard limit family for threshold
excesses.  With location zero, an excess variable Y\ge0 has shape
\xi and scale \beta>0 whenG_{\xi,\beta}(y)
=
1-\left(1+\frac{\xi y}{\beta}\right)^{-1/\xi},
\qquad \xi\ne0,

for y\ge0 with 1+\xi y/\beta>0. For y<0 the CDF is zero;
for \xi<0 it is one at and above -\beta/\xi, by continuity.  The boundary case isG_{0,\beta}(y)=1-e^{-y/\beta}.

For \xi\ge0, the support is y\ge0.  For \xi<0, the support is
0\le y\le -\beta/\xi, so the tail has a finite endpoint.  The survival
function for \xi\ne0 is\bar G_{\xi,\beta}(y)
=
\left(1+\frac{\xi y}{\beta}\right)^{-1/\xi}.

The mean exists only for \xi<1 and equals \beta/(1-\xi).  The variance
exists only for \xi<1/2 and equals\frac{\beta^2}{(1-\xi)^2(1-2\xi)}.

The generalized Pareto distribution is the peaks-over-threshold counterpart of
the generalized extreme-value distribution for block maxima.  Once a threshold
is high enough, the distribution of the excess over that threshold is modeled
with one shape parameter \xi and one scale parameter \beta.

The sign and size of \xi carry the tail story.  Positive \xi gives a


Pareto-type heavy tail.  Zero gives the exponential boundary.  Negative \xi
gives a finite endpoint.  In the fat-tail examples, the most important
boundary values are \xi=1/2 for variance and \xi=1 for the mean.

For \beta=1, the three examples from the survival formula are:

What to notice. Positive \xi gives the slowest-decaying curve, \xi=0
is the exponential boundary, and negative \xi ends at the finite endpoint
-\beta/\xi.

zero; the negative-shape law ends at -\beta/\xi=2.5, marked by a
matching dotted line. Its CDF stays at one beyond that point. Zero
survival is omitted on logarithmic axes; it is never replaced by a small
positive probability. The survival viewport starts at 

10-8.

A GPD is stable under raising the threshold. If Y has parameters
\xi,\beta and u\ge0 satisfies \beta+\xi u>0, then, for admissible
y\ge0 and \xi\ne0,\frac{\bar G_{\xi,\beta}(u+y)}{\bar G_{\xi,\beta}(u)}
=\left(1+\frac{\xi y}{\beta+\xi u}\right)^{-1/\xi}.

For \xi=0, the ratio is e^{-y/\beta}. Thus excesses have the same
shape and updated scale \beta+\xi u. Combining this with the GPD mean
gives the 

mean-excess formula.

The Pareto Type I distribution is an exact generalized Pareto excess model.
If X has Pareto tail exponent \alpha and threshold u\ge x_m, then\mathbb P(X-u>y\mid X>u)
=
\left(1+\frac{y}{u}\right)^{-\alpha}.

This is the generalized Pareto survival function with\xi=\frac1\alpha,
\qquad
\beta(u)=\frac{u}{\alpha}.

The 

Pickands-Balkema-de Haan theorem
explains why the same family appears asymptotically for a much larger class of
threshold exceedances.

A concrete choice of shape and scale illustrates both the survival and moments.

For \xi=0.4 and \beta=2, direct substitution gives\bar G(y)=(1+0.2y)^{-2.5},\qquad
\mathbb E[Y]=\frac{10}{3},\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\frac{500}{9}.

Thus \bar G(0)=1, \bar G(1)=1.2^{-2.5},
\bar G(5)=2^{-2.5}, and \bar G(10)=3^{-2.5}.
These are formula evaluations, with no numerical fitting or simulation.

A GPD fit is a tail model for exceedances, not a model for the full
distribution body.

The threshold u is not chosen by the theorem.  Shape and scale estimates
should be inspected across a range of thresholds.

When \xi\ge1, the fitted excess distribution has no finite mean.  When
\xi\ge1/2, it has no finite variance.

Dependence, truncation, censoring, seasonality, and mixture effects can
distort threshold-excess fits.
