How heavy is the upper tail, and how sensitive is the answer to where we
start fitting it? Hill estimates the exponent of a positive


Pareto-type tail from the largest observations.
Choosing how many observations to retain is part of the estimate.

Read the Pareto and 

regular variation
pages first. The formula uses logarithms and sorted observations; the


extreme-value index \xi is the reciprocal of the
Pareto exponent \alpha. For data analysis, inspect several thresholds and check dependence and
measurement limits before interpreting a stable-looking curve.


Tail threshold selection develops these checks.

Let x_1,\dots,x_n be observed right-tail data with x_i>0 for every i,
and write the ascending realized order statistics asx_{1:n}\le \cdots \le x_{n:n}.

For 1\le k<n, the Hill estimate of the extreme-value index is\widehat\xi_{k,n}
=
\frac1k\sum_{j=1}^{k}
\log\left(\frac{x_{n-j+1:n}}{x_{n-k:n}}\right).

For a 

Pareto-type right tail with exponent
\alpha, the corresponding tail exponent estimate is\widehat\alpha_{k,n}=\frac{1}{\widehat\xi_{k,n}}.

The tuning parameter k is the number of upper order statistics used.  A Hill
stability plot graphs \widehat\xi_{k,n} or \widehat\alpha_{k,n} over a
range of k values.  On this page, we name the plotted coordinate explicitly:
\xi is the extreme-value index, while \alpha=1/\xi is the Pareto tail
exponent.

Here x_{i:n} is the ith ascending observation, and k selects the top
k values above the order-statistic threshold. If all selected values equal
that threshold, \widehat\xi=0 and there is no finite reciprocal estimate.
Ties can also make the strict exceedance count smaller than k.

Hill is a right-tail estimator for strictly positive observations in a
Pareto-type regime, meaning the survival tail is expected to be


regularly varying.  It is appropriate only
after deciding what data transformation makes the tail positive and
one-sided.

Small k means the threshold is very high, so the estimate uses only the most
extreme observations and has high variance.  Large k lowers the threshold,
which adds data but can mix non-tail observations into the calculation.  A
stable region is a practical compromise between those two failures.

Report a range of k values, the corresponding thresholds, and the sensitivity
of the estimated exponent. A plateau can guide further checks, but it does not
establish regular variation or independence.

For a Pareto Type I variable,\mathbb P(X>x)=\left(\frac{x_m}{x}\right)^\alpha,\qquad x\ge x_m.

Define Y=\log(X/x_m). For y\ge0,\mathbb P(Y>y)
=
\mathbb P(X>x_m e^y)
=e^{-\alpha y},

so Y is exponential with mean 1/\alpha.  Equivalently,\mathbb E\left[\log\left(\frac{X}{u}\right)\mid X>u\right]
=\frac1\alpha

for any Pareto threshold u\ge x_m.  The Hill estimator replaces this
conditional expectation by the empirical average of log-excesses above the
random threshold X_{n-k:n}, or by x_{n-k:n} after the sample is realized.

For exact Pareto samples this explains why \widehat\xi_{k,n} targets
1/\alpha.  For a positive iid sample whose right tail is regularly varying
with extreme-value index \xi>0, the standard consistency result uses an
intermediate sequence k=k_n withk_n\to\infty,\qquad \frac{k_n}{n}\to0.

Under these assumptions, \widehat\xi_{k_n,n} converges in probability to
\xi.  The proof of that full theorem belongs to extreme-value asymptotics;
we use the exact Pareto calibration and cite the general result in Resnick


Resnick (2007). Hill’s original estimator is
described in 

Hill (1975),
pp. 1163–1174.

In a distribution with a bounded body and a Pareto tail, increasing k far
enough pulls body observations into the calculation. For empirical data,
a plateau is evidence to inspect, not a certificate.

Two iid samples of 30{,}000 observations: exact Pareto with x_m=1,
\alpha=1.7 (PCG64 seed 20261020), and the


uniform-body/Pareto-tail model
(seed 20261021). The mixture is uniform on [1,3] with probability
0.82 and Pareto with minimum 3, exponent 1.7, otherwise.
Both tail targets are \xi=1/1.7. The marked count of 5,344 is realized,

Hill is a right-tail estimator for strictly positive data: every realized
input must satisfy x_i>0.  Transform or split two-sided data before using

A plateau is suggestive, not a proof of a Pareto tail.  Dependence,

Estimating \alpha and plugging it into moments is dangerous near moment

The reciprocal \widehat\alpha=1/\widehat\xi is unstable when
\widehat\xi is close to zero.  Thin-tail regimes need different tools.

A sample can give an accurate count of what happened while leaving the size
of an unobserved loss almost unconstrained. We make this distinction precise
with two laws whose samples usually coincide but whose means can be far apart.
The 

exceedance note explains why estimating
a fixed event probability does not require a moment of the underlying variable.

Use the 

shared notation: P and
Q are probability laws, X_1,\ldots,X_n are observations, and \alpha
is a positive Pareto exponent. All draws below are iid under the chosen law.

Let P be any probability law and let
Q=(1-\varepsilon)P+\varepsilon R, where R is another law and
0<\varepsilon<1. Define total variation byd_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)=\sup_A|P(A)-Q(A)|,

where the supremum is over measurable events. For every integer n\ge1,d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P^{\otimes n},Q^{\otimes n})
\le 1-(1-\varepsilon)^n\le n\varepsilon.

We prove this bound and its consequence for tests. To generate a Q sample,
independently choose the R component with probability \varepsilon at each
draw. With probability (1-\varepsilon)^n, no such choice occurs and the
conditional sample law is exactly P^{\otimes n}. Thus
Q^{\otimes n}=(1-d)P^{\otimes n}+dH for some probability law H, where
d=1-(1-\varepsilon)^n. For any event A, the probability difference is
d|H(A)-P^{\otimes n}(A)|\le d. The union bound on the n component
choices gives d\le n\varepsilon.

More generally, a measurable test \varphi taking values in [0,1] obeys\left|\mathbb E_{Q^{\otimes n}}\varphi-
\mathbb E_{P^{\otimes n}}\varphi\right|\le d.

The same mixture identity proves this, because both expectations under H
and P^{\otimes n} lie in [0,1]. A test with rejection probability at
most \delta under P therefore has power at most \delta+d against this
Q. Here \delta is a test level, not the tail exponent.

A bounded law and a Pareto contamination

records.content:
Take P uniform on [0,1] and R an exact


Pareto law with minimum x_m=b>1 and exponent
\alpha>1. Their supports are disjoint. The event
\max_i X_i>1 has probability zero under P^{\otimes n} and d under
Q^{\otimes n}, so the total-variation bound is an equality.

For x\ge b the contaminated survival and mean are\bar F_Q(x)=\varepsilon(b/x)^\alpha,
\qquad
\mathbb E_Q X=\frac{1-\varepsilon}{2}
  +\varepsilon\frac{\alpha b}{\alpha-1}.

These follow by mixing the two survivals and the two finite means. For
1<\alpha\le2, Q has infinite second moment by the


Pareto moment calculation, although
P is bounded. For any fixed n, any 0<\eta<1, and any desired positive
mean gap, choose 0<\varepsilon\le\eta/n, then increase b until the
gap is exceeded. Sample total variation stays at most \eta. This proves
that a small sample-law discrepancy need not control an unbounded mean
functional over this unrestricted family.

The order of the quantifiers matters. For each fixed \varepsilon>0, the
detection probability tends to one as n\to\infty. The construction
does not say that a fixed alternative can remain hidden indefinitely.

For \varepsilon=10^{-4}, b=10^6, \alpha=3/2 and n=1000,
the mean is 300.49995 instead of 0.5, yet the probability that all
observations come from P is approximately 0.904833. Conditional on that
event, the entire observed vector has the baseline law. The sample mean is
still unbiased under Q: linearity gives
\mathbb E_Q\bar X_n=n^{-1}\sum_i\mathbb E_Q X_i=\mathbb E_Q X.
Rare large values supply its expectation.

If a measurable payoff satisfies 0\le g(x)\le B with finite B, the
one-draw mixture identity gives|\mathbb E_Q g(X)-\mathbb E_P g(X)|\le\varepsilon B.

For |g|\le B, replace the right side by 2\varepsilon B. A common
payoff bound therefore changes the problem; see


asymmetric payoffs. A known uniform
integrability condition or a restricted parametric family can also rule out
the alternatives used here. Such information is an assumption to justify.

An observation outside [0,1] rejects this particular bounded P exactly.
For a nondegenerate Gaussian, every finite upper-tail threshold has positive
exceedance probability. A large value therefore supports a statistical

Iso-density tail geometry studies the level sets of the iid joint densityf_{X_1,X_2}(x_1,x_2)=f(x_1)f(x_2)

near a large-deviation constraint such as x_1+x_2=s.  The diagnostic asks
whether the most likely configurations along the constraint sit near the
diagonal, where both coordinates are moderately large, or near the axes, where
one coordinate is large and the other is ordinary.

Here X_1,X_2 are independent copies of a continuous random variable with
density f, and x_1,x_2 are its coordinate values. The sum level s is
fixed for each comparison. See 

Shared notation.

For two iid standard normal variables, the joint density is proportional to\exp\left[-\frac{x_1^2+x_2^2}{2}\right].

On the line x_1+x_2=s,x_1^2+x_2^2
=
2\left(x_1-\frac{s}{2}\right)^2+\frac{s^2}{2},

so the joint density is maximized at the equal split
(s/2,s/2).  A large Gaussian sum is geometrically a many-moderate-deviation
event.

For two iid standard Cauchy variables,f(x)=\frac{1}{\pi(1+x^2)}.

Compare the equal split (s/2,s/2) with an axial split (0,s).  The axial to
equal density ratio is\frac{f(0)f(s)}{f(s/2)^2}
=
\frac{(1+s^2/4)^2}{1+s^2}
\sim
\frac{s^2}{16}
\to\infty.

Along a large-sum line, the Cauchy geometry increasingly favors one large
coordinate rather than two equal coordinates.  This is the density-contour
version of the one-big-jump intuition in

The axial points are comparison points, not the exact Cauchy maximizers for
finite positive s. To locate those maximizers, minimize the denominator
D(x)=(1+x^2)(1+(s-x)^2) along the line. Its derivative factors asD'(x)=2(2x-s)(x^2-sx+1).

For s>2, the two minima occur atx=\frac{s\pm\sqrt{s^2-4}}{2},

They sit near the axes, while the equal split becomes a local density minimum.

records.content:
The preceding calculation proves a comparison under independence. A
spherical bivariate Cauchy has instead the normalized densityg(x_1,x_2)=\frac{1}{2\pi}(1+x_1^2+x_2^2)^{-3/2}.

The 

multivariate Student construction
derives its normalization and Cauchy marginals at \nu=1. Its density is
strictly decreasing in squared radius. The same completed-square identity
used for the Gaussian therefore proves that, on x_1+x_2=s, its density
is maximized at the equal split for every s. Heavy marginal tails alone
do not determine the constrained density geometry.

There is a probability comparison as well. In polar coordinates, integrating
g over the full circle givesP(X_1^2+X_2^2>u^2)=\int_u^\infty r(1+r^2)^{-3/2}\,dr
=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+u^2}},\qquad u\ge0.

Angle is uniform and independent of radius because the joint polar density
factorizes. A sector of angle width \delta\in[0,2\pi], outside that
circle, has probability \delta/(2\pi\sqrt{1+u^2}).
At u=3 and \delta=\pi/3, this is 1/(6\sqrt{10})\approx0.052705.
Unlike a point-density ratio, this quantity integrates over a region of
positive area. It is not a large-sum probability.

Consider an equal mixture of two centered bivariate normals with unit
marginal variances and correlations r and -r, where 0<r<1.
Its covariance is I_2, and conditioning gives characteristic function\varphi(t_1,t_2)=e^{-(t_1^2+t_2^2)/2}\cosh(rt_1t_2).

We prove that this mixture is not elliptical. For a nondegenerate elliptical
law with finite covariance, covariance is a positive scalar multiple of
scatter: whitening gives a rotationally invariant law, whose covariance
commutes with every orthogonal matrix and hence is scalar. Thus an
elliptical law with covariance I_2 must be spherical. But the displayed
characteristic function at (v,0) is e^{-v^2/2}, whereas at
(v/\sqrt2,v/\sqrt2) it is e^{-v^2/2}\cosh(rv^2/2).
For v\ne0 these differ at the same radius. This disproves sphericality
and hence ellipticality. Both marginal laws remain standard normal.

The iid Cauchy vector gives another distinction: every linear combination
is Cauchy, with scale |a|+|b| for coefficients a,b not both zero,
since its characteristic function is e^{-|t_1|-|t_2|}.
It is a stable vector but not elliptical. To see the latter without moments,
its characteristic function on either axis would force the elliptical
profile to be exponential in the square root of its argument. It is also
unchanged when one coordinate changes sign, forcing off-diagonal scatter
zero. The equal marginal scales would then force circular level sets;
|t_1|+|t_2| instead has diamond level sets. Thus closure under linear
combinations does not require ellipticality.



Exact density contours on the same coordinate window. The first two laws
have identical standard Cauchy marginals but different contours. In the
third, both marginals are standard normal and covariance is the identity,
yet the contours are not elliptical. The color and line-style keys identify
levels at 5%, 15%, 35% and 65% of each panel’s density at the origin;
these are density levels, not equal enclosed probabilities.
The finite window is a plotting range, not a truncation of any law.

How much does averaging reduce mean absolute error at a specified sample
size? Kappa records the growth of the sum’s absolute deviation between two
sizes. It depends on the whole distribution and the chosen sizes. A tail
exponent alone does not determine it.

We use the metric from 

Taleb (2025), ch. 8, §§8.1–8.3, pp. 154–160.
The derivations below establish the stated special cases and corrections;
simulated values are labeled separately. The 

chapter guide
maps the remaining source sections.

Let X_i be iid, with \mathbb E|X_1|<\infty, mean \mu, and sums
S_n=\sum_{i=1}^nX_i, as in the


shared notation. Define\begin{aligned}
M(n)&=\mathbb E|S_n-n\mu|,\\
A(n)&=\mathbb E|\bar X_n-\mu|\\
&=M(n)/n.
\end{aligned}

M is a mean absolute deviation about the population mean, without
Gaussian calibration. It is neither a median deviation nor a deviation
about an estimated center; see the 

dispersion note.
For integers n>n_0\ge1, with M(n)>M(n_0)>0, set\begin{aligned}
\kappa_{n_0,n}
&=2-\frac{\log(n/n_0)}{\log(M(n)/M(n_0))},\\
\frac{M(n)}{M(n_0)}
&=(n/n_0)^{1/(2-\kappa_{n_0,n})}.
\end{aligned}

We always print both indices. The source’s \kappa_1 means
\kappa_{1,2}, whereas \kappa_{1,n} compares size n with one
observation. An adjacent-size comparison \kappa_{n,n+1} is different.
Here “metric” names a concentration index, not a distance satisfying the
axioms of a metric space.

We prove three elementary properties. Adding a constant to every summand
cancels under centering; multiplying by b\ne0 multiplies both deviations
by |b|. Thus kappa is invariant under location and nonzero scale changes.
Conditional Jensen, applied to an independent centered increment, gives
M(n+1)\ge M(n). The triangle inequality gives M(n)\le nM(1).
Consequently \kappa_{1,n}\le1 wherever the displayed definition applies.
There is no universal lower bound of zero.

For a chain n_0<n_1<\cdots<n_r, logarithmic growth adds:\begin{aligned}
&\log\frac{M(n_r)}{M(n_0)}\\
&\quad=\sum_{j=1}^r
\frac{\log(n_j/n_{j-1})}{2-\kappa_{n_{j-1},n_j}}.
\end{aligned}

This is a telescoping identity, with each intermediate kappa defined.
It does not justify averaging the kappas themselves.

The equal-positive case uses an extended limit. Constant laws and laws
without a finite absolute first moment have no kappa under this definition.
In particular, a 

Cauchy law is a limiting
benchmark as the stable index decreases to one, not an admissible endpoint.

For a nondegenerate stable law of index 1<\alpha\le2, the centered sum
has the same distribution as n^{1/\alpha}(X_1-\mu). Taking absolute
expectations proves\begin{aligned}
M(n)&=n^{1/\alpha}M(1),\\
\kappa_{n_0,n}&=2-\alpha,\\
A(n)/M(1)&=n^{1/\alpha-1}.
\end{aligned}

The stable sum identity is the cited structural property; the algebraic
consequence for kappa is proved here. Skewness does not change the exponent,
so it cancels from kappa even though it can change M(1). At \alpha=2
the law is Gaussian and kappa is zero. The growth exponent is 1/\alpha;
it must not be substituted for \alpha in 2-\alpha.
The 

stable-law note
fixes the characteristic-function scale and proves the symmetric MAD formula.

A domain-of-attraction statement is weaker than the exact stable identity.
For example, suppose a centered sum divided by a_n converges in law to
an integrable stable variable Z, the normalized absolute sums are uniformly
integrable, and \log a_n/\log n\to1/\alpha. ThenM(n)/a_n\longrightarrow\mathbb E|Z|

and substitution gives \kappa_{1,n}\to2-\alpha. Uniform integrability
is what permits convergence of expectations; weak convergence alone does
not supply it. This conditional argument does not assert a finite-sample
rate for every regularly varying law. A one-sided Pareto and a symmetric
Student law with the same tail exponent can have different finite kappas:
both their centers and their distribution bodies differ. The numerical
comparison below concerns exponent three only.

Use the ordinary Student law with degrees of freedom \nu>1, location
zero and scale one. Locally \nu is also its power-tail exponent. A direct
beta integral givesM(1)=\sqrt{\frac\nu\pi}\,
\frac{\Gamma((\nu-1)/2)}{\Gamma(\nu/2)}.

For completeness, substitute v=1+x^2/\nu in
2\int_0^\infty x f_\nu(x)\,dx; the remaining integral is
\int_1^\infty v^{-(\nu+1)/2}\,dv=2/(\nu-1).
The gamma recurrence yields the displayed expression.

There is also a two-summand closed form. Write a=\nu/2 and
X_i=\sqrt{\nu/(2G_i)}Z_i, where the G_i are independent
Gamma(a,1) and the Z_i are independent standard normals, independent
of the G_i. Set T=G_1+G_2, B=G_1/T. The change of variables has
Jacobian T and factorizes the joint density into independent
Gamma(2a,1) and Beta(a,a) densities. Conditional normal absolute
moments therefore give\begin{aligned}
M(2)&=\sqrt{\nu/\pi}\,
\mathbb E[T^{-1/2}]\\
&\quad\times\mathbb E[(B(1-B))^{-1/2}],\\
\frac{M(2)}{M(1)}
&=\sqrt\pi\,2^{2-\nu}
\frac{\Gamma(\nu-1/2)}{\Gamma(\nu/2)^2}.
\end{aligned}

The second line follows by the gamma and beta integrals, followed by the
gamma duplication identity. These are finite precisely when \nu>1.

records.content:
At \nu=3, the characteristic function is
\phi(t)=(1+\sqrt3|t|)e^{-\sqrt3|t|}.
One way to verify it is to differentiate the Cauchy Fourier integral
\int_{\mathbb R}e^{itx}(x^2+a^2)^{-1}dx=\pi e^{-a|t|}/a
with respect to a>0 and use the normalized squared-denominator density
at a=\sqrt3. The Cauchy integral follows by closing the contour in the
half-plane where the exponential decays and taking the residue at
ia or -ia; the arc integral tends to zero. Differentiation is justified
by an integrable bound in a neighborhood of any positive a.

We now derive the sum MAD, using the


absolute-moment Fourier identity.
Integration by parts, then u=\sqrt3t, gives\begin{aligned}
I_n&=\int_0^\infty(1+u)^{n-1}e^{-nu}\,du,\\
M(n)&=\frac{2\sqrt3}{\pi}\,nI_n,\\
\frac{M(n)}{M(1)}
&=e^n n^{1-n}\Gamma(n,n),\\
\Gamma(n,n)&=\int_n^\infty t^{n-1}e^{-t}\,dt.
\end{aligned}

The boundary term vanishes at zero because 1-\phi(t)^n=O(t^2),
and at infinity because the numerator is bounded. The substitution
t=n(1+u) gives the incomplete-gamma expression. This also holds at n=1.
Repeated integration by parts yields the independent finite formula\frac{M(n)}{M(1)}
=\frac{n!}{n^n}\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac{n^j}{j!}.

For the limit, e^{-n}\sum_{j<n}n^j/j!=P(N_n<n)\to1/2,
where N_n is Poisson with mean n. Apply the classical CLT to a sum
of n independent Poisson(1) variables. Stirling’s formula then gives\begin{aligned}
\frac{M(n)}{M(1)}&\sim\sqrt{\pi n/2},\\
\log n\;\kappa_{1,n}&\longrightarrow2\log(\pi/2).
\end{aligned}

This constant differs from the one printed in §8.6.1, p. 165.
The calculation concerns the kappa anchored at one observation. It is
not a bound on the CDF error in a normal approximation, nor on tail-quantile
error. It does not prove that a million-term standardized sum is poorly
approximated by a Gaussian at every threshold.

More generally, take any iid law with variance 0<\sigma^2<\infty.
The classical CLT is cited in the


limit-law note.
The normalized centered sums have second moment \sigma^2; hence
\mathbb E[|Y_n|\mathbf1_{|Y_n|>K}]\le\sigma^2/K for
Y_n=(S_n-n\mu)/\sqrt n. This proves uniform integrability, so\begin{aligned}
M(n)/\sqrt n&\longrightarrow c,\\
c&=\sigma\sqrt{2/\pi},\\
\log n\;\kappa_{1,n}
&\longrightarrow4\log\frac{c}{M(1)}.
\end{aligned}

To obtain the last line, write
\log(M(n)/M(1))=\tfrac12\log n+\log(c/M(1))+o(1)
and substitute in the definition. The logarithmic behavior can reflect
the mismatch between the one-observation MAD and its Gaussian calibration.
If c=M(1), the constant vanishes and this argument gives no nonzero
leading rate. Kappa approaching zero does not identify the far tail.

Let each summand have Gamma shape r>0 and scale \theta>0.
Here \theta is a local scale, not a natural parameter. The sum has
shape a=nr, mean a\theta, andM(n)=\frac{2\theta\,a^a e^{-a}}{\Gamma(a)}.

We derive this using
\mathbb E|V-\mathbb EV|=2\mathbb E(V-\mathbb EV)_+.
After scaling by \theta, the integral is\frac{2\theta}{\Gamma(a)}
\int_a^\infty(t-a)t^{a-1}e^{-t}\,dt.

Integration by parts gives
\Gamma(a+1,a)=a\Gamma(a,a)+a^ae^{-a},
which evaluates the integral. At r=1, the parent is exponential
with rate 1/\theta. Stirling’s formula or the preceding finite-variance
argument gives\log n\;\kappa_{1,n}
\longrightarrow4-2\log(2\pi).

Thus even the exponential law has a positive finite kappa and this
logarithmic anchored rate. It still satisfies the


Cramér condition and is not subexponential.

curve uses index 1.5. The Student and exponential curves use exact formulas;

Let X=e^{\mu_\ell+\sigma_\ell Z} with standard-normal Z and
\sigma_\ell>0. These are log-location and log-scale, not the mean and
standard deviation of X. Write m=\mathbb EX=e^{\mu_\ell+\sigma_\ell^2/2}.
Completing the square in the truncated normal integral givesM(1)=2m\left[2\Phi(\sigma_\ell/2)-1\right].

For example, use M(1)=2\mathbb E(X-m)_+ and the threshold
Z=\sigma_\ell/2. Exponential tilting shifts the normal mean by
\sigma_\ell, giving the formula. Sums of independent lognormals are
not generally lognormal. Matching a sum’s first two moments to another
lognormal gives an approximation, not an identity or a proved bound on kappa.

The mismatch can be checked with third moments. For a mean-one lognormal,
put v=e^{\sigma_\ell^2}-1>0. Its moments
\mathbb EV^j=e^{j(j-1)\sigma_\ell^2/2} give variance v and third
centered moment v^2(v+3). Independence makes the variance of the average
v/n and its third centered moment v^2(v+3)/n^2. The skewnesses of
the actual average and a moment-matched lognormal are therefore\begin{aligned}
g_{\rm sum}&=(v+3)\sqrt{v/n},\\
g_{\rm fit}&=(v/n+3)\sqrt{v/n}.
\end{aligned}

They differ for every n>1. This proves that the fitted lognormal cannot
be the exact sum law; it does not quantify its approximation error.

We prove the three limits at the scope used in §8.6.2, pp. 166–168.
For fixed \sigma_\ell, finite variance and the previous argument give
\kappa_{1,n}\to0 as n\to\infty.
For fixed integer n>1, scale invariance lets us use the mean-one variable
V_\sigma=e^{\sigma Z-\sigma^2/2}. Define its Gaussian approximation
error D_\sigma. As \sigma\downarrow0,\begin{aligned}
D_\sigma&=\frac{V_\sigma-1}{\sigma}-Z,\\
\mathbb E D_\sigma^2&=\frac{e^{\sigma^2}-1}{\sigma^2}-1\\
&\longrightarrow0.
\end{aligned}

This identity follows from \mathbb E V_\sigma^2=e^{\sigma^2} and
\mathbb E[ZV_\sigma]=\sigma. A finite sum preserves L^2 convergence,
which implies convergence of absolute expectations. Thus the MAD ratio
tends to \sqrt n, and kappa tends to zero.

As \sigma\to\infty, couple a fixed finite set of normal variables.
Each V_{\sigma,i}\to0 almost surely, although its mean remains one.
For T_\sigma=\sum_{i=1}^nV_{\sigma,i},\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb E|T_\sigma-n|\\
&\quad=2n-2\mathbb E\min(T_\sigma,n),\\
&\mathbb E\min(T_\sigma,n)\longrightarrow0.
\end{aligned}

The last line is bounded convergence. Therefore M(n)/M(1)\to n
and \kappa_{1,n}\to1. The order of limits matters. Every fixed lognormal
law still has all power moments and belongs to the Gaussian domain of attraction.

For nonnegative integrable sums, the exact lower-deviation identity isM(n)=2\mathbb E(nm-S_n)_+.

For the mean-one lognormal, condition on the first n-1 summands and put
a=n-\sum_{i<n}V_{\sigma,i}. If a\le0, the conditional payoff is zero.
For a>0, completing the square gives\begin{aligned}
h(a)&=\mathbb E(a-V_\sigma)_+,\\
d&=\log(a)/\sigma+\sigma/2,\\
h(a)&=a\Phi(d)-\Phi(d-\sigma).
\end{aligned}

The simulated payoff lies between zero and n. Multiplying its sample
average by 2m estimates M(n) without estimating an unbounded upper-tail
payoff. This uses a known model mean. It is not available merely because a
dataset contains only small observations.

Consider the symmetric triangular density f(x)=(2-|x|)/4 on [-2,2].
It has a single mode at zero and can be written as the sum of two
independent Uniform[-1,1] variables. Direct integration gives M(1)=2/3.
The sum of two copies is a sum of four such uniforms and has M(2)=14/15.
Here is an explicit calculation of the second value. If T is a sum of
four Uniform[0,1] variables, symmetry and integration of its CDF give\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E|2T-4|
&=4\int_0^2P(T<t)\,dt,\\
P(T<t)&=\frac{t^4-4(t-1)_+^4}{24},\\
&\hspace{2em}0\le t\le2,\\
\mathbb E|2T-4|&=\frac{4(32-4)}{120}=\frac{14}{15}.
\end{aligned}

The CDF formula is inclusion–exclusion for the volume below
u_1+\cdots+u_4<t in the unit cube. Thus\kappa_{1,2}=2-\frac{\log2}{\log(7/5)}<0.

The source’s separated Gaussian mixture is another example. For

S_n\mid K&\sim N(a(2K-n),n\sigma^2).

If H(b,s)=\mathbb E|b+sZ|, splitting the normal integral at -b/s gives\begin{aligned}
H(b,s)&=s\sqrt{2/\pi}\,e^{-b^2/(2s^2)}\\
&\quad+|b|[2\Phi(|b|/s)-1],\\
M(n)&=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk2^{-n}\\
&\quad\times H(a(2k-n),\sigma\sqrt n).
\end{aligned}

M(1)=H(a,\sigma) and
M(2)=\{H(2a,\sqrt2\sigma)+H(0,\sqrt2\sigma)\}/2.
For fixed \sigma>0 and a\to\infty, their ratio tends to one from
above, so \kappa_{1,2}\to-\infty.

Let L be eventually positive, measurable, locally bounded, and


slowly varying at infinity.  If \rho>-1, then\int_a^x t^\rho L(t)\,dt
\sim
\frac{x^{\rho+1}L(x)}{\rho+1},
\qquad x\to\infty.

If \rho<-1, then\int_x^\infty t^\rho L(t)\,dt
\sim
\frac{x^{\rho+1}L(x)}{-\rho-1},
\qquad x\to\infty.

Here a>0 is fixed in a region where L is locally bounded, and
A(x)\sim B(x) means A(x)/B(x)\to1.
Both integral statements are cited from 

Bingham et al. (1987),
Theorem 1.5.11, p. 28 (direct half); the special case for L and powers
also appears as Propositions 1.5.8 and 1.5.10, pp. 26–27.

For a nonnegative random variable X with


regularly varying survival function
\bar F(x)=x^{-\alpha}L(x) and \alpha>0, integration by parts gives the
moment-test consequences\mathbb E[X^p\mathbf 1_{\{X>x\}}]
\sim
\frac{\alpha}{\alpha-p}x^p\bar F(x),
\qquad 0<p<\alpha,

and\mathbb E[X^p\mathbf 1_{\{X\le x\}}]
\sim
\frac{\alpha}{p-\alpha}x^p\bar F(x),
\qquad p>\alpha.

Thus a 

Pareto-type tail has finite pth moment
for 0<p<\alpha and infinite pth moment for p>\alpha. The boundary case
p=\alpha is not decided by this theorem alone; it depends on the slowly
varying factor L.

Here \bar F(x)=\mathbb P(X>x), \alpha is the positive tail exponent,
and p is the moment order. The integration parameters a and \rho
belong to the integral theorem.

Karamata’s theorem says that, for regularly varying functions, integrals are
asymptotically governed by the endpoint where the mass accumulates.  When
\rho>-1, the integral up to x is controlled by the upper endpoint.  When
\rho<-1, the remaining tail integral beyond x is controlled by the lower
endpoint.

This is the bridge between tail shape and


moment existence.  Once the survival tail behaves
like x^{-\alpha}L(x), multiplying by x^p tests whether the pth moment is
still dominated by ordinary observations or by the far tail.

For an exact 

Pareto tail, L is constant, so
Karamata reduces the moment test to integrating a pure power.

For L(x)=\log x, the same power boundary applies, but the endpoint
asymptotic gains the slowly varying logarithmic factor.

The boundary case p=\alpha needs separate analysis.  Exact Pareto tails
diverge logarithmically, as shown in


Pareto Moment Existence.  More generally,\mathbb E[X^\alpha]<\infty
  \Longleftrightarrow
  \int^\infty \frac{L(t)}{t}\,dt<\infty,

when \bar F(t)=t^{-\alpha}L(t) in the tail.  Thus L(t)=1 gives
logarithmic divergence, L(t)=1/\log t gives \log\log t divergence,
and L(t)=1/(\log t)^2 gives a finite boundary moment.

We use Karamata’s integral asymptotics as a cited theorem, then derive the two
moment consequences by integration by parts.  The boundary case p=\alpha is
not decided by Karamata alone; it depends on the slowly varying factor and is
handled through examples and caveats.

The integral asymptotics are the classical form of Karamata’s theorem for
regularly varying functions.  The full proof uses uniform convergence of slowly
varying functions on compact multiplier intervals and a split of the integral
into a near-endpoint part and a negligible remainder; this page cites the
standard theorem rather than reproducing that argument here.

The moment consequences follow from integration by parts.  For 0<p<\alpha,\mathbb E[X^p\mathbf 1_{\{X>x\}}]
=x^p\bar F(x)+p\int_x^\infty t^{p-1}\bar F(t)\,dt.

Since t^{p-1}\bar F(t)=t^{p-\alpha-1}L(t) and
p-\alpha-1<-1, Karamata’s tail-integral form gives\int_x^\infty t^{p-1}\bar F(t)\,dt
\sim
\frac{x^{p-\alpha}L(x)}{\alpha-p}
=
\frac{x^p\bar F(x)}{\alpha-p}.

Therefore\mathbb E[X^p\mathbf 1_{\{X>x\}}]
\sim
\left(1+\frac{p}{\alpha-p}\right)x^p\bar F(x)
=
\frac{\alpha}{\alpha-p}x^p\bar F(x).

For p>\alpha,\mathbb E[X^p\mathbf 1_{\{X\le x\}}]
=p\int_0^x t^{p-1}\bar F(t)\,dt-x^p\bar F(x).

The part of the integral over any fixed bounded interval is negligible relative
to x^p\bar F(x).  Applying Karamata to
t^{p-\alpha-1}L(t) givesp\int_0^x t^{p-1}\bar F(t)\,dt
\sim
\frac{p}{p-\alpha}x^p\bar F(x),

so subtracting x^p\bar F(x) leaves\mathbb E[X^p\mathbf 1_{\{X\le x\}}]
\sim
\frac{\alpha}{p-\alpha}x^p\bar F(x).

For the exact Pareto special case, L is constant and the same formulas are
obtained by direct power integration.

For a slowly varying example take L(t)=\log t on t>1 and
\rho>-1. Integration by parts gives the exact identity\int_1^x t^\rho\log t\,dt
=\frac{x^{\rho+1}\log x}{\rho+1}
-\frac{x^{\rho+1}-1}{(\rho+1)^2}.

Dividing by Karamata’s leading term yields\frac{\int_1^x t^\rho\log t\,dt}
     {x^{\rho+1}\log x/(\rho+1)}
=1-\frac{1-x^{-(\rho+1)}}{(\rho+1)\log x}\longrightarrow1.

For exact Pareto with x_m=1 and p>\alpha, the ratio of the truncated
moment to its leading term is 1-x^{-(p-\alpha)}\to1.
At p=\alpha, the truncated moment is \alpha\log x instead.
These are exact calculations illustrating the cited theorem.

Write \bar X_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i. Convergence in probability to
\mu means P(|\bar X_n-\mu|>\varepsilon)\to0 for every
\varepsilon>0. Almost-sure convergence means
P(\lim_n\bar X_n=\mu)=1. The second implies the first, by bounded
convergence applied to the deviation indicators. Convergence in law to a
constant also implies convergence in probability to that constant.

For iid X_i with \mathbb E|X_i|<\infty, the strong law gives
\bar X_n\to\mathbb EX_1 almost surely. We cite the strong law from


Durrett (2019), Theorem 2.4.1, p. 76. Variance need not exist.
We prove the weak law under the same iid integrability assumption here.

Let X_i^{(c)}=\max(-c,\min(X_i,c)). For fixed c, independence and
Chebyshev give\begin{gathered}
P\!\left(\left|\overline{X^{(c)}}_n-\mathbb EX^{(c)}\right|>
\varepsilon\right)\\
\le\frac{c^2}{n\varepsilon^2}.
\end{gathered}

Also \mathbb E|X-X^{(c)}|\to0 by dominated convergence, and
|\mathbb EX-\mathbb EX^{(c)}|\le\mathbb E|X-X^{(c)}|.
Markov bounds the probability that the average of the discarded absolute
remainders exceeds \varepsilon by
\mathbb E|X-X^{(c)}|/\varepsilon, uniformly in n. The triangle
inequality, first choosing c large and then n large, proves the weak
law. No variance of X was used.

For a concrete distinction between convergence modes, independent events
B_n with P(B_n)=1/n give \mathbf1_{B_n}\to0 in probability but
not almost surely: the second Borel–Cantelli lemma gives infinitely many
occurrences (

Durrett (2019), Theorem 2.3.7, p. 70). This example concerns a sequence of indicators, not iid sample
means. For dependent centered observations, a sufficient weak-law condition
is \operatorname{Var}(S_n)=o(n^2), directly by Chebyshev; finite marginal
variances alone do not ensure it.

Let X_1,X_2,\dots be independent copies of a nonnegative random variable
X, and letS_n=\sum_{i=1}^n X_i.

If \mathbb E[X]=\infty, then\frac{S_n}{n}\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}\infty.

For a 

Pareto Type I variable with lower cutoff
x_m>0 and tail exponent \alpha, this applies exactly when \alpha\le1.
In that regime the sample mean is not estimating a hidden finite number; the
ordinary law of large numbers normalization has failed.

Here \mathbb E is expectation and a.s. means almost surely. The Pareto
parameters x_m and \alpha are the lower cutoff and positive tail exponent.
See 

Shared notation.

The finite-mean law of large numbers says that many small and moderate
observations eventually average out the noise.  With a nonnegative infinite
mean, every finite truncation has an ordinary average, but those truncation
levels can be pushed higher without bound.  The untruncated average must
eventually dominate each one.

For 

Pareto tails with \alpha\le1, rare
observations are large enough that no finite long-run mean exists.  A running
average may drift downward between records, but the theorem says there is no
stable finite level waiting in the limit.

We prove the statement by truncating the variables, applying the strong law to each
bounded truncation, and then letting the cutoff rise.  The Pareto threshold
condition is not reproved here; it is supplied by


Pareto Moment Existence.

For a cutoff c>0, define the truncated variableX_i^{(c)}=\min(X_i,c).

Each X_i^{(c)} is bounded, so the strong law of large numbers gives\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^{(c)}
\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}
\mathbb E[\min(X,c)].

Since X_i\ge X_i^{(c)},\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{S_n}{n}
\ge
\mathbb E[\min(X,c)]

almost surely for each fixed c.  Apply this on the countable sequence
c=1,2,3,\dots.  By monotone convergence,\mathbb E[\min(X,c)]\uparrow \mathbb E[X]=\infty.

Therefore the liminf of S_n/n is larger than every finite number, almost
surely, which proves S_n/n\to\infty almost surely.

For a Pareto Type I variable,


Pareto Moment Existence proves that
\mathbb E[X] is infinite exactly when \alpha\le1.

sample path. Long downward stretches between records are compatible with the
theorem. The

different quantity: the largest observation’s share of the realized total.

Z_i=|X_i|^p. If \mathbb E|X|^p<\infty, the empirical absolute

For realized nonnegative observations x_1,\dots,x_n with s_n>0, define\begin{gathered}
s_n=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i,\\
m_n=\max_{1\le i\le n}x_i,\\
r_n=\frac{m_n}{s_n}.
\end{gathered}

The realized max-to-sum ratio r_n is the share of the total produced by the
largest observed value.  Its random-sample counterpart is
R_n=M_n/S_n, where S_n=\sum_{i=1}^n X_i and
M_n=\max_{1\le i\le n}X_i. When X_1,X_2,\dots are iid nonnegative
variables with finite positive mean \mu=\mathbb E[X], thenR_n\to0\qquad\text{almost surely}.

Thus a persistent large realized value r_n is a warning sign that the sample
sum is being governed by extremes rather than by aggregation.  For


Pareto Type I samples with \alpha\le1, the
ordinary mean is infinite, so the finite-mean argument below does not apply.

Lowercase symbols describe the observed list; uppercase symbols describe
random samples. For a nonnegative list with positive total,
1/n\le r_n\le1. If the total is zero, the ratio is undefined.
For the almost-sure limit, S_n/n\to\mu>0 ensures that S_n>0
eventually almost surely; any convention on earlier zero totals gives the
same limit.

In a thin-tailed or comfortable finite-mean sample, the largest observation may
be memorable, but it should eventually become a negligible fraction of the
whole.  The total grows like n\mu, while the largest draw grows more slowly
than n on the scale needed to dominate the sum.

Fat-tailed samples can look different.  One observation can represent a large
fraction of all observed mass, especially near or below the Pareto mean
boundary \alpha=1.  This is the same mechanism behind


LLN Failure Under Infinite Mean, but R_n makes
the dominance visible without plotting the entire running average.  It
complements the path view in


Pre-Asymptotic LLN Behavior.

We prove the finite-mean theorem: if the iid nonnegative observations have a
positive finite mean, then the maximum becomes a negligible share of the sum.
The proof uses the strong law and Borel--Cantelli
(

Durrett (2019), Theorem 2.4.1, p. 76, and Theorem 2.3.1, p. 68).  The infinite-mean Pareto
regimes are cited or described heuristically, because their exact limits need
heavier regular-variation machinery.

Assume X_i\ge0 are iid and 0<\mu=\mathbb E[X]<\infty.  The strong law
gives S_n/n\to\mu almost surely.  It remains to show that M_n/n\to0
almost surely.

For any \varepsilon>0, integrability implies\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\mathbb P(X_n>\varepsilon n)<\infty,

because the sum is bounded by a constant multiple of
\int_0^\infty\mathbb P(X>t)\,dt=\mathbb E[X].  By Borel--Cantelli,
X_n/n\to0 almost surely.  Therefore M_n/n\to0 almost surely: after a
random finite index all new observations are at most \varepsilon n, while
the finitely many old observations divided by n vanish.  Hence\frac{M_n}{S_n}=\frac{M_n/n}{S_n/n}\to0

almost surely.

For a Pareto Type I tail,


Pareto Moment Existence shows that
the mean exists exactly when \alpha>1.  The regimes are qualitatively
different:

\alpha>1: M_n/S_n\to0 almost surely by the finite-mean theorem.

Exact Pareto \alpha=1: M_n/S_n\to0 in probability, but slowly;
M_n/(x_m n) is bounded in probability, while
S_n/(x_m n\log n)\to1 in probability; the


Pareto note proves both normalizations.
This is not almost-sure convergence of the ratio.

0<\alpha<1: under standard regular-variation assumptions, M_n/S_n has
a nondegenerate limiting distribution


Darling, 1952.
Infinite mean does not imply that
one observation asymptotically equals the whole sum; several of the largest
observations may keep material shares.

For iid nonnegative variables with P(X>0)>0, the converse to the
finite-mean theorem also holds: R_n\to0 almost surely if and only if
\mathbb E[X]<\infty. This converse is cited from


O'Brien (1980), not proved above.
It does not rule out convergence in probability with an infinite mean,
as the exact Pareto \alpha=1 case shows.

An entropy maximizer answers a constrained optimization question. Specifying
only “maximum entropy” leaves that question incomplete: the support, measure,
and constraints determine the answer. Here all densities are with respect
to Lebesgue measure in the stated coordinate, with natural logarithms and
fixed measurement units.

Appendix B of 

Taleb (2025), printed pp. 127–133, motivates the examples.
We prove the Shannon optima below by a relative-entropy bound. We then derive
the normalization and moments of a q-exponential family and distinguish them
from a global optimization theorem under escort constraints.

records.content:
For a density f on a fixed support D, its differential entropy is
h(f)=-\int_D f(x)\log f(x)\,dx, when defined. Consider a candidateg(x)=\exp\{\theta\mathbin{\cdot}t(x)-\psi(\theta)\},\qquad x\in D,

with finite normalizer and prescribed expectations of the sufficient
statistics t. This is the 

exponential-family form;
\theta, t, and \psi follow the 

shared notation.
Assume the candidate and competitors have the same finite constraints,
and \int f|\log g|<\infty.

We prove the entropy bound and its equality condition. With r=f/g,
r\log r-r+1\ge0 for r\ge0, with equality only at r=1.
Integrating against g gives\mathrm{KL}(f\Vert g)=\int_D f\log(f/g)\,dx\ge0.

Because \log g is affine in the constrained statistics,
\int f\log g=\int g\log g. Consequentlyh(g)-h(f)=\mathrm{KL}(f\Vert g)\ge0.

This identity also permits h(f)=-\infty and infinite KL when the cross
entropy is finite. The negative part of r\log r is integrable against
g, so the right side is well-defined. Equality requires f=g almost
everywhere. This proves a global maximum, once a feasible candidate exists.
It does not assert existence for arbitrary moment constraints.

records.content:
On [a,b] with finite a<b, normalization alone gives
g=1/(b-a) and h(g)=\log(b-a). Its log density is constant, so the
certificate applies to every competing density on that interval. There is
no corresponding uniform probability density on the whole real line.

On \mathbb R, fix \mathbb EX=\mu and
\mathbb E(X-\mu)^2=\sigma^2>0. The Gaussian candidate has\log g(x)=-\tfrac12\log(2\pi\sigma^2)
           -\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2},\qquad
h(g)=\tfrac12\log(2\pi e\sigma^2).

Its normalization is the Gaussian integral, and taking the prescribed
second moment gives the displayed entropy. The certificate proves its
unique maximum among densities with those moments. A half-line support
would be a different optimization problem. These are the scoped versions
of the examples in §B.1.1 and §B.1.3, pp. 128–129.

Fix x_m>0, support [x_m,\infty), and\mathbb E\log(X/x_m)=m,\qquad 0<m<\infty.

Here m is a local log-moment, not \mathbb EX. Put \alpha=1/m.
The 

Pareto candidate is
g(x)=\alpha x_m^\alpha x^{-\alpha-1}. To check feasibility, set
z=\log(x/x_m); its transformed density is \alpha e^{-\alpha z}
on z\ge0. Thus \mathbb E_g z=1/\alpha=m. Also\log g(x)=\log(\alpha/x_m)-(\alpha+1)\log(x/x_m),
\qquad h(g)=\log(x_m m)+1+m.

The entropy certificate proves that this Pareto law is the unique maximum
for the stated log-moment constraint. No ordinary mean is required: it is
finite only when m<1, by the 

moment theorem.
This supplies a complete proof for the model considered in §B.1.2, p. 129.

The constraint uses a dimensionless logarithm. Changing units from X to
cX changes entropy by \log c and changes x_m by the same factor.
More generally, a differentiable increasing coordinate change U=T(X)
with positive derivative gives h(U)=h(X)+\mathbb E\log T'(X) whenever
the terms are finite, by substitution in the density integral. A nonlinear
change of coordinates therefore need not preserve an entropy ranking.
For the logarithm above the correction is fixed by the constraint, which
is why maximizing in either coordinate gives the same candidate here.

For a local parameter q>0, q\ne1, defineS_q(f)=\frac{1-\int f(x)^q\,dx}{q-1},\qquad
f_{[q]}(x)=\frac{f(x)^q}{\int f(y)^q\,dy},

provided 0<\int f^q<\infty. The second expression is an escort density.
Its mean \int x f_{[q]}(x)\,dx is a different functional from
\mathbb EX. Differential densities can exceed one, so inequalities between
f^q and f require the value of f, as well as the sign of q-1.

For independent variables with densities f,g and finite integrals of their
qth powers, Tonelli gives \int(fg)^q=(\int f^q)(\int g^q).
Substitution provesS_q(f\otimes g)=S_q(f)+S_q(g)+(1-q)S_q(f)S_q(g).

This concerns the joint density of the pair. It is not an entropy
identity for the distribution of their sum. Since differential entropies
can be negative, a universal superadditive/subadditive label needs further
conditions. This distinction matters in §B.2, pp. 129–130.

To see where the family in that section comes from, write J=\int f^q
and prescribe an escort mean m_q. For admissible variations at a positive
density, differentiation of the numerator and denominator gives\delta\left(\frac{\int xf^q}{J}\right)
=\frac qJ\int (x-m_q)f(x)^{q-1}\delta f(x)\,dx.

A stationary density for S_q subject to normalization and that constraint
therefore satisfies, for Lagrange multipliers \lambda_0,\lambda_1,-q f(x)^{q-1}\left[\frac1{q-1}
       +\frac{\lambda_1}{J}(x-m_q)\right]-\lambda_0=0.

This is a necessary interior stationarity calculation, with variations for
which differentiation under the integral is justified. On an admissible
branch it produces a power of an affine function. The escort constraint
is nonlinear in f; we do not infer a global maximum from this calculation.

Take \beta>0. The following family is a probability density for 0<q<2:f_{q,\beta}(x)=\beta(2-q)
 [1+(q-1)\beta x]^{-1/(q-1)}.

For 1<q<2 its support is [0,\infty); for 0<q<1 it is
[0,1/((1-q)\beta)], with density zero beyond that endpoint.
At q=1 define f_{1,\beta}(x)=\beta e^{-\beta x} for x\ge0.
We now prove normalization, the tail exponent, and the mean distinctions.

Substitution v=1+(q-1)\beta x gives an unnormalized integral
1/[\beta(2-q)] in both ranges. On the infinite support it converges
only for q<2; q=2 diverges logarithmically and q>2 also fails.
The survival on the interior of the support is\bar F_{q,\beta}(x)
=[1+(q-1)\beta x]^{-(2-q)/(q-1)}.

For 1<q<2, this is a Lomax survival with
\alpha=(2-q)/(q-1) and scale 1/[(q-1)\beta].
The same power comparison as in the Pareto moment proof shows
\mathbb EX^p<\infty exactly when 0<p<\alpha; equality diverges.
All nonnegative power moments exist in the compact-support case.
Integrating this survival gives\mathbb EX=\frac1{\beta(3-2q)},\qquad 0<q<3/2.

The ordinary mean is infinite for 3/2\le q<2. In contrast, dividing
f_{q,\beta}^q by its integral gives a density proportional to
[1+(q-1)\beta x]^{-q/(q-1)}. Integration gives\int f_{q,\beta}^q=\beta^{q-1}(2-q)^q,\qquad
\mathbb E_{[q]}X=\frac1{\beta(2-q)},\quad 0<q<2.

These formulas also have the stated exponential values at q=1 by limits.
For q=5/4 and \beta=2, the survival exponent is 3, ordinary mean
is 1, and escort mean is 2/3. A zero escort mean on [0,\infty)
would force the escort law to concentrate at zero, impossible for this nondegenerate
density. Centering a coordinate shifts the support too; it cannot set that
mean to zero while preserving the same half-line. These restrictions qualify
the normalization step in §B.2, pp. 132–133.

For a random variable X and a threshold u with \mathbb P(X>u)>0 and finite
conditional expectation above u, the mean excess function ise(u)=\mathbb E[X-u\mid X>u].

It measures the expected overshoot beyond u after the threshold has already
been crossed.  For a 

Pareto Type I tail with
exponent \alpha>1 and u\ge x_m,e(u)=\frac{u}{\alpha-1}.

For a 

generalized Pareto variable
with location zero, shape \xi, scale \beta>0, and
threshold u in its support with \beta+\xi u>0, the mean excess function is
linear when \xi<1:e(u)=\frac{\beta+\xi u}{1-\xi}.

The exponential distribution is the boundary case \xi=0, where e(u) is
constant. Here u is the threshold, \xi the GPD shape, and \beta
its scale at threshold zero.

The mean excess function asks what remains after an event is already large.
Thin-tail intuition often expects the remaining excess to be tame once a high
threshold has been crossed.  A Pareto tail says the opposite: the expected
additional excess grows in proportion to the threshold itself.

The exponential, positive-shape GPD with \xi<1, and negative-shape GPD
models have constant, increasing linear, and decreasing linear population
mean excess functions, respectively. Curvature departs from an exact GPD model
over that threshold range. An empirical plot can also bend because of sampling
noise, especially when few observations exceed the threshold; its shape alone
does not identify a model failure or a body-to-tail transition.

We derive the Pareto mean-excess formula from the conditional survival
function.  The generalized Pareto linear formula follows from standard GPD


threshold stability
and the GPD mean formula. The GPD page derives the stability identity; its
moment formulas are cited rather than reproved here.

For Pareto Type I,\mathbb P(X>x)=\left(\frac{x_m}{x}\right)^\alpha,
\qquad x\ge x_m.

For u\ge x_m and \alpha>1,e(u)
=
\mathbb E[X-u\mid X>u]
=
\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X-u>y\mid X>u)\,dy.

Taking the ratio \bar F(u+y)/\bar F(u) for y\ge0 gives\mathbb P(X-u>y\mid X>u)
=
\left(1+\frac{y}{u}\right)^{-\alpha}.

Thereforee(u)
=
\int_0^\infty \left(1+\frac{y}{u}\right)^{-\alpha}\,dy
=
u\int_1^\infty z^{-\alpha}\,dz
=
\frac{u}{\alpha-1}.

For a generalized Pareto distribution, the threshold-stability property gives
another generalized Pareto distribution above threshold u with updated scale
\beta+\xi u, provided u is in the support and \beta+\xi u>0.  Its mean
exists only for \xi<1, and equals (\beta+\xi u)/(1-\xi).

A Gaussian conditional model need not give a Gaussian marginal law. Let
Z\sim N(0,1) and let Y>0 be independent of Z. We study\begin{gathered}
X=\sqrt Y Z,\\
X\mid Y=y\sim N(0,y).
\end{gathered}

Here Y is variance, so \sqrt Y is conditional standard deviation.
This is the centered scalar case of the


Normix normal-mixture construction.
We use its shared mixing symbol Y and the


notation canon.
A one-observation mixture specifies no temporal dependence: volatility
clustering requires a model for a sequence of mixing variables.

For every real q>0, the absolute moment factors, including infinite values:\begin{gathered}
\mathbb E|X|^q=c_q\mathbb E[Y^{q/2}],\\
c_q=\frac{2^{q/2}\Gamma((q+1)/2)}{\sqrt\pi}.
\end{gathered}

We prove this identity by independence and Tonelli’s theorem applied to the
nonnegative product Y^{q/2}|Z|^q. In the normal integral for c_q, the
substitution t=z^2/2 gives the displayed gamma integral. Thus the moment
exists exactly when the mixing moment exists. Symmetry alone does not make
an odd signed moment exist; absolute integrability is still required.

If 0<\mathbb EY<\infty, then \mathbb E|X|<\infty, \mathbb EX=0 and
\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb EY. If also \mathbb EY^2<\infty, its
Pearson kurtosis is\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathbb EX^4}{(\mathbb EX^2)^2}
&=3\frac{\mathbb EY^2}{(\mathbb EY)^2}\\
&=3\left(1+\frac{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}{(\mathbb EY)^2}\right).
\end{aligned}

The Gaussian reference is 3. For fixed mean variance, nonconstant Y
raises kurtosis. This comparison is specific to centered normal variance
mixtures; it is not an ordering of arbitrary distributions by tail risk.

Choose equal probabilities for Y=1-a and Y=1+a, with 0\le a<1.
Conditioning gives variance 1 and fourth moment 3(1+a^2). At a=0.6
these are 1 and 4.08. The density is the average of two Gaussian densities.
Its moment generating function (MGF) and characteristic function are\begin{aligned}
M_X(t)&=\tfrac12e^{(1-a)t^2/2}\\
&\quad+\tfrac12e^{(1+a)t^2/2},\\
\varphi_X(t)&=\tfrac12e^{-(1-a)t^2/2}\\
&\quad+\tfrac12e^{-(1+a)t^2/2}.
\end{aligned}

They follow from the two conditional Gaussian transforms. They are different
functions, even though the mean is zero. For a>0, division by the unit-normal
density \phi(x) gives\begin{gathered}
\frac{f_a(x)}{\phi(x)}
\sim \frac{1}{2\sqrt{1+a}}
\exp\left(\frac{ax^2}{2(1+a)}\right),\\
|x|\to\infty.
\end{gathered}

The narrower component’s ratio tends to zero; the wider component’s ratio
increases without bound. Nevertheless M_X(t) is finite for every real t.
The mixture has more far-tail density than the unit normal and still satisfies
the 

Cramér condition. It is not a power law.
At a=1 the lower state is an atom at zero and the full law no longer has
a Lebesgue density.

Unequal probabilities remove the equal-weight example’s kurtosis ceiling.
For a different worked case, take\begin{gathered}
P(Y=0.5)=0.99,\\
P(Y=50.5)=0.01.
\end{gathered}

Then \mathbb EY=1, \mathbb EY^2=25.75 and kurtosis is 77.25.
All moments and the MGF remain finite. More generally, fixing 0<c<1 and
putting probability 0<p<1 on b=[1-(1-p)c]/p and 1-p on c preserves
\mathbb EY=1, while \mathbb EY^2 diverges as p\downarrow0.
Each fixed p>0 still gives a finite Gaussian mixture. A rare state can
make a finite moment hard to estimate without making it infinite.



Exact mixture densities and two-sided probabilities. All three laws have
variance 1. The rare wide component is visible in the survival plot even
where its contribution to central density is small. No samples or data fits
are used.

records.content:
Three explicit constructions show why the distribution of the mixing
variable matters. All parameters below are local to this section.

Gamma variance. Let Y have gamma shape k>0 and scale 1/k, so
\mathbb EY=1. Integrating its density gives\begin{gathered}
\mathbb EY^r=k^{-r}\frac{\Gamma(k+r)}{\Gamma(k)},\\
r>-k,\\
M_X(t)=\left(1-\frac{t^2}{2k}\right)^{-k},\\
|t|<\sqrt{2k}.
\end{gathered}

For the MGF, condition on Y and integrate e^{t^2Y/2} against the gamma
density. The integral diverges at and beyond the endpoints. All positive
power moments exist, and kurtosis is 3(1+1/k). At k=1, the MGF is that
of a centered Laplace law with scale 1/\sqrt2; this law has exponential
tails. The density calculation below gives the general gamma-mixture decay.

Lognormal variance. Let Y=\exp(\tau U-\tau^2/2), where U is standard
normal, independent of Z, and \tau>0. Completing the square gives\begin{gathered}
\mathbb EY^r=e^{(r^2-r)\tau^2/2},\\
\mathbb E|X|^q=c_q e^{q(q-2)\tau^2/8}.
\end{gathered}

Every positive power moment exists, yet M_X(t)=\mathbb E e^{t^2Y/2}=\infty
for every t\ne0. To see divergence, write the expectation as an integral
over u; its exponent contains a positive multiple of e^{\tau u} minus
u^2/2, and is eventually positive on an infinite half-line. Finite moments
of every order therefore do not imply a finite MGF. Nor does this construction
have a finite power-tail exponent: a regularly varying survival with finite
positive exponent would force sufficiently high moments to diverge.

Gamma precision. Let Q=1/Y have gamma shape \nu/2 and rate \nu/2,
with \nu>0. Integrating the conditional density gives\begin{aligned}
f_X(x)&=\frac{\Gamma((\nu+1)/2)}{\sqrt{\nu\pi}\Gamma(\nu/2)}\\
&\quad\times\left(1+\frac{x^2}{\nu}\right)^{-(\nu+1)/2}.
\end{aligned}

Indeed the integrand is proportional to
q^{(\nu+1)/2-1}e^{-(\nu+x^2)q/2}, a gamma integral. This is Student’s
t law at unit scale. Its density is asymptotic to a positive constant
times |x|^{-\nu-1}; integrating that comparison gives a survival exponent
\alpha=\nu. The moment identity above reduces to an integral of
q^{(\nu-q_0)/2-1} near zero for moment order q_0>0, so
\mathbb E|X|^{q_0}<\infty exactly when q_0<\nu.
For \nu>2 its variance is \nu/(\nu-2), not 1.

These are proved model calculations. SCoFT v4 §4.2, pp. 74–75 supplies the
variance-versus-precision question; it is not a claim that every stochastic
volatility model produces a power law. Recursive uncertainty belongs to a
later treatment and requires a specified limiting construction.

Use 

normal_mixture_absolute_moment, 

normal_mixture_log_abs_survival.import numpy as np
from xmath.incerto.finite_moments import (
    normal_mixture_absolute_moment, normal_mixture_log_abs_survival,
)

for variances, weights in (([1], [1]), ([0.5, 50.5], [0.99, 0.01])):
    m2 = normal_mixture_absolute_moment(2, variances, weights)
    m4 = normal_mixture_absolute_moment(4, variances, weights)
    tail = np.exp(normal_mixture_log_abs_survival(4, variances, weights))
    print(f"Variance / kurtosis / P(|X|>4): {m2:.4g} {m4 / m2**2:.4g} {tail:.4g}")

All moments of these two finite Gaussian mixtures exist.

The script also checks moment formulas and reports a bounded, seeded

Body and shoulder geometry explains which
parts of a density gain or lose under a small variance perturbation.

The following extension permits a moving conditional mean.

For a gamma mixture, let Y\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\lambda,\vartheta)
(shape and scale) and X=\gamma Y+\sqrt{Y}Z. The local parameters satisfy
A>|\gamma|, \lambda>0, and \vartheta=2/(A^2-\gamma^2).
The helper 

univariate_variance_gamma(alpha, beta, lam) uses
alpha for A, beta for \gamma, and lam for \lambda; its alpha
is not the Pareto exponent. Conditioning and the gamma MGF give\begin{gathered}
M_X(t)\\
=\left(1-\vartheta\gamma t-\tfrac12\vartheta t^2\right)^{-\lambda},\\
-A-\gamma<t<A-\gamma,
\end{gathered}\begin{gathered}
\mathbb E[X]=\gamma\lambda\vartheta,\\
\operatorname{Var}(X)=\lambda\vartheta(1+\gamma^2\vartheta).
\end{gathered}

The interval follows by solving the positive-quadratic-base inequality.
The variance follows from conditional variance plus the variance of the
conditional mean. For x\ne0, integrating the conditional Gaussian density
against the gamma density gives\begin{aligned}
f(x)&=\frac{(A^2-\gamma^2)^\lambda |x|^{\lambda-1/2}}
{\sqrt\pi\,\Gamma(\lambda)(2A)^{\lambda-1/2}}\\
&\quad\times K_{\lambda-1/2}(A|x|)e^{\gamma x}.
\end{aligned}

To obtain this expression, substitute \nu=\lambda-1/2,
a=x^2/2, b=A^2/2 in the Bessel integral
\int_0^\infty y^{\nu-1}e^{-a/y-by}\,dy
=2(a/b)^{\nu/2}K_\nu(2\sqrt{ab}) for a,b>0.
The standard Bessel asymptotic K_\nu(z)\sim\sqrt{\pi/(2z)}e^{-z}
then gives right and left density decay rates A-\gamma and A+\gamma,
each with a power factor |x|^{\lambda-1}. These are exponential tails,
not regularly varying ones. The integral representation and special-function
asymptotics are used as standard identities, not proved here


DLMF 10.32.10 and


DLMF 10.40.2.

At the origin, the same density integral is a gamma integral when
\lambda>1/2, givingf(0)=\frac{(A^2-\gamma^2)^\lambda\Gamma(\lambda-1/2)}
{2\sqrt\pi\,\Gamma(\lambda)A^{2\lambda-1}}.

For smaller shapes it diverges: the Bessel limits give a logarithmic
singularity at \lambda=1/2 and an integrable power singularity below it.
Here the small-argument Bessel limits are cited from


DLMF 10.30.2–3. The symmetric case \gamma=0, \lambda=1 reduces to the Laplace density
(A/2)e^{-A|x|}. The general family relationships remain in the


Normix family tour.

Appendix C of 

Taleb (2025), §C.1, pp. 183–185, concerns transforming
a growth rate. The 

fixed-horizon calculation
shows that X=x_m e^{TR} with R\sim\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda) has Pareto
exponent \lambda/T. A distribution over rates must be specified before
claims about the outcome tail follow.

Here is a finite uncertainty extension, proved by conditioning. First choose
a state J with P(J=j)=w_j>0, \sum_jw_j=1. Conditional on J=j,
draw R\sim\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda_j), with \lambda_j>0. For fixed
T>0 and x\ge x_m>0,P(X>x)=\sum_jw_j(x_m/x)^{\lambda_j/T}.

Factoring the smallest power shows that the tail exponent is
\min_j\lambda_j/T, with coefficient equal to the combined weight of
the states attaining that minimum. Tonelli and the conditional moment
formula give, for p>0,\begin{gathered}
\mathbb EX^p=x_m^p\sum_jw_j\frac{\lambda_j}{\lambda_j-pT}\\
\text{if }pT<\min_j\lambda_j;
\end{gathered}

otherwise the moment is infinite. For rates 1 and 3 with equal weights
and T=1, the outcome mean is infinite, although the rate has finite mean
2/3. This is a finite mixture, not an unspecified infinite hierarchy of
uncertainty. A continuous rate mixture near zero needs a separate analysis.

Use

for horizon in (.5, 1):
    means = [pareto_type1(rate/horizon).mean() for rate in (1, 3)]
    print(f"T={horizon:g}: mixture mean={sum(means)/2:.4g}")

2025, ch. 4, §§4.1–4.2, printed pp. 69–75: mixture mechanisms. The
calculations above state their own hypotheses and proofs.

The linked DLMF identities supply the Bessel integral and asymptotics used

A finite sample produces a finite empirical moment in exact arithmetic.
It does not establish that the corresponding population moment exists.
Even when that moment exists, the estimator can have infinite variance or
be dominated by events that most samples miss. We separate these questions
using an exact Pareto model and a finite Gaussian mixture.

The sample notation follows the 

shared canon.
For iid X_i\ge0 and order q>0, write\begin{aligned}
m_q&=\mathbb E X^q,\\
\widehat m_{q,n}&=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i^q.
\end{aligned}

These are raw moments. For a signed variable, replace X^q by |X|^q;
a signed odd moment requires separate integrability conditions.

records.content:
For 

Pareto with \alpha,x_m>0,\begin{aligned}
m_q&=\frac{\alpha x_m^q}{\alpha-q},\\
&\hspace{2em}q<\alpha,\\
m_q&=\infty,\\
&\hspace{2em}q\ge\alpha.
\end{aligned}

Assume q<\alpha. Then the sample moment is unbiased for every n\ge1,
but it has finite variance only if 2q<\alpha. In that regime,\begin{aligned}
n\operatorname{Var}(\widehat m_{q,n})
&=\frac{\alpha x_m^{2q}}{\alpha-2q}\\
&\quad-\left(\frac{\alpha x_m^q}{\alpha-q}\right)^2.
\end{aligned}

We prove both assertions. Linearity gives the expectation whenever m_q
is finite. For 2q<\alpha, independence makes the cross-covariances zero.
For q<\alpha\le2q, nonnegativity gives
\widehat m_{q,n}^2\ge X_1^{2q}/n^2, whose expectation is infinite.
Since the estimator has finite mean, its variance is infinite too. Equality
at 2q=\alpha is excluded by the logarithmic divergence of the Pareto
moment integral.

For example, \alpha=3,x_m=1 gives m_2=3, but
\widehat m_{2,n} has infinite variance at every finite n.
At \alpha=6, m_2=3/2, m_4=3, and the estimator variance is
3/(4n). A simulated finite standard error in the first model cannot
certify the population variance of the estimator.

We prove convergence in probability when m_q<\infty, without a finite
2qth moment. Set T_i=X_i^q and T_i^{(B)}=\min(T_i,B).
For fixed B, Chebyshev’s inequality gives convergence of the average of
T_i^{(B)} to its expectation, because these variables are bounded and iid.
The omitted nonnegative part has expected average
\mathbb E(T_1-B)_+\to0 as B\to\infty. Markov’s inequality controls
that average uniformly in n. For any error tolerance, first choose B
to make this expectation small, then n to control the bounded average.
The triangle inequality proves \widehat m_{q,n}\to m_q in probability.
This argument supplies no uniform rate over all integrable laws.

When m_q=\infty, the stronger almost-sure divergence follows from the


nonnegative infinite-mean theorem, applied to
X_i^q. That linked note proves the result by truncation. Finite observed
values and floating-point overflow are separate matters; neither determines
which population regime applies.

records.content:
Let R_n=\sqrt{\widehat m_{2,n}}. If m_2<\infty, then\begin{gathered}
\mathbb E R_n^2=m_2,\\
\mathbb E R_n\le\sqrt{m_2},\\
\operatorname{Var}(R_n)<\infty.
\end{gathered}

The identity is immediate from the definition. Cauchy–Schwarz gives the
inequality and integrability of R_n; hence its variance is finite.
Thus infinite variance of the empirical second moment does not imply
infinite variance of the empirical root mean square. For the sample
standard deviation s_n^2=n^{-1}\sum(X_i-\bar X_n)^2, the identity
s_n^2=\widehat m_{2,n}-\bar X_n^2\le\widehat m_{2,n} gives the same
finite-second-moment conclusion for s_n. A fixed n/(n-1) correction
for n>1 does not change this conclusion.

The square root can introduce downward bias through concavity. The sample
raw moment remains unbiased. Bias, estimator variance, and the frequency
of an underestimate are different properties.

records.content:
Here we know the center is zero and assume iid X_i\sim N(0,\sigma^2),
with \sigma>0. Compare the root mean square R_n with the
Gaussian-calibrated mean absolute deviation
A_n=\sqrt{\pi/2}\,n^{-1}\sum|X_i|. Both target \sigma under these
assumptions. We can compute their mean squared errors without simulation.

The normal absolute-moment integrals give
\mathbb EA_n=\sigma and
\operatorname{Var}(A_n)=\sigma^2(\pi/2-1)/n.
For T=\sum(X_i/\sigma)^2, changing variables from a normal density gives
a gamma shape 1/2, scale 2 for each square. Independence and the


gamma convolution identity
give shape n/2, scale 2 for T. Integrating \sqrt T against that
density yields\begin{aligned}
b_n&=\frac{\mathbb ER_n}{\sigma}\\
&=\sqrt{\frac2n}\frac{\Gamma((n+1)/2)}{\Gamma(n/2)},\\
\frac{\mathbb E(R_n-\sigma)^2}{\sigma^2}
&=2(1-b_n).
\end{aligned}

The last identity uses \mathbb ER_n^2=\sigma^2. The corresponding MSE
for A_n, divided by \sigma^2, is (\pi/2-1)/n.
These are exact finite-n risks under squared-error loss, including
R_n’s bias. The demo prints them for n=10,100,1000.

This comparison does not carry over unchanged to the rare-state mixture:
\mathbb E|X|=\sqrt{2/\pi}\,\mathbb E\sqrt Y, so the same A_n now
targets \mathbb E\sqrt Y, whereas the population standard deviation is
\sqrt{\mathbb EY}. Jensen’s inequality makes these unequal for
nonconstant Y with finite mean. Changing the model can change both the
sampling error and the target of a calibrated statistic.

and fourth moment is 77.25, so\operatorname{Var}\left(\frac1n\sum X_i^2\right)=\frac{76.25}{n}.

and the empirical second moment has expectation 0.5. At n=50, this event
has probability about 0.605. Rare samples compensate in the unconditional
mean; the raw second moment estimator is still unbiased.

Under an exact iid Pareto model with \alpha>1, the log-excess average has
a gamma density that is positive and continuous at 1. Consequently even
conditional on a finite fit,\begin{gathered}
\mathbb E\left[\frac{x_m}{1-\widehat\xi_n}
\;\middle|\;\widehat\xi_n<1\right]\\
=\infty.
\end{gathered}

The linked note derives that density. Its positive lower bound on a small
left neighborhood of 1 makes the expectation at least a positive multiple
of \int_{1-\delta}^1(1-t)^{-1}\,dt=\infty. The squared estimator diverges
there as well. A concentrated central part of a sampling distribution can
coexist with divergent moments. Simulations must count non-finite fits;
removing them does not remove the singularity of the remaining distribution.
No universal ranking of the sample mean and this plug-in follows.

records.content:
For fixed observations and positive weights w_i summing to 1, define
A_p=(\sum_iw_i|x_i|^p)^{1/p}. For 0<p<q,A_p\le A_q.

We prove this with Jensen’s inequality for the strictly convex function
t\mapsto t^{q/p} on [0,\infty), then take a qth root. Equality holds
exactly when all |x_i| are equal. The inequality also holds below 1;
those expressions are not norms. At fixed positive weights,
A_p\to\max_i|x_i| as p\to\infty: bound the weighted sum above by
M^p and below by w_jM^p at a maximizing coordinate j.

For equal weights and observations (0,0,0,4),
A_1=1, A_2=2, A_4=2\sqrt2, and A_\infty=4.
The order changes which quantity is summarized; a larger value alone
neither proves a power law nor diagnoses estimation failure.

For geometric unit balls, use the unnormalized norm
\|x\|_p=(\sum|x_i|^p)^{1/p}. Its value decreases with p at fixed
x. To prove this for x\ne0, divide each coordinate by \|x\|_p;
the resulting magnitudes are at most 1, so their qth powers sum to at
most their pth powers, namely 1. The p-unit balls therefore expand.
In two dimensions, p=1,2,\infty give a diamond, circle, and square,
with areas 2, \pi, and 4. The factor n^{-1/p} in A_p explains
why its monotonicity goes in the other direction.



Exact geometric contours. These use the sum of powers, whereas the
empirical power mean uses the average of powers. No probability model
is needed for this comparison.

records.content:
If \mu=\mathbb EX and \mathbb E|X|<\infty, then
\mathbb E|X-\mu|\le\mathbb E|X|+|\mu|<\infty.
If the variance is finite, Cauchy–Schwarz gives
\mathbb E|X-\mu|\le\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)}.
Equality requires |X-\mu| to be constant almost surely.
These are unscaled deviations; Gaussian calibration multiplies the mean
absolute deviation by \sqrt{\pi/2}, so that universal inequality does
not apply to the calibrated value.

For example, the symmetric law on \{-1,1\} has standard deviation and
unscaled mean absolute deviation both equal to 1. Its Gaussian-calibrated
Std/MeanAD ratio is \sqrt{2/\pi}<1. The Gaussian benchmark 1 in the


dispersion diagnostic is a model reference,
not a universal lower bound. Mean and median absolute deviations also
answer different questions. Neither universally replaces a second-moment
estimand or dominates every estimator under every loss.

records.content:
For iid integrable observations, let M(n)=\mathbb E|S_n-n\mu| and
assume M(1)>0. The 

kappa note
compares this sum deviation at two sizes. Here the target is the
relative mean absolute error of the sample mean:R(n)=\frac{M(n)}{nM(1)}.

Scaling two parent laws to the same single-observation MAD makes R(n)
a comparison in common units. A Gaussian sample of size n_g has
R_g(n_g)=n_g^{-1/2}. Define the minimum matching integer by\begin{aligned}
\mathcal N_g&=\{n\ge1:R(n)\le n_g^{-1/2}\},\\
n_*&=\min\mathcal N_g.
\end{aligned}

This criterion matches one expectation of an estimation error. It does
not equate variances, quantiles, or confidence coverage. For example,
Markov’s inequality gives only\begin{gathered}
P(|\bar X_n-\mu|>\varepsilon)
\le\frac{M(n)}{n\varepsilon},\\
\varepsilon>0.
\end{gathered}

The bound may be loose. There is no universal kappa cutoff that certifies
a normal confidence interval. Under variance matching, every iid law
with the same finite variance has the same variance of its sample mean
at the same size; that is a different comparison.

records.content:
We prove that R(n) is nonincreasing. Center n+1 observations and
form the n+1 averages that each omit one observation. Their average is
the full (n+1)-observation average. Convexity of absolute value and
identical distributions therefore give\mathbb E|\bar X_{n+1}-\mu|
\le\mathbb E|\bar X_n-\mu|.

It also tends to zero under integrability. To see this, clip each centered
variable to [-B,B] and center the clipped variable again. Its average
has expected absolute value at most its standard deviation divided by
\sqrt n. The remaining centered part has expected absolute value at
most twice the expected clipping error, uniformly in n, and this tends
to zero as B\to\infty. First take n\to\infty, then B\to\infty.
Thus n_* exists for every finite integer n_g under these assumptions.
A finite computational search can still stop before reaching it.

Use 

gaussian_equivalent_n
with deterministic population MADs, such as


student_sum_mad and

    print(f"{name}: n={n}")
    for j in (n-1, n):
        print(f"  n={j}: relative error={mad(j)/(j*mad(1)):.4f}")

If a model has the exact power relation
M(n)/M(1)=n^{1/(2-\kappa)} at every size, with constant \kappa<1,
solving the matching inequality gives\begin{aligned}
n_*&=\left\lceil n_g^{\,p}\right\rceil,\\
p&=\frac{2-\kappa}{2(1-\kappa)}.
\end{aligned}

For an integrable stable law, \kappa=2-\alpha and
p=\alpha/[2(\alpha-1)]. At \alpha=1.5 this is p=1.5.
For a general law, substituting a small-size kappa into this formula is a
heuristic. Its kappa changes with size, so the exact equation is implicit.
The cubic Student and exponential examples use their full MAD curves.

For independent, identically distributed centered exposures X_i-\mu,
the equally weighted portfolio fluctuation is
n^{-1}\sum_i(X_i-\mu). Its MAD is exactly M(n)/n.
The 

aggregation figure therefore
also quantifies this narrowly specified diversification calculation.
A smooth sample path or a visually concentrated center can still conceal
substantial expected absolute error.

Dependence changes the result. If every exposure equals the same integrable
random variable Y, then the portfolio average is Y at every size and
its MAD never decreases. More generally, writing X_i=C+\epsilon_i with
an integrable common component C independent of iid centered integrable
\epsilon_i gives an average converging to C in L^1. Its MAD about
\mathbb EC consequently tends to \mathbb E|C-\mathbb EC|: apply
the reverse triangle inequality and the L^1 averaging argument above.
Increasing the number of components cannot remove the common fluctuation.

Two coordinates can have the same marginal distributions and quite different
joint extremes. 

Density geometry
compares their contours; this note constructs a joint law and asks which
dependence summaries exist. The context is SCoFT v4 §§6.1–6.7,

the semicircle limit is a separately cited theorem.

We use dimension d, location vector \mu, positive definite scatter matrix
\Sigma, and Student degrees of freedom \nu>0. Scatter specifies shape
and scale; it is a covariance matrix only when we explicitly say so.
Here I_d is the identity matrix; all densities use Lebesgue measure.
Symbols follow the 

shared notation.

An elliptical law has characteristic function\varphi_X(t)=e^{it^T\mu}\Psi(t^T\Sigma t),

for t\in\mathbb R^d, where \Psi is a scalar function for which this is a
characteristic function.
The definition can allow positive semidefinite \Sigma and singular laws;
our density calculations use positive definite \Sigma.
It does not require moments or independence of coordinates.

Let Z\sim N_d(0,I_d), let Y>0 be independent of Z, and choose
AA^T=\Sigma. The 

normal variance-mixture construction
extends toX=\mu+\sqrt Y\,AZ,\varphi_X(t)=e^{it^T\mu}\mathbb E e^{-Yt^T\Sigma t/2}.

Conditioning on Y proves ellipticality. It also proves
\operatorname{Cov}(X)=\mathbb EY\,\Sigma when \mathbb EY<\infty.
For a deterministic matrix B and vector b, substitution of B^Tt
in the characteristic function gives location B\mu+b and scatter
B\Sigma B^T for BX+b. This proves closure under linear maps, including
singular images. It does not assert that every stable vector is elliptical.

For example, let Y equal 1-a or 1+a with equal probabilities,
0<a<1. Covariance remains \Sigma, whereas the density at \mu is
multiplied, relative to N_d(\mu,\Sigma), by\frac{(1-a)^{-d/2}+(1+a)^{-d/2}}2>1.

Strict convexity of y\mapsto y^{-d/2} proves the inequality.
This finite mixture has finite exponential moments in every direction:
its MGF is an average of two Gaussian MGFs. Increased central density
and kurtosis do not imply an asymptotic power tail.

Take a precision G=1/Y with gamma shape and rate both \nu/2.
Conditioning on G=g gives the normal density with covariance \Sigma/g.
Writing q=(x-\mu)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu), integration over g>0 gives\begin{aligned}
f_d(x)
&=\frac{(\nu/2)^{\nu/2}}
 {(2\pi)^{d/2}|\Sigma|^{1/2}\Gamma(\nu/2)}\\
&\quad\times\int_0^\infty
 g^{(\nu+d)/2-1}e^{-(\nu+q)g/2}\,dg\\
&=\frac{\Gamma((\nu+d)/2)}
 {\Gamma(\nu/2)(\nu\pi)^{d/2}|\Sigma|^{1/2}}\\
&\quad\times\left(1+\frac q\nu\right)^{-(\nu+d)/2}.
\end{aligned}

The gamma integral proves both the constant and normalization, since the
integrated conditional densities each have mass one. Every nonzero linear
projection is a univariate Student with the same \nu, location b^T\mu,
and scale \sqrt{b^T\Sigma b}. This follows directly from b^TAZ being
normal, independent of the same G.

The 

univariate moment gate
therefore applies to each coordinate: a mean exists for \nu>1, and
finite covariance requires \nu>2. Gamma integration gives\begin{gathered}
\mathbb E G^{-1}=\frac{\nu}{\nu-2},\\
\operatorname{Cov}(X)=\frac{\nu}{\nu-2}\Sigma\quad(\nu>2).
\end{gathered}

For \nu\le2, a finite sample scatter matrix can still be calculated;
it does not estimate a finite population covariance matrix under this model.

Set d=2, \mu=0, and \Sigma=I_2. The two marginal Student laws
share their random precision. Bayes’ rule givesG\mid X_1=x\sim\operatorname{Gamma}\left(\frac{\nu+1}{2},
                                      \frac{\nu+x^2}{2}\right).

Mixing the conditional normal for X_2 thus gives a Student law with
\nu+1 degrees of freedom and scale \sqrt{(\nu+x^2)/(\nu+1)}.
This scale varies with x on sets of positive probability, which proves
dependence for every finite \nu>0. For \nu>2 the Pearson correlation
is nevertheless zero. For \nu\le2, zero off-diagonal scatter is not
a zero Pearson correlation: that population coefficient is undefined.

There is also a direct joint-tail test without moment assumptions. For
u>0, put p_u(y)=2\bar\Phi(u/\sqrt y), with \bar\Phi the standard
normal survival. Conditional independence gives\begin{aligned}
&P(|X_1|>u,|X_2|>u)\\
&\quad-P(|X_1|>u)^2
=\operatorname{Var}(p_u(Y))>0.
\end{aligned}

The variance is positive because p_u is strictly increasing and the
mixing law is nondegenerate. Independent Student coordinates have zero
excess instead. These bounded indicator probabilities exist even for Cauchy
marginals. They do not by themselves specify an asymptotic tail-dependence
coefficient.

For a bivariate density f with marginals f_1,f_2, mutual information is\begin{aligned}
&I(X_1;X_2)\\
&=\int_{\mathbb R^2}f(x_1,x_2)\\
&\quad\times\log\frac{f(x_1,x_2)}{f_1(x_1)f_2(x_2)}\,dx_1dx_2.
\end{aligned}

It is KL divergence from the joint law to the product of its marginals.
The 

KL inequality
gives nonnegativity and equality exactly at independence. No variance
appears in the definition, but integrability must still be checked.

We derive the Student value. Write h_d=-\mathbb E\log f_d(X) and let
\psi_0(z)=d\log\Gamma(z)/dz denote the digamma function, distinct from
the shared canon’s log-partition symbol. In whitened polar coordinates,
Q=(X-\mu)^T\Sigma^{-1}(X-\mu) satisfiesU=\frac{Q}{\nu+Q}\sim\operatorname{Beta}(d/2,\nu/2).

Indeed the radial density is proportional to
q^{d/2-1}(1+q/\nu)^{-(\nu+d)/2}; the displayed substitution gives
the beta density. Differentiating its normalizing integral in the second
parameter gives
\mathbb E\log(1+Q/\nu)=\psi_0((\nu+d)/2)-\psi_0(\nu/2).
The differentiation is justified on compact subsets of positive parameters
by integrable endpoint powers times |\log(1-u)|.
The beta integral is the cited input
(

DLMF 5.12.1). Substitution into the
normalized log density now proves\begin{aligned}
&h_d(\nu,\Sigma)\\
&=\log\frac{\Gamma(\nu/2)}{\Gamma((\nu+d)/2)}\\
&+\frac d2\log(\nu\pi)+\frac12\log|\Sigma|\\
&+\frac{\nu+d}{2}
  \left[\psi_0\!\left(\frac{\nu+d}{2}\right)-\psi_0\!\left(\frac\nu2\right)\right].
\end{aligned}

All these logarithmic expectations are finite for \nu>0. Thus subtracting
entropies is legitimate even when no second moment exists. For unit diagonal
scatter and off-diagonal entry \rho, |\rho|<1,I_\nu(\rho)=-\frac12\log(1-\rho^2)+\lambda_\nu,\lambda_\nu=2h_1(\nu,1)-h_2(\nu,I_2)>0.

The determinant gives the first term; the earlier dependence proof gives
strict positivity of the second. Independent rescaling of either coordinate
cancels from the entropy difference. At \nu=1,
h_1=\log(4\pi) and h_2=\log(2\pi)+3, so
\lambda_1=\log(8\pi)-3\approx0.224171 nats. The Gaussian analogue
has only -\tfrac12\log(1-\rho^2). A single observed sample correlation
near zero cannot establish independence in either model.

exceedances above the independent-marginal probability. All displayed quantities are
