For two nonzero finite data vectors x,y\in\mathbb R^n, the uncentered
cosine is r_0=x^Ty/(\|x\|\|y\|). Cauchy–Schwarz proves |r_0|\le1.
Pearson’s sample correlation applies this formula to x-\bar x\mathbf1
and y-\bar y\mathbf1 and requires both vectors to be nonconstant.
The two statistics are different. A constant column makes the centered
coefficient undefined, rather than zero.

Hold n-1 observations fixed and replace the last pair by (t,ct),
where c\ne0 and n\ge2. For the uncentered cosine the leading
numerator is ct^2, and the norm product is |c|t^2.
For the centered statistic, write H=I_n-\mathbf1\mathbf1^T/n.
Here e_n is the last coordinate unit vector and \mathbf1 is the
all-ones vector. The leading vectors are tHe_n and ctHe_n with
\|He_n\|^2=1-1/n>0. Both coefficients therefore tend to
\operatorname{sign}(c) as t\to\infty. This is a deterministic
contamination limit at fixed sample size, not an iid sampling theorem.

Our repeated Student samples below compare \nu=1.5 and \nu=5 with
scatter parameter \rho=0.6. Only the latter has population Pearson
correlation 0.6. Sampling quantiles quantify this finite experiment;
they are neither confidence intervals nor a universal convergence rate.

Let W_n be the upper-left n\times n block of one infinite real
symmetric matrix, with independent identically distributed
entries on and above the diagonal, mean zero and variance one, mirrored
below it. The semicircle theorem says that the empirical eigenvalue
measure of W_n/\sqrt n converges weakly almost surely to density
\sqrt{4-x^2}/(2\pi) on [-2,2]. This is a cited result, not proved
here: 

Tao, 254A Notes 4, Theorem 1 and §1 truncation reduction.
Finite variance suffices for this empirical-measure limit; an infinite
fourth moment does not automatically invalidate it. Convergence of the
largest eigenvalue is a different question.

Two finite identities explain the sensitivity to a large entry. For any
real symmetric matrix M with eigenvalues \ell_1,\ldots,\ell_n,\sum_j\ell_j^2=\operatorname{tr}(M^2)=\sum_{i,j}M_{ij}^2,\max_j|\ell_j|=\|M\|_2\ge\max_{i,j}|M_{ij}|.

Orthogonal diagonalization proves the first identity, and
|e_i^TMe_j|\le\|M\|_2 proves the second. A single large entry
therefore forces a large spectral radius. Neither identity proves a limiting
heavy-tail spectral law. Nor does a Wigner theorem apply directly to a
sample covariance matrix D^TD/n, with D a centered data matrix;
that matrix is positive semidefinite and has a different construction.



Twelve independent 80\times80 symmetric matrices per law, all divided by
\sqrt{80}. Each thin curve is a matrix’s empirical CDF, computed from all
80 eigenvalues. The Student-1.5 viewport is [-10,10]; 39 eigenvalues lie below
it and 40 above it, out of 960 across all twelve matrices. The CDFs keep those
values in their ranks and denominators. The normal and Student-3 entries have
variance one; Student 1.5 has unit Student scale and infinite variance. The common divisor in the
last panel is a finite comparison convention, not a proposed limit scaling.
The dashed semicircle CDF appears only in the two finite-variance panels.

Consider X\sim N(0,1) and an independent error \varepsilon with
\mathbb E\varepsilon=0 and 0<\tau^2=\mathbb E\varepsilon^2<\infty.
Define the response V=b+aX+\varepsilon; the letter Y remains reserved
for mixing variance. Independence gives\begin{gathered}
\operatorname{Cov}(X,V)=a,\\
\operatorname{Var}(V)=a^2+\tau^2,\\
R^2_{\mathrm{pop}}=\operatorname{Corr}(X,V)^2
=\frac{a^2}{a^2+\tau^2}.
\end{gathered}

For iid pairs, the strong law applied to X,V,X^2,V^2,XV proves that
sample correlation squared converges almost surely to this value. The
product is integrable by Cauchy–Schwarz. In a fitted simple ordinary
least-squares regression with an intercept and nonconstant columns,
write S_{AB}=\sum_i(A_i-\bar A)(B_i-\bar B) for centered sums.
The normal equations give \hat a=S_{XV}/S_{XX} and fitted centered
response \hat a(X_i-\bar X). Its sum of squares is
S_{XV}^2/S_{XX}, so fitted R_n^2=S_{XV}^2/(S_{XX}S_{VV})=r_n^2.
This proves the connection to the population target. For the expectation
statement, extend R_n^2 by zero on samples with a constant column.
The strong law makes both denominators positive eventually almost surely;
this bounded extension therefore satisfies
\mathbb E R_n^2\to R^2_{\mathrm{pop}} by bounded convergence.
The coefficient on a degenerate sample itself remains undefined.
The convergence argument supplies no O(n^{-2}) error or universal upward-bias claim.

Cook (2026), in “Dogs and fat tails”, studies the distribution of dog-name frequencies.
Bella and Luna have plenty of company, while thousands of names appear only
once.  A lognormal describes the overall pattern
reasonably well.  Here we draw the rank-frequency picture too, then examine how tail estimates change across thresholds.

The source is the 

NYC Dog Licensing Dataset


New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene, 2026.  Each source row is an active license period, not
necessarily a unique dog.  A renewal within the same year can add another row
for the same animal.  We therefore call the aggregated values license-period
frequencies, not dog counts.

We use the full public dataset, not a little row sample.  The


Socrata API
does the compacting for us: trim and uppercase the names, drop missing-name
placeholders, and return one count per name.  The result is only about 35,000
rows instead of hundreds of thousands of license records, so the complete aggregate is
small enough to travel with the page.

Let x_i be the number of included license-period records attached to the
ith observed normalized name.  The sample for the tail diagnostics isx_1,\ldots,x_n,

where n is the number of distinct names in the snapshot.  A large x_i
means that a name is popular.  Names that do not occur in the licensing data
are absent, so this is a zero-truncated frequency spectrum rather than a sample
of all possible names.

A whole-sample lognormal fit and a tail estimate answer different questions.
The first summarizes all positive frequencies.  The second requires a high
threshold and asks whether the observations above it behave approximately like
a regularly varying right tail.  We use the


Hill estimator and a generalized Pareto shape
fit across many candidate thresholds, following


Tail Threshold Selection.  No
body/shoulder boundary supplies that threshold automatically.

Sort names from most to least frequent, give them ranks 1,2,\ldots,n, and
plot rank against frequency.  A power law would look roughly straight on
log-log axes.  The dashed line is an ordinary least-squares fit in log space;
it is a visual summary, not a claim that dog naming follows an exact law.

The survival plot compares the data with the blog’s global lognormal baseline.
Below it, two roomier panels use only upper frequencies and expose the
threshold choice.  The generalized Pareto fit uses the


GPD shape parameter \xi; the Hill
panel reports the Pareto tail exponent
\widehat\alpha=1/\widehat\xi.  These symbols follow the shared


notation table.

Let X have a 

Pareto Type I distribution with
lower cutoff x_m>0 and tail exponent \alpha>0:\bar F(x)=\mathbb P(X>x)=\left(\frac{x_m}{x}\right)^\alpha,
\qquad x\ge x_m.

For any moment order p>0,\mathbb E[X^p] < \infty
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
p<\alpha.

When p<\alpha,\mathbb E[X^p]=\frac{\alpha x_m^p}{\alpha-p}.

At p=\alpha, the truncated moment diverges logarithmically.  For
p>\alpha, it diverges as a power of the upper cutoff.  In particular, the
Pareto mean exists only for \alpha>1, and the variance exists only for
\alpha>2.

Here \bar F denotes survival probability and \mathbb E denotes
expectation; p is a positive moment order.

We prove the Pareto Type I moment boundary and the moment formula by direct
integration.  The same calculation also explains the logarithmic boundary and
power-divergent regimes in the truncated-moment section.  The broader
regularly varying moment test is handled by 

Karamata’s Theorem.

For x\ge x_m, the Pareto density isf(x)=\alpha x_m^\alpha x^{-(\alpha+1)}.

For p>0,\mathbb E[X^p]
=
\int_{x_m}^{\infty}x^p\alpha x_m^\alpha x^{-(\alpha+1)}\,dx
=
\alpha x_m^\alpha
\int_{x_m}^{\infty}x^{p-\alpha-1}\,dx.

The integral converges exactly when p-\alpha-1<-1, equivalently
p<\alpha.  Evaluating the convergent case gives\alpha x_m^\alpha
\cdot\frac{x_m^{p-\alpha}}{\alpha-p}
=
\frac{\alpha x_m^p}{\alpha-p}.

Adding \alpha+1 to both sides proves the algebraic equivalence
p-\alpha-1<-1 \Longleftrightarrow p<\alpha.

This exact Pareto calculation is the simplest instance of the


Karamata moment test for regularly varying tails.

For a finite upper cutoff b\ge x_m, defineM_p(b)=\mathbb E[X^p\mathbf 1_{\{X\le b\}}].

Direct integration givesM_p(b)=
\begin{cases}

How quickly does the chance of a large observation fall as we raise the
threshold? The Pareto law models a positive quantity above a lower cutoff.
Its tail exponent \alpha controls that rate: smaller exponents give more
probability to very large observations. Doubling any threshold in its support
multiplies the survival probability by 2^{-\alpha}.

Basic probability and integration are enough for this page. A survival
probability means \mathbb P(X>x). The formulas below define the CDF F,
density f, and quantile Q; the survival table illustrates the exponent.

Let X be a positive random variable with lower cutoff x_m>0 and tail
exponent \alpha>0.  The Pareto Type I distribution is defined by\bar F(x)=\mathbb P(X>x)=
\begin{cases}
1, & x < x_m,\\
\left(\frac{x_m}{x}\right)^\alpha, & x\ge x_m.
\end{cases}

For x\ge x_m, the CDF, density, and quantile function areF(x)=1-\left(\frac{x_m}{x}\right)^\alpha,
\qquad
f(x)=\alpha x_m^\alpha x^{-(\alpha+1)},
\qquad
Q(q)=x_m(1-q)^{-1/\alpha},\quad 0<q<1.

The exact Pareto tail is 

regularly varying
with index -\alpha.  Its raw moment of order p>0 exists exactly when
p<\alpha:\mathbb E[X^p]=\frac{\alpha x_m^p}{\alpha-p},\qquad p<\alpha.

In particular,\mathbb E[X]=\frac{\alpha x_m}{\alpha-1},\qquad \alpha>1,

and\operatorname{Var}(X)
=\frac{\alpha x_m^2}{(\alpha-1)^2(\alpha-2)},\qquad \alpha>2.

Thus the mean exists only for \alpha>1, and a finite variance exists only
for \alpha>2. Here p is the moment order and q is the quantile level.

Above its lower cutoff, the Pareto law has no characteristic upper scale.  Once
both thresholds lie in the Pareto tail, multiplying the threshold by a fixed factor changes the exceedance
probability by a fixed power:\frac{\bar F(tx)}{\bar F(x)}=t^{-\alpha},\qquad t>0,\; x\ge x_m,\; tx\ge x_m.

Smaller \alpha gives a larger exceedance probability at every x>x_m.
The consequences for sums depend on whether the sample size or the exceedance
threshold grows; moment existence also depends on the moment order.

The density also shows how the distribution piles mass near the lower cutoff
while leaving a long right tail. Its values and scaling make this explicit.

At the cutoff, f(x_m)=\alpha/x_m. For x\ge x_m,\frac{f(2x)}{f(x)}=2^{-(\alpha+1)}.

This density exponent differs by one from the survival exponent.

Larger \alpha concentrates more mass near x_m and makes
the density decay faster.  Smaller \alpha keeps more visible mass far from the
cutoff.

so a log-log survival plot is a straight line with slope -\alpha:\log \bar F(x)=\alpha\log x_m-\alpha\log x.

The same scaling appears numerically. For a fixed multiplier t>0, the
ratio \bar F(tx)/\bar F(x) depends only on t, provided both
x\ge x_m and tx\ge x_m. The identity follows by canceling (x_m/x)^\alpha.

For example, with \alpha=1.16, doubling any threshold in the support
multiplies survival by 2^{-1.16}\approx0.4475. This is a direct evaluation
of the scaling identity, not an empirical estimate.

For a positive moment order p, the exact Pareto formula is\mathbb E[X^p]=\frac{\alpha x_m^p}{\alpha-p}\quad (p<\alpha),

and the moment is infinite for p\ge\alpha. The


Pareto moment theorem gives the direct
integration proof and the truncated-moment formulas and table. Truncation
makes each truncated population moment finite: raising the upper cutoff reveals
whether it approaches a limit, grows logarithmically at p=\alpha, or grows
as a power for p>\alpha.

For a general 

regularly varying tail,
\bar F(x)=x^{-\alpha}L(x), the boundary p=\alpha depends on L.


Karamata’s theorem explains this distinction; the
exact Pareto boundary always diverges.

The moment-existence thresholds give a concrete example:

With x_m=1 and \alpha=1.16, the mean is
1.16/(1.16-1)=7.25 and the second raw moment is infinite; the variance
is therefore infinite.

For simulation, inverse transform sampling givesX=x_m U^{-1/\alpha},\qquad U\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1).

When x_m is known and the observations are independent and identically
distributed exact Pareto draws, the maximum-likelihood estimator is\widehat\alpha=\frac{n}{\sum_{i=1}^n\log(X_i/x_m)}.

This formula requires a positive denominator, which holds almost surely under
the continuous model. If every observation equals x_m, the likelihood has
no finite maximizer; it increases as \alpha\to\infty.

This estimator is not a license to fit an exact Pareto from the sample minimum:
empirical tail thresholds are rarely known and must be diagnosed separately.

The 

symmetric shifted double Pareto model
extends the tail construction to signed observations.

For u\ge x_m and y\ge0, cancellation of Pareto survival probabilities
proves the conditional excess law:P(X-u>y\mid X>u)=\frac{\bar F(u+y)}{\bar F(u)}
=\left(1+\frac yu\right)^{-\alpha}.

This is an exact 

generalized Pareto survival
with shape \xi=1/\alpha and scale u/\alpha. It holds at every threshold
u\ge x_m for this model; no limiting approximation is required.
Integrating the nonnegative excess survival givese(u)=\mathbb E[X-u\mid X>u]=\frac{u}{\alpha-1},\qquad
\mathbb E[X\mid X>u]=\frac{\alpha u}{\alpha-1},\quad \alpha>1.

Both expectations are infinite for 0<\alpha\le1, since the integral of
(1+y/u)^{-\alpha} diverges. The first expectation is the


mean excess; the second includes the
threshold itself. In particular, their ratio to u is different.

We also prove the distinction between tail probability and tail contribution
to the mean. For any nonnegative X and u\ge0, the pointwise identity
X\mathbf1_{\{X>u\}}=u\mathbf1_{\{X>u\}}+(X-u)_+ and Tonelli’s theorem
give\mathbb E[X\mathbf1_{\{X>u\}}]
=u\bar F(u)+\int_u^\infty\bar F(v)\,dv.

The equality holds in the extended nonnegative reals, including atoms at
u. For Pareto with \alpha>1 it becomes
\bar F(u)\alpha u/(\alpha-1). For \alpha=3/2, x_m=1, and u=4,
the probability is 1/8, the mean excess is 8, the conditional mean is
12, and the tail contribution is 3/2. Replacing that contribution by
u\bar F(u)=1/2 would discard the entire excess integral.

We prove the estimator stated above for n\ge1 iid exact Pareto observations,
known x_m>0, and observed x_i\ge x_m. Let
D=\sum_i\log(x_i/x_m). Terms independent of \alpha can be omitted from
the log likelihood, leaving\ell(\alpha)=n\log\alpha-\alpha D+\text{constant},\qquad
\ell'(\alpha)=\frac n\alpha-D,\qquad
\ell''(\alpha)=-\frac n{\alpha^2}<0.

If D>0, the unique maximizer is n/D. If D=0, every observation equals
x_m and \ell increases without bound as \alpha\to\infty. Observations
below x_m are outside this model’s support. A threshold estimated from the
same sample changes the problem; this proof supplies no guarantee for that fit.

Let X_1,X_2,\ldots be iid Pareto Type I variables with the same
\alpha>0 and x_m>0, and put S_n=\sum_{i=1}^nX_i and
M_n=\max_{1\le i\le n}X_i. For a growing sample, the


max-to-sum ratio has three regimes:

If \alpha>1, then M_n/S_n\to0 almost surely. The linked
finite-mean proof gives S_n/n\to\mathbb E[X]>0 and M_n/n\to0
almost surely, so their quotient tends to zero.

If 0<\alpha<1, then M_n/S_n\xrightarrow{d}R_\alpha, where
R_\alpha has a nondegenerate distribution on (0,1). In particular,
the ratio does not tend to zero in probability, nor does it tend to one.
This limit theorem is cited rather than proved here


Darling, 1952, Theorem 5.1.


Kevei and Mason (2014), p. 632
restate the iid result and give the corresponding sum/maximum limit law;
our ratio is its reciprocal.

If \alpha=1, the mean is infinite but M_n/S_n\to0 in probability.
More precisely, M_n/(x_m n) is bounded in probability and
S_n/(x_m n\log n)\to1 in probability. The calculation below proves
these exact-Pareto assertions; it does not assert almost-sure convergence
of the ratio.

For every \alpha>0, a different limit holds when the integer n\ge1
is fixed and the threshold grows:\mathbb P(S_n>x)\sim\mathbb P(M_n>x)
\sim n\mathbb P(X>x),\qquad x\to\infty.

This is the 

subexponential rare-event
statement: a fixed-size sum exceeds a sufficiently high threshold mainly when
one summand exceeds it. It holds even when \alpha>1 and the largest share
vanishes along growing samples. For moments, the separate exact criterion is
\mathbb E[X^p]<\infty if and only if p<\alpha, for p>0, as proved in


Pareto Moment Existence.

We prove the two normalizations used above for \alpha=1.
For z>0 and sufficiently large n, independence gives\mathbb P\!\left(\frac{M_n}{x_m n}\le z\right)
=\left(1-\frac{1}{nz}\right)^n\longrightarrow e^{-1/z}.

For the sum, write V_i=X_i/x_m and, for n\ge3, set b_n=n\log n and
T_{i,n}=V_i\mathbf1_{\{V_i\le b_n\}}. Integration of the density
v^{-2} on [1,b_n] gives
\mathbb E[T_{i,n}]=\log b_n and
\mathbb E[T_{i,n}^2]=b_n-1. Hence\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\frac{\sum_{i=1}^nT_{i,n}}{n\log n}\right)
\le\frac{b_n}{n(\log n)^2}=\frac{1}{\log n}\longrightarrow0.

The normalized expectation \log b_n/\log n tends to 1.
Chebyshev’s inequality gives convergence in probability for the truncated sum.
The union bound \mathbb P(\max_{i\le n}V_i>b_n)\le n/b_n=1/\log n
transfers that convergence to S_n/(x_m n\log n). Dividing the tight
normalized maximum by this normalized sum and by \log n proves
M_n/S_n\to0 in probability.

We extend the two-summand bound on the subexponentiality page to prove the
displayed fixed-n result. The case n=1 is immediate. For fixed n\ge2,
choose h=x_m(x/x_m)^\gamma with 1/2<\gamma<1. If S_n>x but
M_n\le x, either one observation lies in (x-(n-1)h,x], or at least two
observations exceed h. Otherwise the sum is at most x. Thus\mathbb P(S_n>x,\ M_n\le x)
\le n\bigl[\bar F(x-(n-1)h)-\bar F(x)\bigr]
  +\binom n2\bar F(h)^2.

After division by \bar F(x), the first bracket tends to zero because
h/x\to0; the second tail ratio is
(x/x_m)^{\alpha(1-2\gamma)}\to0.
Finally, \mathbb P(M_n>x)=1-(1-\bar F(x))^n\sim n\bar F(x).
Nonnegativity makes \{M_n>x\} a subset of \{S_n>x\}, and the
negligible residual probability proves the sum-tail equivalence.

The sum and product discussions in SCoFT v4 §§5.2.1–5.2.2, pp. 98–100


Taleb, 2025, require different assumptions. Here we prove a bounded
claim about sums and exact formulas for independent Pareto products.

Fix n<\infty, positive weights w_i, and nonnegative X_i with
P(X_i>x)=x^{-\alpha_i}L_i(x) eventually, where \alpha_i>0
and each L_i is slowly varying.
Dependence is unrestricted. For S=\sum_{i=1}^n w_iX_i,\max_i P(X_i>x/w_i)\le P(S>x)
\le\sum_{i=1}^nP(X_i>x/(nw_i)).

The lower bound uses nonnegativity; the upper bound holds because a sum
above x has some term above x/n. Put a=\min_i\alpha_i.
The 

logarithmic regular-variation consequence
makes both bounds x^{-a+o(1)}, so
\log P(S>x)/\log x\to-a. These bounds establish a logarithmic
exponent, not a limiting survival constant or full regular variation of
every dependent sum. If one allows signed variables, take a symmetric
power-tailed V and (X_1,X_2)=(V,-V): both have right power tails but
their sum is identically zero.

For products, let X_1,X_2 be independent unit-cutoff Pareto variables
with exponents a,b>0. The symbols a,b are local exponents in this
two-law calculation. For z\ge1, condition on X_1 to obtainP(X_1X_2>z)=z^{-a}+a z^{-b}\int_1^z t^{b-a-1}\,dt
=\begin{cases}
\dfrac{b z^{-a}-a z^{-b}}{b-a},&a\ne b,\\[6pt]
z^{-a}(1+a\log z),&a=b.
\end{cases}

For unequal exponents the smaller one determines the leading power.
Equal exponents introduce a logarithmic factor, which is slowly varying
but never constant. With a=1, b=2, the survival is 2/z-1/z^2;
with a=b=1, it is (1+\log z)/z.
For other Pareto minima, apply the formula to
X_1X_2/(x_{m,1}x_{m,2}).

Independence cannot be suppressed: X_2=X_1 gives the square, with
exponent a/2. Multiplication by a dependent bounded variable can even
remove the tail: X_2=1/X_1 gives product one. Claims that multiplication
always preserves the heavier tail therefore need additional hypotheses.
The 

power-transformation proof
handles deterministic powers separately.

Empirical data rarely follows an exact Pareto law from its minimum value.  A
tail model needs a threshold choice, diagnostic plots, and sensitivity checks.

A finite theoretical mean can still be practically hard to estimate when
\alpha is close to 1.  The issue is pre-asymptotic behavior, not merely the
formal existence of \mathbb E[X].

The exact failure mode depends on the moment order.  At p=\alpha, the
cutoff moment grows like \log b; for p>\alpha, it grows like

The regime question in SCoFT v4 appendix A, §A.1, pp. 122–124


Taleb, 2025, does not by itself specify a Pareto law.
Here is an example that does. With probability
w\in(0,1], draw a Pareto variable with cutoff x_m>0 and exponent
\alpha>0; otherwise draw a uniform variable on [0,x_m].
For u\ge x_m, conditioning on the regime provesP(X>u)=w(x_m/u)^\alpha.

For every positive order q, the mixture moment is
(1-w)x_m^q/(q+1)+w\mathbb E[X_{\rm Pareto}^q].
The 

existing moment proof therefore
implies finiteness exactly when q<\alpha. A small positive mixture
weight changes the survival constant but not the exponent or moment gate.
At w=0 the model becomes bounded and all positive moments exist.

With w=0.02, x_m=1, \alpha=3/2, survival at u=4 is
0.0025, the mean is 0.55, and the second moment is infinite.
These are population values; they do not predict which tail observations
will occur in a small sample. The 

catalog’s normal location mixture
has a different tail class even when its regimes are widely separated.

Let F be a distribution function with finite or infinite right endpoint
x_F=\sup\{x:F(x)<1\}.  For a high threshold u<x_F, define the conditional
excess distributionF_u(y)=\mathbb P(X-u\le y\mid X>u)
=\frac{F(u+y)-F(u)}{1-F(u)},
\qquad 0\le y<x_F-u.

If F is in the maximum domain of attraction of an extreme-value law with
extreme-value index \xi, then there is a positive scale function \beta(u)
such that\sup_{0\le y<x_F-u}
\left|F_u(y)-G_{\xi,\beta(u)}(y)\right|
\to 0,
\qquad u\uparrow x_F.

The comparison is over the excess support, using the full GPD CDF: for
\xi<0, set G_{\xi,\beta}(y)=1 at and beyond -\beta/\xi.  The generalized Pareto term
has scale \beta>0 and isG_{\xi,\beta}(y)
=
1-\left(1+\frac{\xi y}{\beta}\right)^{-1/\xi},
\qquad \xi\ne0,

on the support where 1+\xi y/\beta>0, andG_{0,\beta}(y)=1-e^{-y/\beta}

for \xi=0.  The theorem is the asymptotic justification for the
peaks-over-threshold model: sufficiently high threshold exceedances are modeled
by a 

generalized Pareto distribution.

X denotes a draw from F, u the threshold, x_F its right endpoint,
\xi the extreme-value index, and \beta(u)>0 the excess scale.
The maximum-domain-of-attraction assumption means that for iid draws,
some a_n>0 and b_n give (M_n-b_n)/a_n\Rightarrow H_{\xi,0,1}.
Here M_n is the sample maximum and \Rightarrow is convergence in
distribution. The GEV page defines H. See 

Shared notation.

Block-maxima theory says that properly normalized maxima have only a small
number of possible limiting shapes, collected in the


Generalized Extreme-Value Distribution.
The Pickands-Balkema-de Haan theorem says the matching threshold view has the
same discipline: once we condition on being far enough into the tail, the
remaining excess has an approximately


Generalized Pareto Distribution.

For fat-tail work, the case \xi>0 is the main bridge.  It corresponds to a


regularly varying right tail with exponent
\alpha=1/\xi.  The theorem does not say every high observation is generated
by a clean 

Pareto law.  It says the excess
distribution over moving high thresholds has a universal limit shape under the
same domain-of-attraction assumptions used in extreme-value theory.

The full Pickands-Balkema-de Haan theorem is cited here, not proved.  The
calculation below proves the exact Pareto special case: once the threshold is
above the lower cutoff, the excess distribution is already generalized Pareto,
not merely asymptotically close to it.

The full theorem is a classical result of Balkema and de Haan and,
independently, Pickands.  Its proof uses the equivalence between convergence of
normalized maxima and convergence of normalized threshold excesses.  We
record the statement and use exact Pareto algebra as a checkable special
case.

If X is Pareto Type I with lower cutoff x_m and tail exponent \alpha,
then for u\ge x_m,\mathbb P(X-u>y\mid X>u)
=
\frac{\mathbb P(X>u+y)}{\mathbb P(X>u)}
=
\left(1+\frac{y}{u}\right)^{-\alpha}.

This is exactly a generalized Pareto survival function with\xi=\frac1\alpha,
\qquad
\beta(u)=\frac{u}{\alpha}.

Thus exact Pareto tails do not merely approach the generalized Pareto form;
they have it at every threshold above x_m.

Plug-in tail estimation fits a tail model and evaluates a quantity of interest
under that fitted model. If a distribution family is indexed by a parameter
\theta and the target functional is T(\theta), its plug-in estimate is
T(\widehat\theta). The parameter can include a tail exponent, scale, and tail
probability; an exponent alone generally does not determine the target.

For an exact 

Pareto distribution, estimating the
exponent from logarithms can give more concentrated mean estimates than the
sample mean. This page establishes a comparison of asymptotic error scales and
explains how finite-sample error comparisons must handle non-finite fits. It does not claim uniformly
smaller mean squared error (MSE). The unregularized plug-in mean has its own
singularity at the mean-existence boundary.

A 

regularly varying tail only specifies
limiting tail ratios. Using a 

Hill estimate in a functional
requires a threshold choice, a tail approximation,
and any body contribution to that functional. The exact model below isolates
the estimation mechanism before these modeling uncertainties enter.

Here \alpha is the tail exponent, x_m is the lower cutoff, and the


extreme-value index is \xi=1/\alpha.
We write \mu=\mathbb E[X] and \bar X_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i for the
population and sample means.

records.content:
Assume X_1,\ldots,X_n are independent and identically distributed (iid), with\begin{gathered}
\mathbb P(X_i>x)=\left(\frac{x_m}{x}\right)^\alpha,\\
x\ge x_m>0,
\end{gathered}

where x_m is known and fixed, and the true exponent satisfies \alpha>1.
These are assumptions about the entire distribution. The


Pareto moment formula gives\mu=\frac{\alpha x_m}{\alpha-1}=\frac{x_m}{1-\xi}.

The maximum-likelihood estimate of the exponent and its reciprocal are\begin{gathered}
\widehat\xi_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\log(X_i/x_m),\\
\widehat\alpha_n=\frac1{\widehat\xi_n}.
\end{gathered}

They use all observations above a known cutoff. Hill instead averages the top
k log-excesses above the random order-statistic threshold X_{n-k:n}.
The formulas share a log-excess mechanism, but their sample sizes and threshold
assumptions differ.

The plug-in mean is\begin{gathered}
\begin{aligned}
\widehat\mu_n&=\frac{x_m}{1-\widehat\xi_n}\\
&=\frac{\widehat\alpha_n x_m}{\widehat\alpha_n-1},
\end{aligned}\\
\widehat\xi_n<1.
\end{gathered}

For each fixed \alpha>1, the finite plug-in estimates have the asymptotic law\begin{gathered}
\mathcal L\!\left(\sqrt n(\widehat\mu_n-\mu)
\mid \widehat\xi_n<1\right)\\
\Rightarrow\mathcal N\!\left(0,\frac{x_m^2\alpha^2}{(\alpha-1)^4}\right),\\
n\to\infty.
\end{gathered}

Here \mathcal L(\cdot\mid\cdot) denotes a conditional sampling law,
\Rightarrow denotes convergence in distribution, and \mathcal N(0,v) is
the centered normal law with variance v. The probability of a non-finite fit
tends to zero. Thus central error quantiles shrink on the n^{-1/2} scale.
This is a distributional claim; the variance in the normal limit is not a
claim about the finite-sample variance of \widehat\mu_n.

For 1<\alpha<2, the sample mean remains consistent, but its error scale is
n^{1/\alpha-1}. More precisely, the


generalized central limit theorem
gives a nondegenerate, non-Gaussian \alpha-stable limit for
n^{1-1/\alpha}(\bar X_n-\mu) in this exact Pareto model


Resnick (2007). That scale decays more slowly than n^{-1/2}.
Large observations can continue to move sample means in this regime;


pre-asymptotic LLN behavior illustrates this effect.

We derive the known-cutoff fit and the displayed plug-in limit using the
ordinary iid central limit theorem and the delta method. The general limit
theorems are cited from van der Vaart


1998, Chapters 2–3;
the stable limit for the sample mean is cited above.

Set Y_i=\log(X_i/x_m). For y\ge0,\begin{aligned}
\mathbb P(Y_i>y)&=\mathbb P(X_i>x_m e^y)\\
&=e^{-\alpha y}.
\end{aligned}

Thus Y_i is exponential with mean 1/\alpha and variance 1/\alpha^2,
even when X_i has infinite variance. Up to terms independent of \alpha,
the log likelihood is n\log\alpha-\alpha\sum_iY_i. Its derivative vanishes
at \widehat\alpha_n=n/\sum_iY_i, and its second derivative is
-n/\alpha^2<0. This proves the fit formula when \sum_iY_i>0, an event
of probability one under the continuous model.

The law of large numbers gives \widehat\xi_n\to1/\alpha<1 almost surely.
The central limit theorem gives\sqrt n(\widehat\xi_n-\xi)
\Rightarrow\mathcal N(0,\xi^2).

For the locally smooth function h(t)=x_m/(1-t),
h'(\xi)=x_m/(1-\xi)^2. The delta method therefore gives limiting variance\begin{aligned}
[h'(\xi)]^2\xi^2&=\frac{x_m^2\xi^2}{(1-\xi)^4}\\
&=\frac{x_m^2\alpha^2}{(\alpha-1)^4}.
\end{aligned}

Because \mathbb P(\widehat\xi_n<1)\to1, conditioning on finite fits does
not change this weak limit. The gain comes from averaging exponential
log-excesses and using the assumed Pareto shape to extrapolate the mean.
It depends on that shape being correct.

At \alpha=1.5 and x_m=1, \mu=3 and the normal-limit variance
coefficient for the plug-in mean is 36. Its central absolute error scale
is therefore 6/\sqrt n, or 2/\sqrt n relative to \mu.
The sample mean’s stable-limit scale is proportional to n^{-1/3}.
The unknown comparison constants and finite-sample behavior are not supplied
by comparing these powers of n.

In a repeated-sample experiment with a finite true mean, non-finite fits count
as infinite errors. Removing them changes the sampling law. Below we report
fit frequencies, not an unconditional MSE or a finite-only error comparison.

can occur even when the true mean is infinite. At the boundary \alpha=1,

records.content:
Let X\ge0 and fix a threshold u>0 with tail probability
q_u=\mathbb P(X>u)>0. Suppose the conditional tail is exactly Pareto:\begin{gathered}
\mathbb P(X>x\mid X>u)=(u/x)^\alpha,\\
x\ge u,\quad \alpha>1.
\end{gathered}

The 

mean-excess formula gives
\mathbb E[X\mid X>u]=u+e(u)=u\alpha/(\alpha-1), where
e(u)=\mathbb E[X-u\mid X>u]. Splitting the expectation at u yields\begin{aligned}
\mu&=\mathbb E[X\mathbf1_{\{X\le u\}}]\\
&\quad+q_u\frac{u\alpha}{\alpha-1}.
\end{aligned}

For an iid sample, let k=\sum_i\mathbf1_{\{X_i>u\}} be the exceedance count.
Estimate q_u by k/n and fit \widehat\alpha_u from those exceedances.
When k>0 and \widehat\alpha_u>1, a body-plus-tail estimate is\begin{aligned}
\widehat\mu_u&=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\mathbf1_{\{X_i\le u\}}\\
&\quad+\frac{k}{n}\frac{u\widehat\alpha_u}{\widehat\alpha_u-1}.
\end{aligned}

The first term is the body’s contribution per original observation, not the
mean conditional on being in the body. The second includes the threshold
itself as well as the mean excess. With no exceedances there is no fitted tail
exponent; a missing tail fit should be reported. If the fitted exponent is at
most 1, the fitted conditional mean is infinite.

A mixture calculation shows why both contributions are needed.

Consider a uniform body on [1,3] with probability 0.8, and a Pareto
tail with cutoff u=3 and exponent \alpha=1.5 with probability 0.2.
The body conditional mean is 2, the tail conditional mean is 9, and\mathbb E[X]=0.8\cdot2+0.2\cdot9=3.4.

Using 9 as the whole-distribution mean would omit the body and tail mass.
Fitting every observation as exact Pareto from 1 would also impose the
wrong model. This is a population calculation, not a simulated estimator ranking.

For empirical thresholds, repeat the analysis
over plausible u or k. Regular variation supports a Pareto approximation
far into the tail, not an exact conditional model at a chosen finite threshold.
The known-cutoff \sqrt n calculation does not supply a rate or confidence
interval for a Hill fit with a selected threshold.

The moment boundary is also an estimation boundary. Differentiating the
population mean with respect to the exponent gives\frac{d\mu}{d\alpha}=-\frac{x_m}{(\alpha-1)^2}.

Small exponent errors can therefore produce large mean errors near \alpha=1.
An uncertainty interval for \alpha that reaches 1 cannot be mapped to a finite
upper bound for this Pareto mean. The fixed-\alpha normal approximation above
is not uniform as \alpha\downarrow1.

There is a stronger finite-sample warning: even conditional on a finite fit,
the unregularized plug-in estimator has infinite first and second moments.
To see this under the exact iid model, \widehat\xi_n has a gamma density
f_n(t)=(n\alpha)^n t^{n-1}e^{-n\alpha t}/\Gamma(n) for t>0, obtained by
averaging n independent exponential log-excesses. Here \Gamma is the gamma
function. The density is continuous and strictly positive at t=1.
For any sufficiently small \varepsilon>0, the first-moment integral includes\int_{1-\varepsilon}^1\frac{x_m}{1-t}f_n(t)\,dt=\infty;

replacing x_m/(1-t) by its square gives a divergent second-moment integral.
Conditioning on t<1 only divides these integrals by a positive probability.
Moreover, \mathbb P(\widehat\xi_n
\ge1)>0 for every finite n. Finite simulations can easily miss the
singularity. Clipping or constraining the exponent away from 1 changes the
estimator and must be disclosed, with its bias and any risk claim assessed
separately.

Model uncertainty remains after sampling error shrinks. A fitted exponent
does not determine the scale, tail probability, or body of the distribution.
Truncation, dependence, measurement limits, or an incorrectly chosen threshold
can invalidate the exact-model calibration. Report those assumptions alongside
threshold sensitivity and uncertainty propagated through the functional.
If the true exact Pareto exponent is at most 1, there is no finite population
mean to recover by this method.

A fitted power law answers a conditional question: which exponent best
describes observations above a proposed lower threshold? It does not establish
that the tail is a power law. Clauset, Shalizi, and Newman (CSN)


Clauset et al. (2009) combine maximum likelihood with a threshold search;


goodness-of-fit and model comparisons
then examine the resulting model.

This page develops those calculations for independent, identically distributed
positive observations. The 

Pareto distribution supplies
the exact continuous model. The 

Hill estimator
allows a broader asymptotic interpretation under regular variation, while


threshold diagnostics explain why
choosing the fitting region matters.

Worked example

A worked real-data example will be added later. All examples here are synthetic.

We retain the 

shared notation:
\alpha>0 is the survival-tail exponent and \xi=1/\alpha is the positive
extreme-value index. Write u=x_{\min}>0 for the fitting threshold. On this
page, a is a local symbol for the density or mass exponent used by CSN:\begin{aligned}
a&=\alpha+1,\\
\bar F(x\mid X\ge u)&=(x/u)^{-\alpha},\qquad x\ge u.
\end{aligned}

Every alpha argument or result in the package below uses \alpha, including
for integer data. For an integer power law the survival is a zeta ratio,
not exactly (x/u)^{-\alpha}; its large-x exponent is still \alpha=a-1.
The change of exponent convention must precede any comparison with software
that reports a.

Let N denote the full sample size and n=n_{\mathrm{tail}} the number of
observations satisfying x_i\ge u. All likelihood sums below run over those
n retained values. Equality is included, which matters for integer data and
for thresholds chosen from observations.

records.content:
At a fixed threshold, the conditional density with respect to Lebesgue measure is\begin{aligned}
f(x\mid\alpha,u)&=\frac{\alpha}{u}(x/u)^{-(\alpha+1)},\\
&\qquad x\ge u.
\end{aligned}

We derive the MLE within this exact model. Let
T=\sum_{i=1}^n\log(x_i/u). Its log likelihood and score are\begin{aligned}
\ell(\alpha)&=n\log\alpha-n\log u-(\alpha+1)T,\\
\ell'(\alpha)&=n/\alpha-T,\\
\ell''(\alpha)&=-n/\alpha^2.
\end{aligned}

If T>0, strict concavity gives a unique finite maximum:\begin{aligned}
\widehat\alpha&=n/T,\\
\widehat a&=1+n/T.
\end{aligned}

If every retained value equals u, the likelihood increases without a finite
maximizer as \alpha\to\infty. Reporting a finite exponent in that case would
invent information about the tail’s spread.

The reciprocal estimate is the average log excess used by Hill


Hill, 1975. There is a small but real counting distinction. For distinct
continuous observations, a Hill fit above the order statistic x_{N-k:N}
uses the k larger observations. Setting u=x_{N-k:N} and retaining equality
in the CSN fit includes one more observation with zero log excess. Thus\widehat\alpha_{\mathrm{inclusive}}
=\frac{k+1}{k}\widehat\alpha_{\mathrm{Hill}}.

With a fixed external cutoff and the same retained sample, the reciprocal
mean-log-excess calculation is identical. Ties require the actual counts;
the displayed factor assumes a single threshold observation.

and

Replacing the integer sum by a continuous integral starting halfway below the
first integer suggests\widehat a_{\mathrm{approx}}
=1+\frac{n}{\sum_{i=1}^n\log\!\left(x_i/(u-\tfrac12)\right)}.

The half-unit correction matters: substituting u in this approximation is
a different and generally worse approximation. Neither expression is the
exact zeta MLE. When u is small or a is large, a few lattice points carry
much of the mass, so replacing their sum by an integral can distort the
normalization substantially. Larger u helps only relative to the local
rate of decay. There is no universal cutoff beyond which the approximation
is accurate for every exponent. A large sample reduces sampling error while
leaving this approximation error in place.

records.content:
For each admissible threshold u, fit its own exponent and compute the
Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance between the conditional empirical CDF F_{n,u}
and the fitted model CDF F_{\widehat\alpha(u),u}:\begin{aligned}
D(u)&=\sup_{x\ge u}
\left|F_{n,u}(x)-F_{\widehat\alpha(u),u}(x)\right|,\\
\widehat u&\in\arg\min_{u\in\mathcal U}D(u).
\end{aligned}

Here \mathcal U is the declared candidate set. A usual choice is the distinct
observed values with enough observations above them to permit a fit. A fixed
grid can reduce computation, but then the result minimizes over that grid
only. Record the minimum tail count, candidate rule, selected count, and
nearby values of D(u); a small difference between two minima is not evidence
for a sharply located population boundary.

For continuous data, the supremum checks both sides of every empirical jump.
For integer data the model jumps too:F_{a,u}(k)=1-\frac{\zeta(a,k+1)}{\zeta(a,u)}.

Check k-1 and k for every observed integer k. These endpoints also cover
gaps containing no observations: the empirical CDF is constant there and the
model CDF is monotone. Comparing just the right sides at observed values can
miss the largest discrepancy. Use


ks_distance_powerlaw
and 

select_xmin.

endpoint on log axes. The fitted line starts at the selected minimum and has
height n/N there: it represents the fitted tail’s unconditional mass.
Its height can differ from strict empirical survival by the observations
exactly at the threshold. The population join is known only because we

records.content:
For the exact continuous law at fixed u, \log(X/u) is exponential with
rate \alpha. Consequently the per-observation Fisher information is
1/\alpha^2. The ordinary interior-MLE approximation gives\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{se}(\widehat\alpha)&\simeq\frac{\widehat\alpha}{\sqrt n},\\
\operatorname{se}(\widehat a)&\simeq\frac{\widehat a-1}{\sqrt n}.
\end{aligned}

The second line is the familiar CSN expression, often written
(\widehat\alpha_{\mathrm{CSN}}-1)/\sqrt n. Adding one changes the exponent’s
name and level, but not its standard error. This is asymptotic sampling error
conditional on the threshold and retained count, not a finite-sample unbiased
variance formula.

For the discrete model, the same MLE approximation uses\begin{aligned}
I(a;u)&=\frac{\zeta''(a,u)}{\zeta(a,u)}
-\left[\frac{\zeta'(a,u)}{\zeta(a,u)}\right]^2,\\
\operatorname{se}(\widehat a)&\simeq[nI(\widehat a;u)]^{-1/2}.
\end{aligned}

The variance identity above derives I; asymptotic normality and the MLE
standard-error approximation are cited results, not proved here


Clauset et al., 2009, §3.1 and appendix B. The helper evaluates the discrete
curvature numerically. Very steep laws or extreme numerical scales can make
that calculation ill-conditioned.

When u was selected from the data, both formulas omit selection uncertainty.
For an empirical bootstrap, resample N observations with replacement from
the whole sample, then repeat the threshold search and exponent fit.
Retain the pairs (\widehat\alpha^{*(b)},\widehat u^{*(b)}). Their sample
standard deviations estimate the two marginal errors; their covariance
records how the estimates move together. Resampling only the selected tail
at a fixed cutoff cannot measure uncertainty in choosing that cutoff.

powerlaw_bootstrap_se
performs this full refit. The small replicate count here illustrates the
calculation; it is insufficient for stable interval endpoints.from xmath.incerto.powerlaw import sample_powerlaw, powerlaw_bootstrap_se

x = sample_powerlaw(1.6, 2, 240, random_state=330)
boot = powerlaw_bootstrap_se(x, replicates=24, min_tail=40, random_state=331)
print(f"Bootstrap SE(alpha): {boot['alpha_se']:.3f}")
print(f"Bootstrap SE(xmin): {boot['xmin_se']:.3f}")

Bootstrap SE(xmin): 0.185

The threshold selector is discontinuous and may jump between competing
minima. Bootstrap standard deviations are useful sensitivity summaries;
they do not by themselves establish confidence-interval coverage. Inspect
the paired replicates and repeat the analysis under reasonable candidate
rules. This empirical bootstrap is different from the fitted-null bootstrap
used for 

goodness of fit.

An exact power tail above some finite threshold is stronger than


regular variation. A slowly varying correction
may remain detectable at every available threshold. Raising the cutoff can
hide that discrepancy by leaving little data; report the retained fraction
alongside the fit.

Rounded continuous measurements need a measurement model; integer support
alone does not make the zeta mass correct. Censoring, reporting floors, and a
hard upper limit change the likelihood. A multiplicative change of continuous
units preserves the fitted exponent when the cutoff changes with it, whereas
adding a constant changes the model. Integer units fix the lattice and cannot
be rescaled arbitrarily while preserving the zeta family.

The likelihood and resampling calculations assume iid observations.
Dependence requires an appropriate sampling model or resampling design.
Least-squares slopes of logged histograms do not reproduce these likelihoods:
binning changes weights, empty bins vanish, and the errors are not those of
ordinary linear regression. Finally, a small fitted KS distance needs its own
calibration. It is a discrepancy statistic, not a p-value.

Power-law goodness of fit and alternatives.

Hill estimator and


tail threshold selection.

of exponent uncertainty near moment boundaries.

and uncertainty. The derivations and synthetic examples above are written
for this note’s notation and scope.

records.content:
A best-fitting power law can still fit badly. Two questions follow the


exponent and threshold fit: how unusual is
its discrepancy under a power-tail model, and does another tail family fit
better? The first asks about absolute goodness of fit; the second compares
specified alternatives. Neither can be answered by a straight-looking
log-log plot.

We use iid positive observations, a full sample of size N, and
n=n_{\mathrm{tail}} retained values x_i\ge u=x_{\min}. As in the


shared notation, \alpha>0 is the
survival exponent. The local density exponent is a=\alpha+1; CSN uses its
symbol \alpha for this a. All package alpha values below follow the
survival convention.

Worked example

A worked real-data example will be added later. All examples here are synthetic.

records.content:
Let (\widehat\alpha,\widehat u) be the fit obtained by minimizing the
refitted KS distance over the declared candidate rule, and let D_{\mathrm{obs}}
be that minimum. A textbook KS p-value for a fully specified continuous CDF
is inappropriate: the exponent and cutoff were learned from these same data.
Discrete data also lack the continuous distribution-free KS reference law.

The semiparametric bootstrap of 

Clauset et al. (2009), §4.1, constructs a null
population with an empirical body and a fitted power-law tail. For each of
B independent replicates:

Generate N independent observations. For each draw, choose the fitted
tail with probability n/N and the body with probability 1-n/N.

A tail draw follows the fitted continuous Pareto or discrete zeta law above
\widehat u. A body draw is sampled uniformly, with replacement, from the
original observations strictly below \widehat u.

Fit the replicate from the beginning, including its own threshold search
and exponent estimate. Use the same minimum tail count and candidate
rule as before; an observed-value rule uses this replicate’s values.

Calculate D_b^* against that replicate’s fitted model on its selected tail.

The tail count before refitting is binomial with parameters N and n/N.
Fixing it at the observed count would define a different resampling experiment.
If the body is empty, every draw comes from the fitted tail. The model leaves
the body’s shape unspecified; it does not pretend the whole sample is Pareto.

We estimate the tail probability by\widehat p=\frac1B\sum_{b=1}^B
\mathbf1\{D_b^*\ge D_{\mathrm{obs}}\}.

The inclusive comparison records ties conservatively, particularly for integer
data. The helper uses this empirical fraction, which can equal zero; zero
means no exceedance in these B replicates, not a proven zero probability.
Fitted-null bootstrap calibration is an approximation to the composite testing
problem, not an exact finite-sample uniform-p theorem.

A small p-value rejects this power-tail fitting procedure at a chosen
significance level. A large value means the observed discrepancy was not
unusual in the fitted-null experiment. It neither proves a power law nor gives
the probability that the hypothesis is true. Small tail samples can have little
power to distinguish curved tails. Choosing a new candidate rule after seeing
the p-value introduces another selection step.

records.content:
Conditional on the fitted null and data, the indicators are iid Bernoulli
with some Monte Carlo target probability p_*. Hence\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}_{\mathrm{MC}}(\widehat p)
&=\frac{p_*(1-p_*)}{B},\\
\operatorname{se}_{\mathrm{MC}}(\widehat p)&\le\frac1{2\sqrt B}.
\end{aligned}

Requiring this worst-case standard error to be at most \varepsilon gives
B\ge1/(4\varepsilon^2). This is a one-standard-error precision rule,
not a guarantee of absolute error within \varepsilon. For an approximate
95% margin, the corresponding normal calculation multiplies the requirement
by 

1.962. Near zero or one, a binomial interval is more informative than a
plug-in standard error of zero. Increasing B reduces simulation noise; it
does not repair model bias, dependence, or threshold-selection uncertainty in
the original observations.

powerlaw_gof_bootstrap
refits every replicate and fails explicitly if a fit fails. It does not discard
difficult replicates. Here the small sample and B=39 keep the demonstration
fast. Its worst-case Monte Carlo standard error is about 0.08, so these
outputs are illustrations rather than precise testing decisions. We use


sample_powerlaw to generate
the synthetic tail.

Codeimport numpy as np
from xmath.incerto.powerlaw import sample_powerlaw, powerlaw_gof_bootstrap

rng = np.random.default_rng(340)
x = rng.uniform(1, 3, 240)
tail = rng.random(x.size) < 0.4
x[tail] = sample_powerlaw(1.8, 3, int(tail.sum()), random_state=rng)
result = powerlaw_gof_bootstrap(x, replicates=39, min_tail=40, random_state=341)
fit = result["fit"]
print(f"xmin={fit['xmin']:.3f}; tail count={fit['n_tail']}")
print(f"KS={fit['ks']:.3f}; bootstrap p={result['p_value']:.3f}")
print(f"Worst-case Monte Carlo SE: {result['worst_case_mc_se']:.3f}")
print(f"Distinct refitted thresholds: {len(np.unique(result['xmins']))}")

Outputxmin=3.315; tail count=89
KS=0.066; bootstrap p=0.410
Worst-case Monte Carlo SE: 0.080
Distinct refitted thresholds: 33

records.content:
Select a common threshold u and keep exactly the same observations for every
comparison. If a candidate has unconditioned density g(x;\theta) and survival
\bar G(u;\theta), its conditional tail density is\begin{aligned}
q(x;\theta,u)&=\frac{g(x;\theta)}{\bar G(u;\theta)},\qquad x\ge u,\\
\ell(\theta;u)&=\sum_{i=1}^n\log g(x_i;\theta)\\
&\quad-n\log\bar G(u;\theta).
\end{aligned}

This display assumes a continuous law. For an integer law the denominator is
P_\theta(X\ge u), and numerator and denominator must both use counting
measure. Do not compare log probability masses with log densities, or let
one model discard observations that another model must explain.

Conditioning changes the fit, not merely its reported likelihood. For example,
fitting an ordinary lognormal to the retained values and subtracting a tail
normalizer afterward is generally not maximum likelihood for the conditional
model, because that normalizer depends on the parameters.

The following continuous alternatives all have support [u,\infty) after
conditioning. Each parameter is fitted on that same retained sample.

Write y=x/u, shape k>0, and \beta=(u/\tau)^k>0, where \tau is the
parent Weibull scale. Thenq_{\mathrm W}(x)
=\frac{k\beta}{u}y^{k-1}\exp[-\beta(y^k-1)].

The name stretched exponential usually refers to 0<k<1; the implementation
fits the full Weibull family, including the exponential case k=1. At fixed
k, differentiating the conditional log likelihood gives\widehat\beta(k)=
\left[\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i^k-1)\right]^{-1}.

Profiling out \beta leaves a one-dimensional numerical shape fit. Comparing
Weibull against exponential is a nested problem; comparing Weibull against
Pareto requires the non-nested conditions discussed below.

records.content:
The cutoff law is sometimes called a truncated power law. Here “cutoff” means
an exponential damping factor, not a hard finite upper endpoint. Define the
dimensionless cutoff b=\lambda u, with \lambda>0, and\begin{aligned}
C(a,b)&=\int_1^\infty z^{-a}e^{-b(z-1)}\,dz,\\
q_{\mathrm C}(x)&=\frac{(x/u)^{-a}e^{-b(x/u-1)}}{uC(a,b)}.
\end{aligned}

For b>0, any real a gives an integrable density. At b=0, normalization
requires a>1 and C(a,0)=1/(a-1), recovering the pure Pareto law. The
coefficient a-1 in an interior cutoff fit is not its asymptotic survival
exponent: the exponential factor eventually dominates. All positive moments
of an interior cutoff law exist.

The normalizing integral is part of the optimization. Omitting it rewards
arbitrary changes of scale in the purported density and invalidates a
likelihood-ratio comparison.

records.content:
For two fitted conditional densities evaluated on the same n observations,
let\begin{aligned}
d_i&=\log\widehat q_1(x_i)-\log\widehat q_2(x_i),\\
R&=\sum_{i=1}^n d_i,\qquad \bar d=R/n,\\
s_d^2&=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(d_i-\bar d)^2,\\
Z_V&=\frac{R}{\sqrt n\,s_d}.
\end{aligned}

Positive R favors model 1; negative R favors model 2. The normalized
statistic Z_V is sometimes also called normalized R. Under the null that
the two pseudo-true models have equal expected log likelihood, Vuong’s
non-nested result gives an asymptotic standard normal reference and the
two-sided p-valuep_V=2\{1-\Phi(|Z_V|)\}.

We cite the fitted-model asymptotic result in 

Vuong (1989) rather than
prove it. Its conditions include iid sampling, regular interior parameter
estimation, distinguishable non-nested models, and a finite, strictly positive
variance of the limiting per-observation contrast. The heuristic central
limit argument applies to that limiting contrast; fitted scores sharing
estimated parameters are not themselves independent observations.

These qualifications matter for heavy tails. Against an exponential, a
Pareto log-likelihood contrast contains a term proportional to X. Under an
exact Pareto generator, its variance is infinite if \alpha\le2, and even its
expectation can fail for \alpha\le1. A finite array of scores cannot verify
the population moment assumptions. Overlap, a nearly vanishing s_d, or an
optimizer drifting toward a family boundary also requires different analysis.

A small p_V and the sign of R distinguish relative fit under those
conditions. They do not establish that the preferred model fits well in an
absolute sense. A large p_V leaves the comparison unresolved; it does not
establish equivalence. The statistic below uses the unpenalized log likelihoods,
not an AIC or BIC adjustment.

If u was selected on the same data, the fixed-threshold reference theorem
does not automatically cover that selection. Report such p-values as
conditional approximations, or use an independent threshold choice or a
simulation design that repeats the selection procedure. Several pairwise
tests add a multiplicity issue; a collection of unadjusted p-values is not a
single calibrated family-selection decision.

fit_tail_model supplies fitted
per-observation log likelihoods, and


likelihood_ratio_test
computes the comparison. This example fixes u=1 before sampling. The Pareto
generator has \alpha=3, so the exponential contrast has finite variance.
Both samples have 2500 observations; each comparison uses the entire sample.

Codeimport numpy as np
from xmath.incerto.powerlaw import (
    sample_powerlaw, fit_tail_model, likelihood_ratio_test,
)
rng = np.random.default_rng(350)
samples = {
    "Pareto": sample_powerlaw(3, 1, 2500, random_state=rng),
    "Exponential": 1 + rng.exponential(size=2500),
}
for name, x in samples.items():
    pl = fit_tail_model(x, 1, "powerlaw")
    exp = fit_tail_model(x, 1, "exponential")
    lr = likelihood_ratio_test(pl["loglik"], exp["loglik"])
    print(f"{name}: R={lr['R']:.2f}, Z={lr['normalized_R']:.2f}, p={lr['p_value']:.3g}")

OutputPareto: R=233.67, Z=4.31, p=1.6e-05
Exponential: R=-206.54, Z=-11.82, p=2.93e-32

A separate lognormal simulation illustrates conditional fitting of every
alternative. We use the same realized tail for all five fits. Lognormal
likelihoods can be close to other families in a finite sample; this table
reports optimization outcomes and log likelihoods, without assigning a

x = np.random.default_rng(360).lognormal(1, 0.6, 1000)
models = ("powerlaw", "lognormal", "exponential",

    print(f"  status: {fit['status']}")

records.content:
The pure power law is the \lambda=0 boundary of the cutoff family. If both
optimizations find their maxima, the larger family cannot have lower maximized
likelihood. With model 1 the pure law and model 2 the cutoff law,\begin{aligned}
R&=\ell_{\mathrm{PL}}-\ell_{\mathrm C}\le0,\\
T_{\mathrm{LR}}&=2(\ell_{\mathrm C}-\ell_{\mathrm{PL}})=-2R.
\end{aligned}

The sign therefore gives no evidence by itself for a cutoff. Under an ordinary
regular interior restriction with one extra parameter, Wilks’ reference is
\chi_1^2. Here \lambda\ge0 and the null sits at its boundary. With one
regular constrained direction and interior identifiable nuisance parameters,
a common reference is the mixture\tfrac12\delta_0+\tfrac12\chi_1^2,

where \delta_0 is a point mass at zero. This boundary result is cited from


Self & Liang (1987), §3, Case 5. For a positive observed statistic its upper-tail
p-value is half the \chi_1^2 upper tail; at zero the inclusive upper-tail
probability is one.

That mixture is not a universal cutoff test. The cutoff score at the
Pareto null involves X-\mathbb E X; ordinary finite-information regularity
already fails when the null tail has \alpha\le2. An estimated threshold,
other boundary parameters, or failure to find a likelihood maximum introduces
further issues. A null simulation calibrated for the actual fitting procedure
is preferable when the reference-law assumptions are unsupported: simulate
under the null, repeat every fitted step, and compare refitted LR statistics.
The KS goodness-of-fit bootstrap above is a different statistic and does not
supply this nested LR p-value.

The helper’s nested=True option returns T_{\mathrm{LR}} and leaves its
p-value uncalibrated by default. Selecting calibration="chi2" or
calibration="boundary" explicitly asserts the corresponding conditions;
the software cannot verify them from two score arrays.import numpy as np
from xmath.incerto.powerlaw import fit_tail_model, likelihood_ratio_test

x = 2 + np.random.default_rng(370).exponential(size=600)
pure = fit_tail_model(x, 2, "powerlaw")
cutoff = fit_tail_model(x, 2, "truncated_powerlaw")
lr = likelihood_ratio_test(pure["loglik"], cutoff["loglik"], nested=True)
print(f"Nested LR statistic: {lr['statistic']:.2f}")
print(lr["status"])

Clauset, Shalizi, and Newman, Power-law distributions in empirical data


Clauset et al. (2009): §4.1 for the fitted-null bootstrap, §5 and appendix C
for relative fit. We qualify reference distributions where boundary or
infinite-moment cases need separate treatment.

Vuong, Likelihood Ratio Tests for Model Selection and Non-Nested Hypotheses


Vuong (1989): fitted-model non-nested asymptotics; the full technical
theorem is cited, not proved here.

Self and Liang, Asymptotic Properties of Maximum Likelihood Estimators and
Likelihood Ratio Tests under Nonstandard Conditions 

Self & Liang (1987):
the regular boundary-mixture result, not a blanket claim about heavy-tail
cutoff fits.

The speed of a uniformly sampled particle in a two-dimensional equilibrium
gas has a Rayleigh distribution. Each signed velocity component is
Gaussian; taking the length of the velocity vector changes the law.
This answers Taleb’s distribution challenge 

Taleb, 2026: the density
already written in the accompanying animation is Rayleigh 

Matharium, 2026.
No extra physical parameter is needed.

The sampling rule matters. An event recorded when a particle crosses a small
hole favors faster particles. We derive the chamber law first, then the
effusion law and the finite-system correction. A seeded simulation compares
seven fitted families; it illustrates these distinctions without testing
whether the animation implements equilibrium dynamics.

Assume a classical, nonrelativistic gas of equal-mass particles at canonical
equilibrium, with no bulk flow and no constraint on total momentum. Let
m>0 be particle mass, T>0 temperature, and k Boltzmann’s constant.
Let d\ge1 be an integer. Write the velocity as \mathbf u\in\mathbb R^d,
the speed as V=\|\mathbf u\|, and its realized value as v. Set\sigma^2=\frac{kT}{m},\qquad c=\frac1{2\sigma^2}.

Here \sigma is component standard deviation; it is not speed standard
deviation. Densities below use Lebesgue measure in their stated coordinates.
These symbols agree with the 

shared notation.

For N particles at positions \mathbf q_i and a velocity-independent
potential U, the Hamiltonian is
H=\sum_{i=1}^N m\|\mathbf u_i\|^2/2+U(\mathbf q_1,\ldots,\mathbf q_N),
and the canonical weight e^{-H/(kT)} separates into kinetic and positional
factors 

Tong, n.d., §2.3. Integrating the positions and the
other particles leaves the single-particle density\begin{aligned}
\phi_d(\mathbf u)&=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-d/2}\\
&\quad\times\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|\mathbf u\|^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).
\end{aligned}

The factorization proves that the d components are independent
N(0,\sigma^2) variables. This follows from the equilibrium measure;
it does not require a central limit argument about collisions.
The 

maximum-entropy note explains why the
constraint and the coordinate measure must be specified in an entropy argument.

We now derive the speed density, its moments, and its mode. The surface area
of the unit sphere in d dimensions is
S_{d-1}=2\pi^{d/2}/\Gamma(d/2). Polar coordinates contribute the shell
factor S_{d-1}v^{d-1}, giving\boxed{
\begin{gathered}
f_d(v)=\frac{2c^{d/2}}{\Gamma(d/2)}v^{d-1}e^{-cv^2},\\
v>0.
\end{gathered}
}

The density is zero for v<0, and V/\sigma\sim\chi_d.
Substitution t=cv^2 gives\begin{gathered}
\int_0^\infty v^{d+r-1}e^{-cv^2}\,dv\\
=\frac{\Gamma((d+r)/2)}{2c^{(d+r)/2}},\\
r>-d.
\end{gathered}

Taking r=0 proves normalization. For every real r>-d,\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb E[V^r]\\
&\quad=(2\sigma^2)^{r/2}\frac{\Gamma((d+r)/2)}{\Gamma(d/2)}.
\end{aligned}

For r\le-d the integral diverges at zero. Every positive moment exists.
For d>1, differentiating the log density gives
(d-1)/v-v/\sigma^2, so the unique mode is \sigma\sqrt{d-1}.
For d=1 the law is half-normal and its mode is zero.

Dimension

Law and density for v>0

Mean

Variance

Mode

2

Rayleigh: v\sigma^{-2}e^{-v^2/(2\sigma^2)}

\sigma\sqrt{\pi/2}

(4-\pi)\sigma^2/2

\sigma

3

Maxwell: \sqrt{2/\pi}\,v^2\sigma^{-3}e^{-v^2/(2\sigma^2)}

2\sigma\sqrt{2/\pi}

(3-8/\pi)\sigma^2

\sqrt2\sigma

In two dimensions, integration also gives
F(v)=1-e^{-v^2/(2\sigma^2)} for v\ge0.
This is a Weibull law with shape 2 and scale \sqrt2\sigma.
Its right tail decays faster than any exponential, placing it on the light
side of the 

tail-class catalog.

For a local shape s>0, define\begin{gathered}
h_s(v)=\frac{2c^s}{\Gamma(s)}v^{2s-1}e^{-cv^2},\\
v>0.
\end{gathered}

This is a generalized Gamma density with power 2; the chamber law has
s=d/2. The generalized inverse Gaussian


GIG family
is a different family. In the shared convention its kernel is
v^{p-1}\exp[-(av+b/v)/2], with p\in\mathbb R and a,b>0.

We can exclude Gamma, inverse Gamma, inverse Gaussian, and GIG by their
tails, without fitting any data. In the following kernels, shapes and
scales are positive, and all parameters are fixed as v\to\infty.

Candidate

Density kernel on v>0

Gamma, shape s_0, scale \vartheta

v^{s_0-1}e^{-v/\vartheta}

Inverse Gamma, shape s_0, scale b_0

v^{-s_0-1}e^{-b_0/v}

Inverse Gaussian, mean \mu, shape \kappa

v^{-3/2}e^{-\kappa v/(2\mu^2)-\kappa/(2v)}

\operatorname{GIG}(p,a,b)

v^{p-1}e^{-(av+b/v)/2}

After taking logarithms, each candidate has only constant, logarithmic,
linear, and reciprocal terms. Consequently, for each such density q,\begin{gathered}
\lim_{v\to\infty}\frac{\log q(v)}{v^2}=0,\\
\lim_{v\to\infty}\frac{\log h_s(v)}{v^2}=-c<0.
\end{gathered}

The unequal limits prove that none of these fixed-parameter laws equals
h_s. The argument includes the normalizable Gamma and inverse Gamma
boundaries of GIG. Log densities refer to a fixed choice of speed units;
changing units changes the negative constant but preserves the distinction.

Gaussian exclusion needs a separate argument: a nondegenerate Gaussian
assigns positive probability to negative speeds. Its log-density limit
is also negative, so the preceding tail test alone would not exclude it.
For d\ge2, even an ordinary Gaussian conditioned to be nonnegative fails:
its density has a positive right limit at zero, whereas f_d(0+)=0.
Positive support and skewness alone do not identify a family.

Let Q=V^2 and let \varepsilon=mV^2/2 be kinetic energy. The change
of variable from v to q has Jacobian 1/(2\sqrt q), so under h_s,\begin{gathered}
\begin{aligned}
p_Q(q)&=\frac{h_s(\sqrt q)}{2\sqrt q}\\
&=\frac{c^s}{\Gamma(s)}q^{s-1}e^{-cq},
\end{aligned}\\
q>0.
\end{gathered}

Using Gamma’s shape, scale convention, this proves\begin{gathered}
V^2\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(s,2\sigma^2),\\
\varepsilon\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(s,kT).
\end{gathered}

For the 2D chamber, s=1: squared speed is exponential with mean
2kT/m, and kinetic energy is exponential with mean kT.
For R=1/Q, a second Jacobian gives\begin{gathered}
p_R(r)=\frac{c^s}{\Gamma(s)}r^{-s-1}e^{-c/r},\\
r>0.
\end{gathered}

Thus 1/V^2\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(s,c).
Similarly 1/\varepsilon has inverse Gamma scale 1/(kT).
The reciprocal speed 1/V instead has an exponential factor e^{-c/r^2};
it is not inverse Gamma.

If the normalizable boundaries are included,
\operatorname{Gamma}(s,\vartheta)=\operatorname{GIG}(s,2/\vartheta,0)
and \operatorname{InvGamma}(s,b_0)=\operatorname{GIG}(-s,0,2b_0).
For the strict a,b>0 family these are limits. Transforming a Gamma
variable by a square root does not preserve membership in Gamma or GIG.

Crossing a hole changes the sample

records.content:
Assume the hole is small compared with the mean free path, the gas near it
is isotropic and equilibrated, and detection efficiency does not depend on
speed. In time dt, particles that can cross a small area come from a layer
of thickness v\cos\theta\,dt, where \theta is the angle to the outward
normal and \cos\theta>0. This is the flux factor in the usual effusion
calculation 

Fitzpatrick, n.d..

Multiplying the equilibrium velocity measure by this factor and integrating
over outward directions leaves one extra factor v. Normalizing proves\begin{gathered}
g_d(v)=\frac{vf_d(v)}{\mathbb E_f V}\\
=\frac{2c^{(d+1)/2}}{\Gamma((d+1)/2)}v^d e^{-cv^2},\\
v>0.
\end{gathered}

The effusing speed divided by \sigma therefore has law \chi_{d+1}.
In particular,g_2(v)=\sqrt{\frac2\pi}\frac{v^2}{\sigma^3}
e^{-v^2/(2\sigma^2)}=f_3(v).

Two-dimensional effusion has the same speed law as a three-dimensional
chamber. The change comes from sampling, not an added spatial dimension.
Its mode is \sigma\sqrt d, and its squared speed and energy use
s=(d+1)/2 in the preceding Gamma formulas. Selecting only an outward
direction would not introduce the factor v; counting crossings does.

The animation shows particles leaving an opening and accumulating in a
histogram 

Matharium, 2026. If those are physical crossing events, the
effusion law is the appropriate equilibrium prediction. If the opening
merely conveys uniformly selected particles to a histogram, Rayleigh is
appropriate. The displayed formula specifies the chamber law; without the
sampling algorithm, the drawing does not resolve this distinction.

Canonical velocities have the preceding Gaussian components even for finite
N. An isolated finite system with fixed total kinetic energy has a different
joint measure. Assume N>1 ideal particles, or elastic hard disks or spheres,
in reflecting hard walls, with total kinetic energy E>0 and no imposed
total-momentum constraint. The velocity measure is uniform on the sphere\begin{gathered}
\sum_{i=1}^N\|\mathbf u_i\|^2=\frac{2E}{m}\\
\text{in }\mathbb R^{dN}.
\end{gathered}

We derive its one-particle marginal. Integrating the remaining d(N-1)
coordinates against the energy-shell delta function supplies the factor
(E-mv^2/2)^{d(N-1)/2-1}. The first particle’s radial element contributes
v^{d-1}\,dv. Put v_{\max}=\sqrt{2E/m} and
B(x,y)=\Gamma(x)\Gamma(y)/\Gamma(x+y). Substitution
z=v^2/v_{\max}^2 normalizes the density to\begin{gathered}
\begin{aligned}
&f_{N,d}(v)\\
&\quad=\frac{2v^{d-1}}{v_{\max}^{d}B(d/2,d(N-1)/2)}\\
&\qquad\times\left(1-\frac{v^2}{v_{\max}^2}\right)^{d(N-1)/2-1},
\end{aligned}\\
0<v<v_{\max}.
\end{gathered}

Equivalently,\boxed{\frac{mV^2}{2E}\sim
\operatorname{Beta}\!\left(\frac d2,\frac{d(N-1)}2\right).}

This is a scaled Beta energy law, with a finite upper endpoint


Scalas et al., 2015. For the instantaneous effusion measure, multiplication
by v changes the first Beta shape to (d+1)/2, leaving the second unchanged.

Define the kinetic temperature by E=dNkT_{\rm kin}/2. At fixed
T_{\rm kin} and fixed speed, the finite-system factor tends to
e^{-mv^2/(2kT_{\rm kin})} as N\to\infty, and the Gamma-ratio
asymptotic \Gamma(z+a)/\Gamma(z)\sim z^a gives the canonical normalizer.
This proves the chi limit; it is not a uniform relative approximation all
the way to v_{\max}. Fixing total momentum as well would change the
available degrees of freedom and the Beta law.

Hard-core exclusion affects the allowed positions but introduces no
velocity-dependent potential, so it does not alter the canonical
factorization. Elastic collisions conserve energy; that alone does not
prove that an arbitrary initial condition has equilibrated. Noninteracting
point particles reflecting in a fixed box retain their individual speeds.

The moment formula gives mean energy dkT/2 inside and (d+1)kT/2
among effusing particles. A leak therefore removes more energy per particle
than the chamber average. In a large, unheated chamber that re-equilibrates
between losses, treat N as continuous and use dots for time derivatives.
Energy balance gives\begin{gathered}
\frac d2 k(N\dot T+T\dot N)\\
=\frac{d+1}{2}kT\dot N,\\
N\dot T=\frac{T\dot N}{d}.
\end{gathered}

Since \dot N<0, temperature falls. Starting at N_0,T_0, integration gives
T/T_0=(N/N_0)^{1/d} within this quasistatic approximation.
If the outgoing event rate is J(t), the accumulated speed
density over an observation interval ish_{\rm collected}(v)=
\frac{\int J(t)g_d(v;T(t))\,dt}{\int J(t)\,dt}.

It generally mixes temperatures. The


variance-mixture note explains why averaging
over scales can change a marginal law. A fixed-temperature effusion density
does not describe an entire cooling history.

We draw 50,000 independent pairs of Gaussian components with kT/m=1, seed
20261022, and take their Euclidean lengths. All first components are drawn
before all second components. This samples the canonical chamber law directly;
it is neither molecular dynamics nor a sample extracted from the animation.

We fit Gaussian, Gamma, inverse Gamma, inverse Gaussian, GIG, Rayleigh, and
Weibull laws by maximum likelihood. Positive families have location fixed
at zero. Gaussian estimates mean and standard deviation; Rayleigh estimates
one scale; Weibull, Gamma, and the two inverse families estimate two parameters.
With K estimated parameters and maximized log likelihood \ell, the
reported score is \mathrm{AIC}=2K-2\ell in these fixed speed units.



The same 50,000 speeds in 80 bins. Curves use 401 points from -0.5 to
the sample maximum. The log panel displays densities down to 

10-5;
this plotting limit does not truncate the fitted laws. Rayleigh and Weibull
nearly coincide, as do Gamma and the GIG boundary fit.

The table’s KS distance is D=\sup_v|F_n(v)-F_{\hat\theta}(v)|,
where F_n is the empirical CDF. Its p-values are the ordinary two-sided
KS calculation without correction for parameter fitting. They are
descriptive diagnostics, not calibrated tests of the fitted families.
Calibration would require, for example, a parametric bootstrap with refitting
in each replicate 

SciPy developers, 2026. Zeros below are numerical underflow,
not exact zero probabilities.

fit_speed_models,


speed_fit_table, and


squared_speed_ks.

records.content:
The Gamma MLE has shape \hat s=3.1513 and scale
\hat\vartheta=0.3964. At its GIG representation
(p,a,b)=(\hat s,2/\hat\vartheta,0), the inward derivative of log
likelihood per observation is\begin{aligned}
&\left.\frac1n\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial b}\right|_{b=0+}\\
&\quad=\frac12\Bigl(\frac1{(\hat s-1)\hat\vartheta}\\
&\qquad-\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\frac1{v_i}\Bigr)<0.
\end{aligned}

This expression is finite because \hat s>1. Differentiating the
normalizing integral supplies the model reciprocal mean in the first term.
The other two score components vanish at the Gamma MLE. Log likelihood is
concave in the natural coordinates (p-1,-a/2,-b/2): the Hessian of its
log normalizer is the covariance of (\log V,V,1/V) in the interior.
The supporting-plane inequality therefore certifies a maximum on the
Gamma boundary. For strict a,b>0, this value is a supremum as b\downarrow0.

The helper uses that boundary law directly for its density and CDF. It
does not present tiny positive GIG parameters as a distinct distribution.
The table retains GIG’s nominal K=3, hence a score exactly 2 above
Gamma’s. Ordinary regular-model AIC theory does not apply unchanged at
this boundary; the score here is a stated comparison convention.

Theoretical quantiles are horizontal and empirical quantiles vertical, at
199 equally spaced probabilities from 0.005 to 0.995. All displayed
quantiles are retained. These QQ
plots use the same observations as the fit table; they are not independent
validation data.



The same probabilities and observations, with one panel per inverse family.
Their much larger fitted upper quantiles need separate horizontal ranges;
no quantiles are clipped to make the central fits look closer.

The squared-speed test compares against the specified exponential mean
2, without estimating it. Its KS statistic is 0.0058 and its p-value is
0.0696, so it does not reject this simple null at the 5% level.
This p-value has the usual iid continuous-null calibration. It is not the
probability that the exponential model is true. The different Rayleigh
p-value in the table uses a fitted scale.

records.content:
Embrechts et al. (1997), Modelling Extremal Events.

Resnick (2007), Heavy-Tail Phenomena.

An exact 

Pareto tail has the same probability
ratio whenever we multiply a threshold by a fixed amount. Regular variation
asks for this behavior only in the limit as the threshold grows. It allows
slow corrections to a power law while retaining a limiting tail exponent.

Read the Pareto survival example first for a concrete example. This page uses
limits and positive measurable functions; the proof below establishes the
power-times-slowly-varying characterization directly from the definition.

A positive measurable function f is regularly varying at infinity with index
\rho, written f\in RV_\rho, if, for every fixed t>0,\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{f(tx)}{f(x)}=t^\rho.

The case \rho=0 is called slow variation: a positive measurable function
L is slowly varying when L(tx)/L(x)\to1 for every fixed t>0.  Equivalently,
regularly varying functions can be written asf(x)=x^\rho L(x)

with L slowly varying.  A survival function
\bar F has a regularly varying right tail with exponent \alpha>0, written
\bar F\in RV_{-\alpha}, when\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{\bar F(tx)}{\bar F(x)}=t^{-\alpha},
\qquad t>0.

Here \bar F(x)=\mathbb P(X>x), L is the slowly varying factor,
\alpha is the positive tail exponent, and t is a fixed multiplier.

Regular variation is the mathematical version of


Pareto-style scale invariance.  At high
thresholds, multiplying the threshold by t has an asymptotically stable
effect on exceedance probabilities.  The slowly varying factor L allows
departures from an exact 

Pareto law while
preserving the same tail exponent.

The ratio statement is stronger than saying that large observations are more
frequent than under a Gaussian baseline.  It says that the relative penalty for
raising a large threshold settles to a power t^{-\alpha}.

Constant functions are slowly varying.  If L(x)=c>0, then
L(tx)/L(x)=1 for every x and t>0.

Logarithmic corrections are slowly varying.  For fixed
\beta\in\mathbb R, L(x)=(\log x)^\beta on x>1 satisfies
L(tx)/L(x)\to1.

A nonzero power is not slowly varying.  If L(x)=x^\beta, then
L(tx)/L(x)=t^\beta, which equals 1 for all t only when \beta=0.

Lognormal right tails are heavy-tailed and subexponential, but not regularly
varying: their fixed-multiplier survival ratios do not settle to
t^{-\alpha} for any finite \alpha.

Exponential tails are neither regularly varying nor subexponential.  For a multiplier t>1, their
survival ratios decay exponentially in x.

We prove the algebraic characterization used throughout these notes: a regularly
varying function is a power times a slowly varying function.  The proof is only
an unwinding of the ratio definition. The 

Karamata note
develops the related integral asymptotics and their moment consequences.

If f(x)=x^\rho L(x) with L slowly varying, then for fixed t>0,\frac{f(tx)}{f(x)}
=
t^\rho\frac{L(tx)}{L(x)}
\to t^\rho.

Conversely, if f\in RV_\rho, define L(x)=x^{-\rho}f(x).  Then\frac{L(tx)}{L(x)}
=
t^{-\rho}\frac{f(tx)}{f(x)}
\to 1,

so L is slowly varying and f(x)=x^\rho L(x).

For survival tails, set \rho=-\alpha in the same equivalence:
\bar F(x)=x^{-\alpha}L(x), with L(x)=x^\alpha\bar F(x) slowly varying.
No separate survival-tail argument is needed.

For the 

Pareto distribution with lower cutoff
x_m,\bar F(x)=x_m^\alpha x^{-\alpha},

so L(x)=x_m^\alpha is constant and therefore slowly varying.

The elementary equivalence above defines L; it does not prove Karamata’s
representation theorem. For positive measurable slowly varying L, that
theorem gives, eventually,L(x)=c(x)\exp\left\{\int_a^x\frac{\varepsilon(v)}v\,dv\right\},
\qquad c(x)\to c\in(0,\infty),\quad \varepsilon(x)\to0,

with measurable c and locally integrable \varepsilon(v)/v.
We cite the existence of this representation: 

Bingham et al. (1987),
Theorem 1.3.1, p. 12. This is a different result from the


integral theorem.

Its sufficiency follows directly. For fixed t>0, the logarithm of
L(tx)/L(x) is \log[c(tx)/c(x)]+\int_x^{tx}\varepsilon(v)\,dv/v.
The integral’s absolute value is at most |\log t| times the supremum
of |\varepsilon| between x and tx, which tends to zero.
Also \log L(x)/\log x\to0: split the integral at a fixed point beyond
which |\varepsilon|<\delta, divide by \log x, and then let
\delta\downarrow0. Hence a regularly varying survival satisfies
\log\bar F(x)/\log x\to-\alpha. This is a ratio of logarithms;
convergence of a derivative of a log-log plot needs extra smoothness.
