We prove the transformation rule used in SCoFT v4 §5.2.3, p. 100


Taleb, 2025, without differentiating a density. Let X\ge0 have
\bar F(x)=x^{-\alpha}L(x) eventually and let r>0. ThenP(X^r>y)=\bar F(y^{1/r})=y^{-\alpha/r}L(y^{1/r}).

For fixed t>0, the ratio of the last slowly varying factors has arguments
t^{1/r}y^{1/r} and y^{1/r}, so it tends to one. Thus X^r has
survival exponent \alpha/r. Units may be fixed first by applying this
argument to X/x_m. Negative powers concern the behavior near zero and
are outside this right-tail rule. The exact Pareto payoff case is already
derived in 

asymmetric payoffs.

The fixed-multiplier ratio can be compared algebraically for an exact Pareto
tail and a power law with a slowly varying logarithmic correction.

For an exact Pareto tail and a logarithmically corrected tail, respectively,\frac{\bar F(2x)}{\bar F(x)}=2^{-\alpha},
\qquad
\frac{(2x)^{-\alpha}(\log(2x))^\beta}
     {x^{-\alpha}(\log x)^\beta}
=2^{-\alpha}\left(1+\frac{\log 2}{\log x}\right)^\beta.

For \alpha=1.5 and \beta=1, the correction multiplier is 2 at x=2,
3/2 at x=4, and 5/4 at x=16. The second expression is used only
sufficiently far into the tail, where it is decreasing and at most one
before taking the ratio; a full distribution also needs a body below that range.

The exact Pareto ratio is constant at 2^{-\alpha}; the log-corrected
ratio approaches the same target slowly. A finite diagnostic curve can
suggest regular variation, but the definition is about the asymptotic limit.



Figure 1:This reused chapter-2 figure uses \bar F(u)=u^{-2}(1+\log u) for
u\ge1, extended by one below 1. It has exponent 2 and slowly
varying factor 1+\log u, differing from the preceding exponent-1.5
example with factor \log u. Its doubling ratio is
\tfrac14[1+\log 2/(1+\log u)], which approaches 1/4.
All values are population evaluations; the threshold axis is logarithmic.

The 

chapter 5 demo compares
multiplier ratios for Student and shifted double-Pareto tails. Their finite
threshold differences are explained by the


matching calculation.

Regular variation is an asymptotic property.  It does not say that every
moderate observation follows a power law.

Estimating \alpha from finite samples is threshold-sensitive; the


Hill estimator and log-log plots are
diagnostics, not certificates.

A nonnegative law with a regularly varying right tail and \alpha>0
is subexponential (Foss, Korshunov, and Zachary, 2nd ed., §3.5,
Theorem 3.29 and following paragraph, p. 57); see


Subexponentiality for the one-big-jump
principle.

Moment implications require assumptions on the full tail and should point to


Karamata’s theorem or to a Pareto-specific proof.

Foss, Korshunov, and Zachary, An Introduction to Heavy-Tailed and
Subexponential Distributions, 

Foss et al. (2013),
§3.5, Theorem 3.29, p. 57: cited subexponential classification.

Bingham et al. (1987), Regular Variation, Theorem 1.3.1, p. 12:
the cited representation theorem; the elementary power-times-L
characterization is proved on this page.

Taleb (2025), §5.1.1, pp. 95–97, and §5.2.3, p. 100:
scaling and transformation context.

Embrechts, Klueppelberg, and Mikosch, Modelling Extremal Events

An absorbing state changes which future payoffs a path can receive. Let T
be the first ruin time, taking values in \{1,2,\ldots\}\cup\{\infty\};
the process stays ruined after T. The probability law P and expectation
\mathbb E follow the 

shared notation.

Suppose trials are independent and each causes ruin with the same
probability q\in(0,1] if reached. For every integer N\ge0,P(T>N)=(1-q)^N,\qquad P(T\le N)=1-(1-q)^N,

with survival at N=0 defined as one. We prove both the finite formula and
the limit: survival through N is the intersection of N independent
nonruin events, hence the product. The events \{T>N\} decrease to
\{T=\infty\}, so continuity of probability and (1-q)^N\to0 give
P(T<\infty)=1. At q=0, survival is one at every horizon instead.

For q=0.02, ruin probabilities at horizons 10, 100 and 1000 are
approximately 0.182927, 0.867380 and 0.9999999983.
No heavy-tail assumption enters this calculation.

What the dependence assumption can be replaced by

records.content:
When P(T\ge k)>0, define the conditional hazard
h_k=P(T=k\mid T\ge k). The chain rule givesP(T>N)=\prod_{k=1}^N(1-h_k).

This identity needs no independence assumption. If 0\le h_k<1 for all
k, eventual ruin has probability one if and only if
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}h_k=\infty. We prove the equivalence. If the sum
diverges, \log(1-h_k)\le-h_k forces the product to zero. If the sum
converges, eventually h_k\le1/2 and
\log(1-h_k)\ge-2h_k. The tail log-sum then has a finite lower bound;
the finite initial product is positive, so the infinite product is positive.
If some reached hazard is one, ruin is certain by that step separately.

A positive hazard at every step is insufficient. For
h_k=1/(k+1)^2,P(T>N)=\prod_{k=1}^N\frac{k(k+2)}{(k+1)^2}
=\frac{N+2}{2(N+1)}\longrightarrow\frac12.

The formula follows by cancelling successive factors. It gives eventual
ruin probability 1/2, although every conditional hazard is positive.
For a different boundary, let all potential trial-failure indicators equal
one Bernoulli variable B with P(B=1)=q. Each marginal failure
probability is q, but P(T\le N)=q for every N\ge1: surviving
the first trial reveals B=0. Marginals alone do not determine repeated risk.

hierarchy.lvl2: Growing ensemble expectation and a terminating path
Growing ensemble expectation and a terminating path

records.content:
Take q\in(0,1), a>1, and starting resource W_0>0.
Here W_k denotes resources at step k, not a mixing variable. LetW_k=W_0a^k\mathbf1_{\{T>k\}}

under the constant-hazard model. This gives
\mathbb E W_k=W_0[a(1-q)]^k. If a(1-q)>1, the expectation grows
without bound. Nevertheless T<\infty almost surely, so on almost every
path W_k=0 eventually and\frac1N\sum_{k=1}^NW_k\longrightarrow0.

The proof is pathwise: after the finite ruin time the sum has only finitely
many nonzero, finite terms, while its denominator grows. There is no
contradiction with the expectation, which is carried by the increasingly
rare surviving paths. With W_0=1, q=0.02 and a=1.04, the ensemble
factor per step is 1.0192. This example proves a particular failure of
interchanging a path limit and expectation; it is not a general ergodic theorem.

An absorbing barrier can also make the order of additive payoffs matter.
Starting at 3, the increments (-4,4) lead to permanent ruin at the
first step. Reversing them gives resources (3,7,3) with no ruin.
Both increment sums are zero. The rule here sets resources to zero on
first reaching a nonpositive value and ignores all later increments.

Exact finite-horizon curves. The summable-hazard model retains positive
infinite-horizon survival. The lower panel uses q=0.02, a=1.04;
it compares ensemble expectation with survival, not with simulated paths.

The chapter context is 

Taleb (2025), ch. 3, §3.11, pp. 63–66.
The attached 

precaution paper, v1,
§II.B and §III, pp. 2–3, discusses irreversible failure and repeated risk.
Our proofs supply explicit hazard assumptions and counterexamples to an
unqualified eventual-ruin claim. The paper’s policy and infinite-cost
arguments are not conclusions of these probability calculations.

The Prologue asks what changes in statistical reasoning when extreme outcomes
matter. Its terminology is deliberately broader than a single asymptotic tail
class. We use that question to separate three properties: a large fourth
moment relative to variance, the existence of exponential moments, and the
scaling of a survival function.

The source uses “thick” in a Gaussian-relative, kurtosis-based sense, and
“fat” more broadly than a strict power-law definition (ch. 1, pp. 4–5).
Here we name the mathematical property explicitly. The

asks about the tail of an iid sum. None is defined by the word “fat” alone.

For a variable with finite fourth moment and positive variance, define its
Pearson kurtosis, locally denoted by K, asK=\frac{\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E X)^4]}{\operatorname{Var}(X)^2}.

This is kurtosis, not excess kurtosis K-3. A standard Gaussian has K=3:
integration by parts with \phi'(z)=-z\phi(z) gives
\int z^4\phi(z)\,dz=3\int z^2\phi(z)\,dz=3, where both integrals run
over \mathbb R and \phi is the standard normal density.

We prove that arbitrarily large kurtosis is compatible with bounded support
and finite exponential moments. Fix a local probability 0<\varepsilon\le1
and give X the three-point lawP(X=0)=1-\varepsilon,\qquad
P(X=\varepsilon^{-1/2})=P(X=-\varepsilon^{-1/2})=\frac{\varepsilon}{2}.

Symmetry gives \mathbb E X=0. Summing over the three atoms gives\mathbb E X^2=\varepsilon\varepsilon^{-1}=1,\qquad
\mathbb E X^4=\varepsilon\varepsilon^{-2}=\varepsilon^{-1},\qquad
K=\varepsilon^{-1}.

For every real \theta, the same finite sum gives\mathbb E e^{\theta X}
=1-\varepsilon+\varepsilon\cosh(\theta/\sqrt{\varepsilon})<\infty.

For each fixed \varepsilon the right tail ends at
\varepsilon^{-1/2}. It therefore cannot have a regularly varying tail
with positive exponent, or belong to the unbounded-support subexponential
class used here. Choosing smaller \varepsilon produces a different
bounded law with larger kurtosis. It does not turn any one of these laws
into a power-tailed distribution. For example, \varepsilon=0.01 gives
variance 1, kurtosis 100, and support \{-10,0,10\}.

The catalog supplies a second contrast: a lognormal variable has all positive
power moments finite but has no finite positive exponential moment. It is
subexponential, yet not regularly varying. An exact Pareto variable has a
positive power moment of order q precisely when q<\alpha.
The catalog 

proves the lognormal moment calculations and separates the cited
classifications;
the

Pareto integral proof.

These examples answer different questions. A finite population variance
requires a finite second moment. The kurtosis comparison requires a finite
fourth moment as well. A finite Chernoff bound requires an exponential moment at
the chosen positive parameter. A multiplier-ratio claim requires information
arbitrarily far into the tail. A finite empirical fourth moment alone
establishes none of those population assumptions.

The normalized expression in the first table fails the triangle inequality
when 0<p<1: for (1,0) and (0,1) it gives 1 for their sum but
2^{1-1/p}<1 for the sum of their values. Independence can always be
expressed by P(X\in A,Y\in B)=P(X\in A)P(Y\in B) for measurable sets.
A density ratio can express it only where the denominator is positive and
the densities exist. An elliptical scatter matrix is a model parameter;
identifying it with a covariance additionally requires second moments and
the appropriate scalar normalization.

For random variables Y_n,Y, convergence in probability means
P(|Y_n-Y|>\varepsilon)\to0 for every \varepsilon>0.
Almost-sure convergence means P(\lim_nY_n=Y)=1.
Convergence in distribution means convergence of the CDFs at continuity
points of the limiting CDF. These are the conventions behind the arrows in
§2.1, p. 8.

For iid X_i with \mathbb E|X_1|<\infty, the weak LLN gives
\bar X_n\xrightarrow{P}\mu, where \mu=\mathbb E X_1.
With the stronger assumption 0<\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(X_1)<\infty,
the classical CLT gives\frac{\sqrt n(\bar X_n-\mu)}{\sigma}\xrightarrow{d}N(0,1).

These two general theorems are cited, not proved here (SCoFT v4
§§2.2.2–3, p. 10). Neither statement gives a universal finite-sample error
bound. The

pointwise probability bound for its bounded indicators.

By contrast, the subexponential relation compares P(S_n>x) and P(M_n>x)
as x\to\infty with n fixed. It does not say that M_n/S_n tends to one
as n grows. The

keeps the growing-sample regimes and moment orders separate.

For Pareto (\alpha=3/2,x_m=1), threshold u=4 is the quantile

gives mean excess 8 and tail contribution 3/2.
All four numbers describe the same distribution and threshold.

For an integrable nonnegative loss, define expected shortfall at level
0<q<1 by (1-q)^{-1}\int_q^1Q(v)\,dv.
When there is no atom at the quantile, this agrees with the conditional tail
mean. At an atom, conditioning on X>Q(q) generally selects a different
probability mass. For the empirical law of (1,2,2,4) and q=1/2, the upper
half consists of equal masses at 2 and 4, so the quantile integral gives
3. Strict conditioning on X>2 instead gives 4. This calculation explains
why the probability level, sign convention, and treatment of ties must accompany
the terms VaR and expected shortfall.

Even uniform CDF accuracy does not control a mean without additional tail
conditions. To prove this, let P_j put mass 1-1/j at zero and 1/j at
j^2, for integers j\ge2. Its CDF differs from that of a point mass at
zero by at most 1/j, yet its mean is j. This deterministic sequence of
laws is a counterexample to such an implication; it is not a simulation of
an iid empirical process. It isolates the probability-versus-moment issue
behind §§2.2.27–28, pp. 19–20, without importing a uniform convergence theorem.

The Darwin College lecture connects statistical evidence to the consequences
of acting on it. We study four questions: what a finite sample can exclude,
how a payoff transforms a tail, how repeated exposure reaches an absorbing
barrier, and how splitting exposure changes aggregate damage.

The section locators below refer to that version. Our concept notes develop
models and proofs; the lecture supplies their context. Empirical
and policy assertions in the lecture are outside these calculations.

In the 

contamination example,
a uniform law on [0,1] is mixed with probability \varepsilon of a
Pareto draw starting at b>1. For n iid observations,d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P^{\otimes n},Q^{\otimes n})=1-(1-\varepsilon)^n.

Raising b changes the mean without changing this discrepancy. That is an
explicit limit on inference over the proposed family, not a claim that all

payoff’s expectation rises by s^2, whereas the negative quadratic falls
by s^2. Both follow by finite sums. Curvature compares responses to a
specified spread; downside protection needs a separate payoff bound.

The

q\in(0,1). Its ensemble expectation is\mathbb E W_k=W_0[a(1-q)]^k,

at every shock is divided by m, but a Pareto shock’s transformed tail

convexity in variance holds only above a threshold relative to that variance,
not for every tail event and every mixing interval.

the following local ratios:A_t(u)=\frac{\bar F(tu)}{\bar F(u)},\qquad

For nonnegative variables and positive fixed weights, a union bound and a
one-coordinate lower bound preserve the smallest logarithmic tail
exponent of a finite sum. That statement does not require independence.
Signed variables can cancel: (V,-V) has sum zero even when both marginals
have power tails. The 

sum proof
states exactly what the bounds establish.

Products are more sensitive to dependence. Two independent unit-cutoff
Pareto variables with common exponent \alpha have product survivalP(X_1X_2>z)=z^{-\alpha}(1+\alpha\log z),\qquad z\ge1.

The 

product derivation
also handles unequal exponents. With identical observations X_2=X_1,
the product is a square and its exponent is \alpha/2 instead. Thus the
unqualified product principle in §5.2 cannot be used under arbitrary
dependence.

For a nonnegative variable with regularly varying survival and r>0,
X^r has exponent \alpha/r. Applying this to |T_\nu|, where T_\nu
is a Student variable with degrees of freedom \nu>0, gives exponent
\nu/2 for T_\nu^2. Its mean exists for \nu>2 and its variance for
\nu>4. These moment conditions do not identify a stochastic-volatility
process from a fluctuating sample statistic. Chapter 4 already supplies
the 

estimator-moment distinction.
The special-function expression and mean-deviation table in §5.6 are not
needed for this argument and are not claimed verified here.

not equate finite moments. Our double-Pareto density includes the required

A limit \mathbb E[X\mid X>u]/u=1 does not establish a positive
exponential moment. For survival e^{-\sqrt u}, direct integration gives
\int_u^\infty e^{-\sqrt t}\,dt=2(\sqrt u+1)e^{-\sqrt u}.
Dividing by survival gives e(u)=2\sqrt u+2, so the conditional-mean
ratio tends to one despite subexponentiality.

constraints. The appendix’s escort-mean calculation requires positive
normalization and an admissible entropic index; stationarity alone is not
a proof of a global optimum for a nonlinear constraint.

varying function. We reserve \alpha>0 for a survival exponent, use \nu
for Student degrees of freedom, and use local q for the entropic index.

For a bivariate Student with degrees of freedom \nu>0 and scatter
\Sigma=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&\rho\\\rho&1\end{smallmatrix}\right),
setting \rho=0 means the scatter axes are orthogonal. If \nu>2,
Pearson correlation also equals zero. Independence still fails for every
finite \nu, because the two coordinates share the scale.

At \nu=1 this is the spherical Cauchy. Its Pearson coefficient is
undefined but its mutual information is finite:I(X_1;X_2)=\log(8\pi)-3\approx0.224171\quad(\rho=0).

The 

entropy calculation
proves the value. Independent Cauchy coordinates instead have mutual
information zero and nonelliptical contours. Thus a marginal family and
one matrix parameter do not specify the dependence model.

A Student scatter matrix is \Sigma, while covariance, when finite,
is \nu\Sigma/(\nu-2). The density needs its normalizing constant.
The

keeps both distinctions explicit.

Stable vectors need not be elliptical. The


independent Cauchy counterexample
has stable linear projections and nonelliptical level sets. A singular
law need not have a density, but stability alone does not imply its absence.

A semicircle statement needs a matrix ensemble and scaling. A finite
fourth moment is not necessary for the cited empirical spectral limit;
extreme eigenvalues and sample covariance spectra are separate questions.

The uncentered cosine in §6.6 differs from centered sample Pearson
correlation. Neither finite statistic creates a missing population moment.

For V=b+aX+\varepsilon with independent, centered finite-variance
error and standard normal X, the population target is
a^2/(a^2+\operatorname{Var}\varepsilon). The


proof
gives consistency but no universal upward-bias or O(n^{-2}) rate.
An undefined infinite-variance target must not be assigned zero by a ratio
of infinities. The source’s historical regressions are not reproduced.

An absorbing state is eventually reached in our homogeneous model only
when its conditional failure probability is positive. Irreversibility
without persistent risk is insufficient, as the appendix example shows.

These qualifications bound the teaching claims. They do not assess portfolio
performance, historical data quality, or the source’s broad prescriptions.
Notation follows the 

shared canon:
\alpha denotes a survival exponent, while \nu denotes Student degrees
of freedom (equal to each marginal’s exponent here). Y is mixing variance,
G=1/Y precision, V a regression response, and T a transition matrix.
The appendix’s state probabilities must not be read as point densities.

Let X_1,X_2,\dots be iid nonnegative random variables with distribution F
and unbounded right support, so \bar F(x)=\mathbb P(X>x)>0 for every
finite x. The distribution is
subexponential when, for two independent copies,\begin{gathered}
\frac{\mathbb P(X_1+X_2>x)}{2\mathbb P(X>x)} \to 1,\\
x\to\infty.
\end{gathered}

Equivalently, for every fixed integer n\ge2 (and trivially for n=1), with
S_n=X_1+\cdots+X_n and M_n=\max_{1\le i\le n}X_i,\mathbb P(S_n>x)
\sim
\mathbb P(M_n>x)
\sim n\bar F(x).

For those same fixed integers, equivalently,\mathbb P(S_n>x,\; M_n\le x)=o(\bar F(x)).

This is the one-big-jump principle: for a fixed number of summands, a very
large sum is usually caused by one summand being very large, not by all
summands moving moderately together.

The maximum-tail asymptotic
\mathbb P(M_n>x)\sim n\bar F(x) is not the distinctive part of the theorem:
it follows for every iid distribution with an unbounded right tail and fixed
n.  The subexponential content is that the sum tail has the same first-order
asymptotic as the maximum tail.

Regularly varying survival tails with positive
exponent, \bar F\in RV_{-\alpha} for \alpha>0, are a standard
subexponential class.  We cite that theorem and use the exact


Pareto family as a checkable
example.

Here F is the common CDF, n is fixed while x grows, and
\alpha>0 and x_m>0 are the exponent and cutoff in the Pareto example.
The notation a(x)\sim b(x) means a(x)/b(x)\to1; o(b(x))
denotes a term negligible after division by b(x).

Figure 1:Coordinates are X_1/u and X_2/u, for a fixed positive threshold u.
Green marks \max(X_1,X_2)>u; gold marks
X_1+X_2>u with both summands at most u. Their union is the sum event.
The diagonal itself is excluded by the strict inequality. Colored area
is geometry, not probability: the parent joint law supplies probability mass.
For a subexponential law the gold region has negligible probability relative
to \bar F(u) as u\to\infty, with two summands fixed.

Subexponential does not mean “lighter than exponential,” and it is unrelated
to the concentration-theory phrase “sub-exponential random variable” for a
light-tailed \psi_1 condition.  In this context it means the opposite: the
tail is heavy enough that convolution barely changes the leading-order tail
probability.

For two iid summands, a sufficiently large sum is about twice as likely as
one summand exceeding the same threshold. For n fixed summands, the leading
factor is n.

This is the mathematical version of a recurring Incerto warning.  In thin-tail
settings, a large aggregate deviation is often the result of many small
coordinated deviations.  In subexponential settings, the aggregate tail is
usually dominated by a single large term.  That changes how sums, ruin events,
insurance losses, and sample moments should be read.

The statement collects several equivalent forms and one important sufficient
class.  We prove the elementary maximum-tail asymptotic and an exact Pareto
two-summand check.  The full equivalence theory and the theorem that regularly
varying tails are subexponential are cited, because their proofs need more
convolution-tail machinery than we develop here.

For the general fixed-n extension and its converse, we cite Foss,
Korshunov, and Zachary (2013), §3.3, Corollary 3.20 and Theorem 3.21,
p. 52. Their nonnegative case agrees with the definition here. The
fixed-size Pareto proof for arbitrary n is already on the


Pareto page.

The theorem that regularly varying tails are subexponential goes back to
Chistyakov’s convolution-tail criterion for sums of independent positive random
variables 

Chistyakov (1964).  Standard modern references with proofs are
Embrechts, Klueppelberg, and Mikosch, Appendix A3


Embrechts et al. (1997), and Foss, Korshunov, and
Zachary, second edition, §3.5, Theorem 3.29 and its following paragraph,
p. 57 

Foss et al. (2013) for the
regular-variation implication.
We do not reprove the full theorem, but the exact 

Pareto
case gives the right calibration.

For any distribution with unbounded right tail, \bar F(x)\to0 as
x\to\infty.  For fixed n, iid independence gives\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb P(M_n\le x)\\
&\quad=\mathbb P(X_1\le x,\dots,X_n\le x)\\
&\quad=F(x)^n\\
&\quad=\left(1-\bar F(x)\right)^n.
\end{aligned}

Therefore\mathbb P(M_n>x)
=1-\left(1-\bar F(x)\right)^n

Set u=\bar F(x).  Since u\to0 and n is fixed, the binomial expansion
gives\begin{aligned}
&1-(1-u)^n\\
&\quad=nu-\binom{n}{2}u^2+O(u^3),
\end{aligned}

and therefore\begin{aligned}
&\frac{1-(1-u)^n}{nu}\\
&\quad=1-\frac{n-1}{2}u+O(u^2)\\
&\quad\to1.
\end{aligned}

Substituting back,\mathbb P(M_n>x)
\sim n\bar F(x).

This maximum formula only uses iid independence, fixed n, and
\bar F(x)\to0.  For nonnegative variables, M_n>x implies
S_n=X_1+\cdots+X_n>x, so it is a lower bound for the sum tail.  What is
special about subexponential tails is the matching upper bound:\mathbb P(S_n>x,\;M_n\le x)=o(\bar F(x)).

Those are the configurations where several observations are moderately large
but none exceeds x.  Subexponentiality says this residual event is negligible
at the scale of one tail probability.

For the Pareto tail \bar F(x)=(x_m/x)^\alpha with x\ge x_m, the missing
upper-bound step can be checked directly for n=2.  LetA_x=\{X_1+X_2>x,\;M_2\le x\}.

Choose h=x_m(x/x_m)^\gamma with 1/2<\gamma<1. This keeps the units
consistent and gives h/x\to0 and h\to\infty.

The residual event A_x is the region in [0,x]^2 above X_1+X_2=x.
It is covered by two thin strips and a region where both coordinates exceed
h. The following table replaces the geometric plot.

Cover event

Probability or bound

x-h<X_1\le x

\bar F(x-h)-\bar F(x)

x-h<X_2\le x

\bar F(x-h)-\bar F(x)

X_1>h and X_2>h

\bar F(h)^2 by independence

Outside the cover region, a point has neither coordinate in (x-h,x] and not
both coordinates above h.  Thus at least one coordinate is \le h, and the
other is \le x-h, so X_1+X_2\le x.  Therefore any point in A_x must lie
in the cover: either one summand lies in (x-h,x], or both summands
exceed h.  Hence\begin{aligned}
\mathbb P(A_x)&\le 2\mathbb P(x-h<X\le x)\\
&\quad+\mathbb P(X_1>h,\;X_2>h).
\end{aligned}

For the first term,\begin{aligned}
&\frac{\mathbb P(x-h<X\le x)}{\bar F(x)}\\
&\quad=\frac{\bar F(x-h)-\bar F(x)}{\bar F(x)}\\
&\quad=\left(\frac{x}{x-h}\right)^\alpha-1\\
&\quad\to0,
\end{aligned}

because h/x\to0.  For the second term, independence gives\begin{aligned}
&\frac{\mathbb P(X_1>h,\;X_2>h)}{\bar F(x)}\\
&\quad=\frac{\bar F(h)^2}{\bar F(x)}\\
&\quad=(x/x_m)^{\alpha(1-2\gamma)}\\
&\quad\to0,
\end{aligned}

because \gamma>1/2.  Thus \mathbb P(A_x)=o(\bar F(x)).  Since
\{S_2>x\} is the disjoint union of \{M_2>x\} and A_x,\mathbb P(X_1+X_2>x)\sim 2\bar F(x).

The regularly varying theorem cited above generalizes this Pareto calculation:
the maximum formula is universal, while the negligible residual event is the
heavy-tail property.

The 

Tail Class Catalog gives a broader comparison. The lognormal and stretched
Weibull entries are cited examples, not consequences of the Pareto proof.

The exponential is an exact nonexample.  If
X_i\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda), then the universal maximum formula still
holds:\begin{aligned}
\mathbb P(M_2>x)&=2e^{-\lambda x}-e^{-2\lambda x}\\
&\sim2e^{-\lambda x}.
\end{aligned}

But the sum tail is much larger:\mathbb P(X_1+X_2>x)=e^{-\lambda x}(1+\lambda x),

so\frac{\mathbb P(X_1+X_2>x)}{2\mathbb P(X>x)}
=\frac{1+\lambda x}{2}\to\infty,

not 1.

The fixed-n assumption is load-bearing.  If n grows with x, additional
large-deviation regimes can appear.

For a right-tail survival function \bar F(x)=\mathbb P(X>x), the survival
tail-ratio diagnostic isQ_F(x)=\frac{\bar F(x)^2}{\bar F(2x)},

where \bar F(2x)>0.  With iid copies X_1 and X_2, the numerator is\bar F(x)^2=\mathbb P(X_1>x,\ X_2>x).

Thus Q_F(x) compares a two-coordinate moderate-extreme event with a
one-coordinate double-threshold event.  It is a tail-geometry diagnostic, not
an estimator by itself.

Here x>0 is the comparison threshold, F is the CDF, and
\alpha>0, x_m>0 are the Pareto exponent and lower cutoff.
Q_F is distinct from the regular-variation ratio \bar F(tx)/\bar F(x).

Taleb, 2025, motivates
this event comparison with exponential and sigmoid survivals. We derive
their values here and keep them separate from a convolution-tail criterion.

For centered logistic survival \bar F(x)=1/(1+e^{2kx}), k>0,Q_F(x)=\frac{1+e^{4kx}}{(1+e^{2kx})^2}\longrightarrow1.

This law is light-tailed. Its density is bounded by a constant times
e^{-2k|x|}, so its MGF is finite for |\theta|<2k by comparison
with an exponential integral on each half-line. The density is
\tfrac{k}{2}\operatorname{sech}^2(kx), the 

hypsecant2 helper’s law
with loc=0, scale=1/k.
The name identifies this squared-secant convention, not the ordinary
hyperbolic-secant distribution.

For a centered Laplace law with scale b>0, the right survival is
\tfrac12e^{-x/b} on x\ge0, giving Q_F(x)=1/2.
More generally, \bar F(x)\sim c e^{-\lambda x} implies Q_F(x)\to c.
Translating X by d changes that constant to ce^{\lambda d}.
Thus the value one is not an invariant boundary between light and heavy
tails. It reflects the tail prefactor as well as its decay.

For Weibull survival e^{-x^\beta} on x\ge0,\log Q_F(x)=(2^\beta-2)x^\beta.

It tends to -\infty, zero, or +\infty as \beta<1, \beta=1,
or \beta>1. The

separate subexponential classification for the first range. A vanishing
Q_F is not a proof of the full convolution condition.

SCoFT v4 §§2.2.1 and 2.2.11, pp. 9 and 13, discuss a practical transition
to a nearly constant tail factor 

Taleb, 2025. Such a transition is an
extra modeling assumption. The definition of slow variation does not imply
a finite constant limit, or an exact Pareto tail beyond a finite threshold.

Here is a complete counterexample, in dimensionless units:\bar F(x)=
\begin{cases}
1,&x<1,\\
x^{-2}(1+\log x),&x\ge1.
\end{cases}

We prove that this is a survival function with a regularly varying tail.
It is continuous at 1, tends to zero at infinity, and its derivative on
x>1 is -x^{-3}(1+2\log x)<0. Thus it defines a probability law on
[1,\infty). Its factor L(x)=1+\log x tends to infinity, while for every
fixed t>0 and sufficiently large x,\frac{L(tx)}{L(x)}=1+\frac{\log t}{1+\log x}\longrightarrow1,
\qquad
\frac{\bar F(tx)}{\bar F(x)}\longrightarrow t^{-2}.

The 

chapter 2 worked cases evaluate
this ratio alongside the exact Pareto ratio 1/4 at multiplier 2.
A finite curve cannot establish where a tail approximation becomes adequate;


threshold selection requires its own
diagnostics. The example disproves a constant-limit requirement analytically.

\mathbb E e^{\theta X}<\infty for at least one \theta>0. Ordinary moments

We prove both entries in the lognormal row. Let Z\sim N(0,1) and
X=e^Z. Completing the square gives, for every real q,\mathbb E X^q
=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{qz-z^2/2}\,dz
=e^{q^2/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
  \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-(z-q)^2/2}\,dz
=e^{q^2/2}.

In contrast, for any fixed \theta>0,\mathbb E e^{\theta X}
=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
  \exp(\theta e^z-z^2/2)\,dz=\infty.

Indeed, e^z/z^2\to\infty as z\to\infty, so the integrand is at
least 1 for all sufficiently large z. The integral over that half-line
diverges. This establishes failure of the Cramér condition despite all
positive power moments being finite. Subexponentiality is a separate,
cited result; it does not follow just from this failure.

For a Pareto model with \alpha=5/2 and x_m=1, the mean is 5/3
and the variance is 20/9, but the fourth moment diverges. The formulas
follow from the linked integral: \mathbb E X^2=5 and
5-(5/3)^2=20/9. Pearson kurtosis is therefore not a finite summary for
this model. Having a finite variance does not imply a finite fourth or
positive exponential moment.

Thus the multiplier diagnostic separates power tails from all four other
examples, but cannot distinguish subexponential lognormal and stretched-Weibull

stretched Weibull are cited results; a ratio table is not a proof of their
subexponentiality.

We prove the two negative classifications in the table. Write
\operatorname{Gamma}(k,\lambda) in shape–rate notation, with k,\lambda>0.
At rate one, convolution of the densities with shapes k and \ell>0
gives\frac{e^{-x}}{\Gamma(k)\Gamma(\ell)}
\int_0^x y^{k-1}(x-y)^{\ell-1}\,dy
=\frac{e^{-x}x^{k+\ell-1}}{\Gamma(k+\ell)},\qquad x>0,

using the beta integral (

NIST DLMF, Eq. 5.12.1).
Thus independent shapes add. Scaling by
1/\lambda gives the same rule at a common rate \lambda.
The survival integral, compared with its leading integrand by l’Hôpital’s
rule, gives\bar F(x)\sim\frac{(\lambda x)^{k-1}e^{-\lambda x}}{\Gamma(k)},
\qquad x\to\infty.

For completeness, at rate one the derivatives of
\int_x^\infty y^{k-1}e^{-y}\,dy and x^{k-1}e^{-x} have ratio
[1-(k-1)/x]^{-1}\to1; both functions tend to zero. Consequently,
for fixed t>1,A_t(x)\sim t^{k-1}e^{-\lambda(t-1)x}\to0,\qquad
R(x)\sim\frac{\Gamma(k)}{2\Gamma(2k)}(\lambda x)^k\to\infty.

This proves that every positive-shape gamma law, including the exponential
case k=1, is neither regularly varying with a finite positive exponent
nor subexponential.

The positive-exponent convention in the table does not exhaust regularly
varying functions. To examine the index-zero boundary, let
V be Pareto with minimum v_m>0, exponent a>0, and dimensionless
values, and put X=e^V. Here a,v_m are local parameters; the survival
exponent of X will be zero. This construction is motivated by SCoFT v4
§5.5, pp. 102–103 

Taleb, 2025. Inverting the increasing transform
provesP(X>x)=\left(\frac{v_m}{\log x}\right)^a,\quad x\ge e^{v_m},
\qquad f_X(x)=\frac{a v_m^a}{x(\log x)^{a+1}}.

For every fixed t>0, its survival ratio tends to one because
\log(tx)/\log x\to1. Thus \bar F_X\in RV_0, outside this catalog’s
positive-power rows. Every positive power moment diverges:
\mathbb EX^p=\mathbb E e^{pV}, and the exponential factor eventually
exceeds every polynomial in the Pareto density integral.

We also prove subexponentiality directly for this example. For iid
nonnegative X_1,X_2, with M_2=\max(X_1,X_2),P(M_2>x)\le P(X_1+X_2>x)\le P(M_2>x/2).

Both bounds divided by 2\bar F_X(x) tend to one: the maximum-tail
formula is 2\bar F_X-\bar F_X^2 and
\bar F_X(x/2)/\bar F_X(x)\to1. The squeeze proves the claim.
Thus a regularly varying survival can be subexponential even when its
index is zero. There is no finite positive 1/\alpha
calibration at this index-zero boundary.

The chapter demo evaluates this survival using \log x=2,4,8 with
a=2, v_m=1, obtaining 1/4,1/16,1/64. It keeps the thresholds in
logarithmic coordinates to avoid overflowing e^V. Finite evaluations
do not stand in for the moment-divergence or convolution proofs.

maximum-entropy note gives another
construction of power tails, conditional on specified information constraints.
Neither construction establishes a tail law for observed data.

Appendix A of SCoFT v4, §A.1, pp. 122–124 

Taleb, 2025,
considers distributions with separated regimes. We can check the effect on
kurtosis without assuming a power tail. Let B take -1 and 1 with
equal probabilities, let Z\sim N(0,1) be independent, and set
X=mB+\sigma Z, with m\ge0 and \sigma>0. Symmetry gives mean zero.
Expanding and discarding the odd terms proves\mathbb EX^2=m^2+\sigma^2,\qquad
\mathbb EX^4=m^4+6m^2\sigma^2+3\sigma^4,
\qquad
K=3-\frac{2m^4}{(m^2+\sigma^2)^2}.

Here K is Pearson kurtosis. For m>0 it lies below three and tends
to one as m/\sigma\to\infty. Yet
\mathbb E e^{tX}=\cosh(mt)e^{\sigma^2t^2/2}<\infty for every real
t. This location mixture is light-tailed. Its density has a local
minimum at zero when m>\sigma: differentiating the two normal densities
gives f''(0)=f(0)(m^2-\sigma^2)/\sigma^4>0.
Thus low kurtosis can accompany a valley around the expectation.
It is not evidence of a small probability of a large regime change.

For m=2, \sigma=1, the variance is 5 and K=43/25=1.72.
The 

variance-mixture note holds the location
fixed and mixes variances; these are different experiments. A finite normal
mixture has positive density everywhere, so a valley is not a forbidden
interval and every individual point still has probability zero.

For the §A.2 context, pp. 124–125, take a homogeneous two-state Markov
chain with states intact and failed. The failed state is absorbing and
an intact system fails with probability p\in[0,1] at each step,
conditional on still being intact. Its row-stochastic transition matrix isT=\begin{pmatrix}1-p&p\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
T^n=\begin{pmatrix}(1-p)^n&1-(1-p)^n\\0&1\end{pmatrix}
\quad(n\ge1).

Induction proves the power: multiplying by T multiplies the remaining
intact probability by 1-p. Starting intact, eventual failure has
probability one if p>0 and zero if p=0. Irreversibility alone is not
sufficient; reachability and persistent conditional risk matter. With varying
conditional hazards p_j, intact survival is \prod_{j=1}^n(1-p_j).
For example, p_j=2^{-j-1} has sum 1/2, and
\prod_{j=1}^n(1-p_j)\ge1-\sum_{j=1}^n p_j\ge1/2 by induction.
Every step has positive risk but eventual failure is not certain.
The 

existing survival calculation treats this product;
we do not replace it with an independence assumption on unconditional events.



Exact appendix-A examples. The location mixture uses \sigma=1, with
m=0 and 2 in the density panel. The last panel compares conditional
hazard 0.05 each step with p_j=2^{-j-1}, starting intact. The first
survival tends to zero; the second stays at least 1/2. Neither construction
asserts a power-tail law. Figure regeneration: uv run python demos/incerto/multivariate_tails.py.

Regular variation and subexponentiality concern limits, not the shape of
a fitted curve on a finite range.

Very small survival probabilities can underflow in numerical calculations.
Logarithmic ratios help preserve information; rounded zeros do not establish
exact zero probability.

The subexponential definition used here is the right-tail iid version for
nonnegative summands. Two-sided and dependent settings need additional
assumptions.

The finite exact examples above check formulas, not the accuracy of an
upstream sampler, survival-function implementation, or quadrature routine.

This appendix proves the elementary two-summand convolution decomposition used
by the subexponential diagnostic.  We work with independent continuous
variables, then specialize to an iid lower-bounded distribution.  Discrete,
dependent, and two-sided variants require separate assumptions.

For independent continuous random variables X_1 and X_2 with densities
f_1, f_2 and survival functions \bar F_1, \bar F_2,\mathbb P(X_1+X_2>x)
=
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_1(y)\bar F_2(x-y)\,dy.

To see the iid reduction, take a common density f, survival function
\bar F, and lower support endpoint a, with x>2a.  Split the event
\{X_1+X_2>x\} into three cases, ignoring probability-zero boundary points:
first X_2\le x/2, second X_1\le x/2, and third both variables exceed
x/2.  In the first case, conditioning on X_2=y with a\le y\le x/2
leaves the requirement X_1>x-y, so this part contributes
\int_a^{x/2} f(y)\bar F(x-y)\,dy.  The second case contributes the same
quantity by iid symmetry.  The remaining upper-right square has probability
\bar F(x/2)^2 by independence.

For a=0, the partition can be recorded as disjoint regions rather than a
contour plot. Boundaries have zero probability under the continuous-law
assumption.

For iid variables with lower support endpoint a, symmetry gives the more
useful half-line formula\mathbb P(X_1+X_2>x)
=
2\int_a^{x/2} f(y)\bar F(x-y)\,dy+\bar F(x/2)^2.

Dividing by 2\bar F(x) yields a normalized integral:\begin{aligned}
R(x)
&=\int_a^{x/2}\frac{f(y)\bar F(x-y)}{\bar F(x)}\,dy
  +\frac{\bar F(x/2)^2}{2\bar F(x)}\\
&=\int_a^{x/2}
\exp\{\log f(y)+\log\bar F(x-y)-\log\bar F(x)\}\,dy\\
&\quad+\frac12\exp\{2\log\bar F(x/2)-\log\bar F(x)\}.
\end{aligned}

The logarithmic form applies where the factors are positive, with zero terms
understood by limits. It avoids forming tiny unnormalized probabilities before
taking their ratio. The decomposition is an ordinary conditioning argument;
no numerical integration or executable package helper is needed for it.

Tail threshold selection is the modeling step that chooses where the body of a
sample ends and where a tail estimator or peaks-over-threshold model begins.
For a threshold u, the exceedance sample is\{x_i-u:x_i>u\}.

For a 

Hill estimator, the equivalent tuning parameter is
the number k of upper order statistics, with empirical threshold
x_{n-k:n}.  Hill is designed for positive, regularly varying right tails
with extreme-value index \xi>0; for a Pareto-type tail,
\alpha=1/\xi.  A threshold selection report should include at least:

the candidate thresholds or k values;

the number of exceedances retained;

Hill or EVI stability over the candidate range;

mean-excess or GPD-shape stability where relevant;

the reason the selected range was kept or rejected.

The goal is not to find a universally correct threshold.  It is to make the
bias-variance tradeoff visible.

Here x_{1:n}\le\cdots\le x_{n:n} are the sorted observations,
k counts the upper values used by Hill, and \xi is the
extreme-value index. Ties at the threshold can make the strict exceedance
count differ from k and should be reported explicitly.

Every tail model asks the same awkward question: how far out is “tail”?  Set
the threshold too low and the estimator is biased by body observations.  Set
it too high and the estimator is dominated by too few extremes.  A good
threshold analysis therefore looks for a region where several diagnostics stop
moving violently while enough exceedances remain to estimate anything at all.

This page is distinct from the


body-shoulder-tail diagnostic.  Body/shoulder geometry
describes how a distribution’s density responds to variance mixing.  Threshold
selection is an empirical modeling decision for tail estimation.

For a one-sided positive sample:

Choose a grid of candidate thresholds, often empirical quantiles.

Record exceedance counts at each threshold.

Plot Hill estimates over k or threshold values.

Plot the 

mean-excess function for the
same threshold range.

If using a GPD model, fit shape and scale over multiple thresholds.

Prefer a range where estimates are reasonably stable and exceedance counts
are not too small.

The accepted range should be reported, not hidden.  Downstream quantities such
as 

moment existence, return levels, or
expected shortfall can be highly sensitive to \xi. Under an exact GPD model,
finite variance requires \xi<1/2, while finite mean and expected shortfall
require \xi<1. For a general regularly varying tail, moments at the boundary
also depend on the slowly varying factor. High return-level estimates are
sensitive to \xi but do not have mathematical singularities specifically
at those two values.

Consider the population model from the source example: with probability
0.82, X is uniform on [1,3]; with probability 0.18, it is Pareto
with cutoff 3 and exponent \alpha=1.7=17/10. Thus\begin{gathered}
\bar F(u)=\\
\begin{cases}
1, & u<1,\\
\dfrac{0.82(3-u)}2+0.18, & 1\le u<3,\\
0.18(3/u)^{1.7}, & u\ge3.
\end{cases}
\end{gathered}

Above 3, the conditional tail is exactly Pareto. Its shape is \xi=10/17,
its excess scale is \beta(u)=10u/17, and its mean excess is
e(u)=u/(\alpha-1)=10u/7. For an iid sample of size n=30{,}000,
the expected number of exceedances is n\bar F(u).

At thresholds at least 3, raising u introduces no tail-model bias in this
exact construction but still loses observations. In empirical data, the cutoff
is unknown and there may be no exact Pareto region at any finite threshold.
The table therefore does not select an empirical threshold or report an
uncertainty interval.

For a general GPD tail, threshold stability is
\beta(u')=\beta(u)+\xi(u'-u). Hence shape and modified scale
\beta(u)-\xi u should be inspected together. The simpler relation
\beta(u)/u=\xi is specific to the exact Pareto tail. Selected-threshold
uncertainty, dependence, and tail approximation error are additional to the
sampling uncertainty of a fit at a fixed threshold.

One iid sample of 30{,}000 from the model above, PCG64 seed 20261021.
Every panel uses the same threshold axis; dotted lines mark the known
population join u=3. Thresholds are observed order statistics near a
fixed grid, so Hill uses the same baseline as the strict exceedance count.
Dashed references are population quantities; the exact Pareto references
start at 3. The mean-excess and fitted-parameter curves are masked below
50 exceedances, with the excluded threshold region shaded. Counts remain
visible in the companion GPD figure below; numerical fit failures would
appear there as crosses.
The survival panel uses strict empirical survival and omits its zero endpoint
on log axes. No threshold is selected by the plot.



The same sample, thresholds and dotted join at u=3. Shape and modified
scale have population references only above the join. Counts below 50 remain
visible even when fits are masked. The count-panel title reports actual
eligible-fit status: all eligible fits succeeded for this seed; four other
thresholds have too few exceedances to fit. Numerical success is not
validation of the parent model.

The GPD fits hold excess location at zero and check numerical convergence,
positive scale and support for every excess. We plot both fitted shape
and modified scale \widehat\beta(u)-\widehat\xi(u)u. Success of these
checks means the numerical fit is usable for the display; it does not
establish a global likelihood optimum or validate the model.



The same sample at three fixed thresholds. Each panel places fitted GPD
CDF values at the ordered excesses on the horizontal axis and i/(m+1)
on the vertical axis, where m is that panel’s exceedance count and
i=1,\ldots,m. These are plotting positions,
not strict survival probabilities. Parameters are fitted on the displayed
data, so proximity to the diagonal is an in-sample diagnostic with no
confidence-band interpretation. The body affects the fit at u=2;
raising the threshold loses observations. Agreement or a plateau across
these checks does not single out a unique threshold.

Use 

pareto_type1 and


gpd_threshold_fit.
This reproduces the three fixed-threshold fits without writing figures:

Codeimport numpy as np
from xmath.incerto.distributions import pareto_type1
from xmath.incerto.estimators import gpd_threshold_fit

rng = np.random.default_rng(20261021)
tail = rng.random(30000) < 0.18
x = rng.uniform(1, 3, 30000)
x[tail] = pareto_type1.rvs(1.7, scale=3, size=tail.sum(), random_state=rng)
for u in (2, 3, 12):
    fit = gpd_threshold_fit(x, u, min_exceedances=50)
    print(f"u={u:d}: count={fit['count']:d}, status={fit['status']}")
    print(f"  xi={fit['xi']:.4g}, beta={fit['beta']:.4g}, modified_scale={fit['modified_scale']:.4g}")

Threshold selection is a modeling judgment, not a theorem.  Different
diagnostics can disagree.

The Hill estimator is a right-tail regular-variation tool for \xi>0, not a
general estimator for Gumbel-type or bounded-tail domains.

The ratio \hat\beta(u)/u is an exact-Pareto diagnostic.  For a general GPD
threshold model, threshold stability is
\beta(u')=\beta(u)+\xi(u'-u), so \beta(u)-\xi u is the stable quantity.

Very high thresholds may reduce approximation bias but can leave too few
exceedances for stable estimation.

Dependence, volatility clustering, rounding, reporting limits, and
truncation can all make threshold diagnostics misleading.

A selected threshold for one sample window or horizon should not be reused
mechanically for a different dataset.

Thresholds for right-tail positive data do not automatically apply to
two-sided returns or losses without an explicit transformation.

Tail questions begin by specifying an event and the evidence available for it.
A fraction counted in a finite sample and a probability under a proposed model
are different quantities. Keeping both visible makes later estimation arguments
easier to assess.

Start with 

counting exceedances, a
worked example with a short Python demo. It uses only a finite list and strict
inequalities; no moment or distributional assumption is needed for the count.

The following reading path moves from a distributional model
to estimates of tail quantities:

Pareto distribution specifies an exact power tail;


regular variation allows slowly varying
corrections at high thresholds.

Karamata’s theorem connects tail shape to integrals.


Pareto moment existence proves the
exact moment boundaries, and the


mean excess function describes
overshoots beyond a threshold.

The 

Hill estimator estimates a positive tail
index from log-excesses. The


extreme-value index places that estimate
within the wider classification of extreme-value limits.

The 

generalized Pareto distribution
models threshold excesses, and


plug-in tail estimation explains how
a fitted tail model enters a mean estimate, including its moment-boundary
singularity and the contribution of the distribution body.

Power-law fitting develops the continuous
and discrete likelihoods and a KS threshold search. Continue with


goodness of fit and alternatives
for bootstrap calibration and comparisons on a common tail.

The second reading path connects extreme-value limits to diagnostics.

The 

Pickands–Balkema–de Haan theorem
justifies the GPD excess model under a maximum-domain-of-attraction assumption.

The 

generalized extreme-value distribution
describes normalized block-maxima limits; the


Frechet law is its positive-shape member and connects
those limits to regularly varying tails.

Tail threshold selection makes the
finite-sample tuning decision explicit through exceedance counts, shape,
mean excess, and modified-scale stability.

Subexponentiality explains why a large sum
of a fixed number of nonnegative iid terms has the same leading tail as
its maximum.

The 

survival tail ratio compares two
moderate extremes with one doubled extreme. The


max-to-sum ratio measures the largest
observation’s share of a realized total. Their limits answer different
questions and neither diagnostic alone proves an empirical tail class.

Symmetric shifted double Pareto provides a
two-sided power-tail model, with a clear distinction between symmetry and
existence of the mean.

Body, shoulders, and tails derives local
density changes under variance mixing. Its curvature boundaries describe
mixture geometry; choosing a Pareto threshold remains a separate task.

Iso-density tail geometry compares
equal and axial splits of a large sum under normal and Cauchy densities.
Density at a point and integrated tail probability remain distinct.

The third reading path contrasts light-tailed concentration with stable sums
and infinite-mean averages.

LLN failure under infinite mean proves that
averages of nonnegative iid variables with infinite mean diverge almost
surely. Capped Pareto means make the truncation argument explicit.
